title: Julia Roberts' parents couldn't afford bill for her birth. Martin Luther King Jr. and his wife covered it
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: In 1967, Julia Roberts' parents couldn’t afford the hospital bill for her birth, so Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King covered it. Rating: True About this rating A popular internet story claims that Oscar-winning actor Julia Roberts' family had an unusual relationship with Martin Luther King Jr. Snopes readers asked us to verify the story that the Kings paid the hospital bill for Roberts' birth as a gift to her parents. According to one Facebook post from September 2026: Martin Luther King Jr. footed the hospital bill for Julia Roberts's birth in 1967 when her family was facing very tough financial times. Her parents were struggling to make ends meet and could not afford the medical costs, so the King family stepped in out of deep gratitude for Julia's parents, who ran a small theater school in Atlanta and welcomed the King children when few other places would. It is an incredible piece of history that shows how simple acts of kindness can bind people together across generations. This story was confirmed by both Roberts and Bernice King, a daughter of the couple. In a September 2022 interview at an event hosted by A+E Networks and History Channel in Washington, D.C., Roberts recounted the connection to journalist Gayle King (no relation to MLK's family): KING: Let's start with the day you were born. Who paid for your hospital bill? ROBERTS: Okay, her research is very good. […] The King family paid for my hospital bills. KING: Not my family! ROBERTS: Not your family, but … KING: Martin Luther King Jr. … ROBERTS: … and Coretta. KING: And how did that come about? […] Why did they do that? … ROBERTS: Obviously, because my parents couldn't pay for the hospital bill. My parents had a theater school in Atlanta called the Actors and Writers Workshop. One day, Coretta Scott King called my mother and asked if her kids could be part of the school because they were having a hard time finding a place that would accept her kids. My mom was like, "Sure, come on over," and so they just all became friends and they helped us out of a jam. KING: In the '60s, you didn't have little Black children interacting with little white kids in acting school. And your parents were like, "Come on in," and I think that's extraordinary, and it lays the groundwork for who you are. A clip of the interview was shared on Twitter: Bernice King later shared the clip and corroborated Roberts' account, writing , "I know the story well, but it is moving for me to be reminded of my parents' generosity and influence." Roberts' parents, Walter and Betty Roberts, indeed ran a theater company, and the Kings' other daughter, Yolanda King, who died in 2007, spoke publicly about attending classes there. Per a transcript of a 2001 CNN segment that profiled Roberts and included an interview with Yolanda King: DARYN KAGAN: Today's queen of Hollywood began life in modest surroundings, nearly a continent away, in Atlanta, Georgia. Julia Fiona Roberts debuted at Crawford Long Hospital on October 28, 1967. Julia went home to a two-story house in Midtown, one of Atlanta's middle class neighborhood. Her parents, Walter and Betty Roberts, ran a writing and actor's workshop. The children of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., were enrolled there. It was the only integrated children's theater group in Atlanta. Dexter King is now a writer. Yolanda King, an actress and producer. KING: Mr. Roberts was so imposing. I loved him, but I was also a little intimidated by him too. And — but he was — I mean, he taught me so much, and he and Mrs. Roberts, about the work, and just about living and being really open, grabbing life and making the best of it. Yolanda King also described the school in a 1994 interview with the Los Angeles Times: For example, since age 8 she'd been enrolled in what was then the only integrated drama school in Atlanta, run by Walt Roberts, father of actress Julia Roberts. But when she played in a teen-age production of "The Owl and the Pussycat" in 1972, she said, her hometown erupted. "I was 15, my co-star was white, and the white community criticized it because they didn't think (mixing the races) was right. "The black community asked: 'How could you disgrace your dead father's image by playing the role of a prostitute?'" The furor was so great that King said she was forced to stand up at church one Sunday and explain her actions to the whole congregation. Author Phillip DePoy, another former student of the school, described in a 2013 essay how a member of the Ku Klux Klan once attempted to "make trouble" for the aspiring actors: I kissed a girl, and 10 yards away a Buick exploded. I was on the back of a flatbed truck that had been converted into a swamp. I was a fox. The girl was a terrapin. We were in Atlanta, it was a very nice summer day in 1965, and I was 15 years old. The girl was Yolanda King, daughter of Coretta and Martin Luther King Jr. I was primarily Caucasian and Yolanda wasn't. That's what the trouble was about. I don't know who owned the Buick, but I know who blew it up. A man, a tangential member of the Ku Klux Klan, had seen me kiss Yolanda the day before in the same parking lot. She and I were members of a theatrical group called the Actors and Writers Workshop. It was run by Walter and Betty Roberts, the parents of Eric and Julia Roberts. Rob, as Walter was sometimes called, had written his theatrical version of a Joel Chandler Harris story, thanks in part to a Guggenheim grant for children's theater. That's why Yolanda and I were standing in a makeshift swamp on the back of a flatbed truck, dressed as a fox and a terrapin. The Klansman had come around the day before the explosion in order to make trouble. The workshop was offering a free show in the Carver Homes housing project, an exclusively African-American wonderland filled with hammered lives and children with nothing to do. The guy only heckled us the first day, said words that everyone had heard a million times before, finished his case of PBR, and was about to leave when I kissed Yolanda. The school eventually shuttered due to financial reasons. Walter and Betty Roberts divorced before his death in 1977, according to NPR . Given that this story has been told over the years by Roberts and King's children, one of whom recounted her experiences at the school, we rate this claim as true. For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous rumors about Marting Luther King Jr.

title: Is image of Pope Leo XIV wearing Nike sneakers real?
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: An image authentically shows Pope Leo XIV wearing Nike sneakers with his vestments. Rating: True About this rating Context The picture predates the papacy of Leo, whose real name is Robert Prevost. In 2026, people shared an image allegedly showing Pope Leo XIV wearing Nike sneakers with his vestments. For example, on May 9, an Instagram user shared ( archived ) the image with the caption, "Pope Leo XIV wearing Nikes with his vestments from 'Leone a Roma' Trailer by Vatican News (2026)." (@durangoism via Instagram) Other users shared the image on various social media platforms . In today's age of evolving artificial intelligence, some people might question the authenticity of such an image showing the man now serving as pope, whose real name is Robert Prevost, donning such casual footwear. In short, the image is real and predates his time in the papacy. As some users' posts said, the photo originated in "Leone a Roma," a documentary released in 2026 that attempts to "retrace the years Robert Francis Prevost spent in the Eternal City" — a reference to Rome. Vogue identified the shoes as a pair of Nike Franchise Low Plus sneakers. Snopes emailed the Holy See press office to ask for further information, including to confirm exactly when the photo was taken. The picture appears at the 0:51 mark in the film's trailer : The same photo also makes an appearance during a montage in the full documentary (28:28). That montage begins with the brief onscreen title "World Youth Day 2008," as well as pictures of people wearing clothing referencing that day, indicating someone possibly took the photo either at that specific gathering or another past youth event. Leo also appeared on Vanity Fair's 2026 "best dressed list," with the publication referencing the photo with his "most memorable look," reading, "Even prior to the papacy, Leo, FKA Father Bob, took his modest cream cassock to heavenly heights by pairing them with Nikes." For his "fashion claim to fame," the outlet wrote, "Leo has kept his sense of wry casualness, sometimes sporting baseball caps." For further reading, we previously investigated the claim that Leo said no one can use God to justify war , as well as the claim he used AI to write his first encyclical .

title: Story about 'K9 Valor' surviving suicide bomber, saving 47 soldiers isn't what it seems
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: A U.S. military dog named Valor was honored at the Pentagon for surviving a suicide bombing and saving 47 soldiers in 2023. Rating: False About this rating In 2026, people online repeatedly shared a tale framed as a true story about a heroic dog receiving an award for its military service at the Pentagon. For example, one Facebook post ( archived ) included an image depicting a dog with the right side of its face scarred — apparently K9 Valor — receiving the Congressional Medal of Honor. The text of the post read: This is K9 Valor. He saved 47 soldiers. He survived a suicide bomber, then went on to stop three more, fighting tooth against knife. In the end, he placed himself between an explosion and his handler. The blast shattered half his face. He lost his left eye and ear. He was flown to Germany, where surgeons worked to rebuild his jaw. At the Pentagon, he was honored with a standing ovation that lasted over eight minutes. A true American hero This story ( archived ) appeared numerous times ( archived ) on Instagram ( archived ), X ( archived ) and Reddit ( archived ). The same account that shared the above Facebook post in June reposted the story ( archived ) nearly a month later and again the following month ( archived ). Snopes readers sent us emails asking whether it was true. A version of the story shared on LinkedIn ( archived ) went into more detail than the others. That post described the dog, K9 Valor, being wounded by a suicide bomber at Kabul International Airport on Aug. 26, 2021. Even after being injured, Valor supposedly warned soldiers of a second bomb just in time for them to avoid the blast, and then charged and kill three insurgents trying to shoot wounded survivors. According to the post, Valor became the first dog to receive the Congressional Medal of Honor in May 2023. This story, however, was fabricated out of whole cloth. There is no evidence of a K9 Valor present at the Kabul Airport suicide bombing or of a dog being awarded the Congressional Medal of Honor. Therefore, we've rated this claim as false. Since even the less detailed versions of the claim shared an image of a dog receiving the Congressional Medal of Honor, Snopes first searched if a "Valor" or any other dog has received the medal. The Congressional Medal of Honor can be identified by its light blue ribbon with 13 stars and the unique design of the medal itself. A recipient search for "valor" on the Medal of Honor Museum website returned no results. A dog doesn't appear among the Congressional Medal of Honor Society's list of recipients who received the award for serving in Afghanistan . A list of "firsts" among Medal of Honor recipients did not identify a first dog to have received an award. A blog post from the Congressional Medal of Honor Society said it welcomed just two new members to its ranks in 2023. Neither received the award in May and both were humans. The organization Animals in War and Peace awards service animals medals for their duty, often in war. While many of its recipients are Belgian Malinois dogs like Valor apparently is, none of the organization's award recipients have stories about suffering wounds from one bombing and immediately saving soldiers from a second. Its award ceremonies typically occur in March , not May, and at the U.S. Capitol , not the Pentagon. Immediately after the suicide bombing at Kabul International Airport, U.S. officials reportedly believed a second bombing occurred nearby. The U.S. Department of Defense clarified the following day that it no longer believed there was a second explosion , and instead the attack was carried out by a single suicide bomber. That would mean the events as described in the LinkedIn post couldn't have happened, since there was no second bomb from which to save 47 soldiers. Snopes has sent U.S. Central Command an email asking whether any dog with a similar story to the one here was present at the 2021 Kabul bombing. We will update this story if and when we receive a reply. Images show signs of AI generation The images shared with the posts showed signs of being generated or edited using artificial intelligence tools. Some readers may have already noticed one piece of evidence: Even though the posts say Valor lost his left eye, the dog in the image used in the Facebook post above appears to be missing its right eye. In another version of that same image, an insignia that doesn't match any used in the U.S. military is visible on the arm of the service member's jacket. His insignia shows four evenly spaced chevrons pointing up, but across the U.S. military the fourth line in insignias are separated from the others by a space and curve downward. A Google SynthID check , a tool that checks for hidden watermarks Google AI adds to images and video, found that all or part of that image was edited or generated by Google AI. Additionally, various posts used AI-generated images of different dogs that are supposedly K9 Valor. For example, the more detailed story from the LinkedIn post included an image of a different dog with both ears still present, despite Valor allegedly having lost his left ear. Again, a Google SynthID check found that the image was edited or generated by Google AI. Snopes previously reported on this claim in June and July 2026 . We're reporting on it again due to continued interest in the claim.

title: Oklahoma inmates made $2 an hour working for political call centers, documents show
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: The Oklahoma Department of Corrections contracted inmates to work for a call center company that handled making calls for a conservative super PAC. Rating: True About this rating A rumor circulated in early September 2026 that incarcerated people in the state of Oklahoma were contracted to work for a call center company that handled telemarketing for a conservative super PAC. Users on social media shared the rumor, with some claiming the Oklahoma Department of Corrections earned $10 per hour from the vendor but that prison laborers were getting paid only $2 per hour. The rumors circulated as the United States approached the Labor Day holiday, which has celebrated the labor movement since the late 1800s. The claim was true, according to a service contract between the state prison department and telemarketing company HBW Leads , embedded below. The document originated in reporting by Oklahoma Watch , a nonprofit investigative journalism outlet, which published the article on Aug. 24, 2026. One current inmate, Steve Wilbanks, was named as a source. Snopes confirmed Wilbanks was a prisoner at the James Crabtree Correctional Center in Helena and has been in state custody since 2015. Oklahoma Watch cited three other inmates used as sources anonymously. According to the report, inmates earned $2 per hour at call centers located at four state prisons : James Crabtree , Mabel Bassett in McLoud and Lexington Correctional and Joseph Harp , both in Lexington. According to the service contract, tasks inmates could perform were: 1. outbound calls related to marketing lead generation; and 2. conducting or assisting with political opinion polling, subject to applicable laws and regulations. The contract further says Oklahoma Correctional Industries , a division of the Oklahoma Department of Corrections whose website says it "employs offenders who lack marketable job skills," would earn $10 per hour of work per inmate. However, the contract states the corrections department can "withhold up to but not to exceed 80 percent of the wage rate per inmate hour worked," which matches the rates reported. The Oklahoma Watch piece stated: BW Leads agreed to pay the Department of Corrections $10 per inmate hour worked. Prisoners employed at the call centers earn $2 per hour, plus possible bonuses for generating leads or completing surveys. The remaining $8 per hour is allocated as overhead for Oklahoma Correctional Industries, a self-supporting sub-entity of the Department of Corrections that provides work programs and job training to inmates. We reached out to the Oklahoma Department of Corrections for further comment on the report. We also asked for the specific reasoning behind inmate pay structure and why telemarketing doesn't appear on the list of services provided by Oklahoma Correctional Industries. We'll update this article if we hear back. HBW Leads' website identified the Oregon-based company as generating "insurance leads" gained through telemarketing on behalf of the clients who hire them. The website said, "Our lead specialists spend, on average, 4-7 minutes with each potential prospect asking them a series of qualifying questions on your behalf." HBW Leads made no mention of political calling on its website, but a subsidiary company operating out of Toledo, Ohio, Visible Trends , specializes in "polling, fundraising, legislative outreach, or GOTV," referring to get-out-the-vote efforts. A business search on the Ohio Secretary of State's website confirmed Visible Trends to be registered by HBW Leads in January 2025. (Ohio Secretary of State) One of Oklahoma Watch's sources said some of the statements they read during their telemarketing jobs specified that the calls were paid for by conservative super PAC Make Liberty Win , whose website described them as specializing "in mobilizing voters to engage in primary and general elections through direct voter contact." An FEC filing ( archived ) showed at least 38 payments totaling more than $400,000 from Make Liberty Win to Visible Trends between from March 2026 and June 2026, the same term length shown in the service contract between HBW Leads and the corrections department. Though it was clear the Oklahoma Department of Corrections and HBW Leads had established a contract to use inmates as telemarketers, Snopes couldn't independently verify whether the inmates made political calls on behalf of Make Liberty Win specifically. Oklahoma Watch's reported one of its sources said they made political calls that resembled push-polling, in which the caller purports to be asking survey questions but actually aims to influence voters, a practice generally frowned upon in campaigning. We reached out to Make Liberty Win to ask whether it was aware of Visible Trends using prison laborers and will update this article if we hear back. Oklahoma Watch reported that the super PAC's executive director, Barrett Young, told the outlet that the group was unaware of the use of prison labor and has since canceled the contract for performance reasons.

title: Why federal judge ruled First Amendment protects certain AI-generated child sex abuse material
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: A federal judge rule certain AI-generated child sex abuse material is protected by First Amendment. Rating: True About this rating Context In his decision, Judge John Z. Lee of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit, referred to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions from 1969 and 2002. The first says people have the right to keep obscenity in the privacy of their homes and the second says child sex abuse material that does not depict real children is not child pornography and is protected by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. The judge also said that while he is bound by precedent, he is concerned by "the lines these cases draw." A rumor spread in late summer 2026 that a federal judge ruled the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which establishes the right to free speech, protects certain artificial intelligence-generated child sex abuse material. A number of Snopes readers emailed to share an image that relayed the story. "A federal judge has ruled that the First Amendment protects an individual's right to privately possess child sexual abuse content created using Al if it does not depict a real person and remains in the home," the image read. Meanwhile, one X post shared a screenshot of a post by The Washington Post making the claim, saying the judge's decision "normali ses child sexual abuse" and "feeds the depravity" ( archived ): In sum, the claim was true, but it lacked crucial context. In his Aug. 25, 2026, decision , Judge John Z. Lee of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit, said precedent forced him to make this ruling, pointing to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions. He added that the current state of technological advance meant the court had "concerns" about the "lines" set by these two Supreme Court decisions. The U.S. Department of Justice declined to comment on whether the agency intends to take the case to the Supreme Court. Law hasn't caught up with AI, judge suggested In 2024, a man named Steven Anderegg was arrested on charges of fabricating, possessing and distributing AI-generated child sex abuse material, as well as sending some of this material to a minor. Anderegg asked for the charges of production and possession to be dismissed, which a federal district court in Wisconsin granted on grounds that these counts ran against decided caselaw. The prosecutors then appealed this decision, but Lee agreed with the lower court, citing two decisions the Supreme Court rendered in 1969 and 2002. The first decision , Stanley v. Georgia, said the First Amendment protects people who privately keep obscene material. "The First Amendment does not allow a state to criminalize the private possession of obscene matter," read the summary of the case on the Justia website, a free online collection of all U.S. Supreme Court decisions. The second decision — Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition — came six years after the Child Pornography Prevention Act of 1996 . It ruled that child sex abuse material that does not depict real children is not child pornography, and that it is protected by the First Amendment. This decision explicitly covered digital images. "T he statute sought to outlaw all speech that was related to the possibility of child pornography, including images of adults who look like children and computer-generated images," the case's Justia page reads. While Lee said he was compelled by judicial precedent to make this ruling, he also expressed "concerns about the lines these cases draw," given how quickly AI technology is evolving. The judge also said that fabricated child sex abuse material that does not depict real persons was becoming more and more difficult to distinguish from such material that showed real children, making law enforcement more difficult. "Recent data suggests that the influx of AI-generated images reported to the NCMEC [National Center for Missing and Exploited Children] CyberTipline imposes increasing burdens on law enforcement," the judge wrote in his decision. A paragraph in Lee's decision summarized his rationale (Page 3 of this document ): We now live in an age where GenAI [generative AI] models can render images depicting the abuse of virtual children that are virtually indistinguishable from those depicting the abuse of actual children. This case illuminates how this evolving technology complicates the lines drawn by the Supreme Court in Stanley , Osborne , and Free Speech Coalition . Indeed, in Free Speech Coalition , the Supreme Court addressed the scope of First Amendment protections for virtual CSAM, but that was nearly twenty-five years ago, and the image-generation technology available today was likely unimaginable back then. Given the relentless advancement in artificial intelligence models, we have some concerns about the lines these cases draw, but we are not free to redraw them ourselves. In other words, Lee said he could not on his own change a precedent set by the Supreme Court. It would therefore fall upon the Supreme Court to change the interpretation of the law to account for current technology and its consequences. For further reading, Snopes examined the claim that 17 Republican Colorado lawmakers voted against banning AI-generated child sex abuse material .

title: Some Target baskets can track you in-store. Here's what to know
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: Target uses a Bluetooth device on its baskets that tracks shoppers in store. Rating: True About this rating Context Some Target baskets carry a Bluetooth Low Energy Beacon that transmits its location to "smart" lights in the store. The lights can interact with the beacons and Target's app to find a shopper's location, help them navigate around a store or send location-specific offers. Because the basket-mounted beacons transmit only locations and do not collect information about the shopper, it is technically Target's app that tracks shoppers, not the beacons. In August and September 2026, a claim ( archived ) circulated online that the retailer Target used a Bluetooth device on its baskets that tracked shoppers in store. The claim came from an Aug. 29 TikTok video in which a person who appeared to be a Target employee claimed the retailer fitted its baskets with trackers that followed shoppers throughout the store. The alleged employee said: Hello, I just want to make a PSA: You are now being tracked at Target. These baskets, this thing, that's a tracker, so they're now tracking shoppers at Target, at your local Target, for, supposedly, "consumer habits." Other users shared similar claims about Target's alleged tracking on Facebook ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ), Threads ( archived ), X ( archived ) and Reddit ( archived ). Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim. In short, Target does track shopper locations using the basket-mounted Bluetooth beacon that the TikTok user showed in their video. The beacon transmits its location to Target's "smart" overhead LED lights , which in turn can communicate location information to its app. Acuity Brands, which Target said supplied its LED lights, explained in a news release in 2017 that by using its lights and beacons attached to items such as shopping carts it could deliver " highly accurate, real-time positioning services for customers" through a retailer's app. Acuity Brands said Target renewed a multiyear deal for products including its indoor location services in 2020. According to its privacy policy, Target still used LED light and Bluetooth technology to track shoppers in-store in August 2026. The policy advised that customers who did not want to share their store location data could disable location sharing on their device or in the Target app. We contacted Target to confirm how it collected and used data about customers in store using Bluetooth beacons, as well as how customers could opt out of tracking. We await a reply to our query. What we know about Target tracking The TikTok user who shared the video about Target's basket-mounted beacons on Aug. 29 shared another video ( archived ) the day after, identifying the exact product Target used to track shoppers as a Bluetooth beacon from Acuity Brands. A Reddit user who posted ( archived ) about the device six months earlier showed a device with the same FCC ID as the one the TikTok user identified. The Federal Communications Commission grants FCC IDs to products that meet the necessary regulatory standards for wireless communication. The product's user manual said it is a Bluetooth Low Energy Beacon that "communicates its position to Atrius Assets," the software that Target has used since at least 2020 for indoor location services. Bluetooth Low Energy Beacons are small devices that send out radio signals that can be picked up by nearby devices. Beacons can only transmit — not receive — data, so they generally rely on apps to interpret and use the data they are sending. In terms of tracking, if many beacons are sending their location, a device can interpret those signals and triangulate the location of an individual beacon, or individual shopper holding a basket fitted with a beacon. Target wrote in its news release in 2019 that its lights interacted with its app to find customer locations, suggesting that the basket-mounted beacons sent their signals to the lights. It was unclear from the available information whether Target used the data it gathered about individual shoppers' routes through their stores beyond providing location-based offers through the app or guiding customers to specific products. Target used Bluetooth beacons since at least 2015 The technology publication TechCrunch reported that Target and other retailers have used beacon technology to track shoppers in store and send them location-based offers since at least 2015 and that the retailer added Bluetooth beacon-driven indoor mapping to its app in 2017. Target appeared to still use this technology in 2026. Its privacy policy in August 2026 said Target might use location information shared by customers' phones to " help you find nearby Target stores; or, in-store location through the use of your phone's blue tooth signal, LED light chip technologies or other technologies will permit Target to find nearby products for you, get you real-time deals, auto-sort your shopping list and more." Target said in its privacy policy that shoppers who wished to opt out of sharing their in-store location could prevent their devices from sharing their location with Target "by adjusting the permissions on your mobile device or within the relevant app." It did not appear from the beacon's manual that shoppers could turn the device off themselves, meaning Target would still collect information about where the basket traveled if a shopper used it, but could not connect that data to a specific phone or customer if the device's owner turned off location sharing or did not use the Target app. For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated a number of rumors about Target .

title: Did Trump sign executive order changing name of New Mexico to 'New America'? Here's the truth
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: In early September 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change the name of New Mexico to "New America." Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating Context Trump did float the idea of changing New Mexico's name to New America on social media — writing "I Love It!!!" in response to the idea — on Sept. 6, but he did not sign any executive order to change the state's name. Unlike with geographic landmarks and bodies of water, he lacks the authority to change New Mexico's name without majority support from the state's elected officials. A claim that federal officials approved a plan to change the name of the state of New Mexico to "New America" spread online, with one popular post going so far as to claim U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the state's name in early September 2026. The claim emerged following a real order Trump signed Aug. 27, 2026, to change Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in the United States. X user @DailyNoud shared the claim on Sept. 1 that New Mexico's name also would be changed ( archived ), writing: "Donald Trump has signed an executive order to change the name of New Mexico to New America." The post received more than 3.9 million views, as of this writing: Some people seemed to interpret it as true, and Snopes readers contacted us in search of more information. Variations of the claim also spread on Instagram , Threads and Facebook — and soon after, Trump repeated the idea of changing New Mexico's name on social media with a flurry of posts , writing in one, "Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA. So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!" Trump also posted the map of New Mexico seen in the X post above on Sept. 6, showing "Mexico" crossed out and replaced with "America." The map featured a misspelling of Socorro, New Mexico (reading "Sooorro" instead), indicating possible alteration using artificial intelligence. To investigate whether there was any official move to change New Mexico's name, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo and Bing . If officials in Trump's administration had really approved plans to change the state's name — or if Trump had signed any such executive order — these searches would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting about an official move to change the name of New Mexico. Unlike with geographic landmarks and bodies of water, Trump lacks the authority to change New Mexico's name without majority support from the state's elected officials. Democrats in the state indicated they would not support such a move . We identified the claim's original source: satirical social media account Casper Planet, which describes its output as "Snews that doesn't matter." This post didn't explicitly say Trump signed an executive order, rather — it claimed that "federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America." (X user @DailyNoud also was a satire account .) The Facebook page Casper Planet shared the related claim ( archived ) on Aug. 29, 2026: New Mexico To Be Renamed New America Following Federal Geographic Naming Changes WASHINGTON - Federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America, continuing a recent effort to update geographic names across the country. According to officials familiar with the change, the word "Mexico" was identified during a routine review of American maps and was determined to be geographically confusing. The change is expected to affect highway signs, government documents and approximately 14 million souvenir coffee mugs. Residents will officially become New Americans, while people born there before the change will reportedly be allowed to continue identifying as New Mexicans during a two-year transition period. Mexico has not been consulted. In addition to a location tag on "Satire Street," its Facebook bio reads ( archived ): Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up We reached out to the page owner for comment in January 2026 regarding a claim about AI-generated images of massive snow bank on Wyoming's Devils Tower. The account's administrator, Justin Hathaway, told Snopes over the phone: "I just love doing this satire stuff, it's such an outlet for me." He continued: "Another reason is people don't really read things fully anymore, and it's a good way to educate people on reading stories fully if they sound somewhat unbelievable." We also attempted to contact the account's owner regarding this claim, and will update this story if we receive a response. Other Casper Planet posts Snopes has debunked include a claim that Yellowstone National Park rangers warned the public that ravens had learned to open car doors and another that a man received a DUI while riding a bear . Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective , we use " originated as satire " or " labeled satire " ratings based on creators' description of their work.

title: Did Lindsay Clancy GoFundMe amass over $1M, while mom who saved kids from fire raised $42K?
label: Rating: Mixture About this rating
text: Claim: A meme accurately cites facts and fundraising figures in comparing prosecutors charging Lindsay Clancy with killing her three children, with Clancy receiving more than $1 million in fundraising, and the story of Emma Schols sustaining severe burns while rescuing her six children from a house fire, then receiving only $42,000 in fundraising. Rating: Mixture About this rating What's True The meme provides some factual information about both stories and, as of this writing, an accurate GoFundMe tally of donations earmarked to defray Clancy's parents' travel and housing costs as they attended the trial. Also, it's true that a Swedish news outlet reported that a church deacon in that country organized a fundraiser equaling, at current currency conversion rates, about $42,000. However … What's False … the meme omits additional fundraisers and sponsors who pledged to help rebuild Schols' home, according to information found in the same Swedish news outlet mentioned above and her 2022 book. In late August and early September 2026, people shared a meme comparing the alleged stories of two mothers. Emma Schols' story of heroism, which involved sav ing her six children from a house fire and sustaining severe burns in the process, appears on the meme's left side, with a fundraising figure of $42,000. The right side features Lindsay Clancy, the mother at the center of a highly-publicized Massachusetts murder trial — which ended in a mistrial Sept. 4 — in which prosecutors charged her with killing her three young children, along with a purported GoFundMe fundraising figure exceeding $1 million. X user @CodyManners2 posted ( archived ) the meme, which reads under photos of Schols: "Mother pulls all 6 of her children out of raging house fire, going back in three times despite burns covering 93% of her body. Money raised: $42,000." Clancy's caption reads: "Mother kills all 3 of her children by strangling them to death with exercise bands. Claims she is victim. GoFundMe: $1,044,318+." (@CodyManners2 via X) Other users widely shared the meme , or a similar one , on Facebook ( archived ), Reddit ( archived ), TikTok ( archived ) and X ( archived ). In sum, Schols' book and news media outlets' reporting confirm the meme features a few specific facts but also omits key information. For these reasons, we have rated the meme's content as a mixture of true and false information. Snopes emailed Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, and Schols to request comment. A reverse image search found no posts displaying the meme older than X user @CodyManners2's post. We reached out to that user to ask whether they created the meme and will update this article if we receive further information. Breaking down the Schols-Clancy meme Schols, who lives in Sweden, saved all six of her children in a Sept. 3, 2019, house fire, taking three trips to remove all of them from the inferno. Her 2022 coauthored book , "Ärren bär jag med stolthet: branden i Edsbyn och livet efteråt," which translates to "I Carry the Scars with Pride: The Fire in Edsbyn and Life Afterwards," tells her harrowing story, including the fact that 93% of her body sustained burns, as the meme claims. In September 2019, Swedish news media outlet SVT, quoting church deacon Christer Schwartz, reported Schols' fundraising total at 400,000 Swedish krona, or at current exchange rates about $42,000. According to that report, Schwartz's fundraiser was one of several on Schols' behalf but no other figures were reported. On top of Schwartz's and other fundraisers, a February 2020 charity hockey match reportedly collected an additional 200,000 Swedish krona ($21,000). Schols says in her book that people and companies also initially pledged to sponsor the rebuilding of her house, though she adds some of those sponsors pulled out after she separated from her partner. As for Clancy, The Associated Press , Reuters and other outlets reported she admitted strangling her children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023, and pleaded not guilty to her initial charges , which included three counts each of first-degree murder, strangulation and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Prosecutors later dropped the strangulation charges, saying they were redundant to the murder charges. The organizer of the Clancy case GoFundMe ( archived ), titled "The Musgrove Family Fund," described the purported recipients of the fundraiser as Clancy's parents, Mike and Paula Musgrove, citing their hotel, travel and relocation costs to stay close to their daughter over more than three years. The in-question meme does not mention Clancy's parents, instead making the allegation that Clancy herself will one day collect the funds. At last check, the fundraiser had grown to more than $1.1 million with a goal of $2 million, bringing in more than 33,500 individual donations. The meme adds that Clancy has claimed she's the victim. During her criminal trial in summer 2026, Reddington, her attorney, said "there is evidence of lack of criminal responsibility" and suggested "a required finding of not guilty should be entered on the case." He repeatedly argued Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis , a disorder an estimated one or two in 1,000 women experience after giving birth that can include delusions, depression, hallucinations, insomnia, paranoia and other changes in behavior. Prosecutors, on the other hand, argued she knew what she was doing. Schols' harrowing rescue story On Sept. 3, 2019, Schols awoke before 6 a.m. in her home to early-morning light shining through her window, with the faint memory of minutes earlier hearing some of her children playing in another room. In Schols' book, which we translated to English, she said her then-partner, Anders, was working a night shift, leaving her to sleep alone. She wrote of the morning, "Great, I think, now I have a few minutes to lie down and catch up before I have to start my morning routine." Moments later, the book recounts, she felt a very different sense of "fear, panic and desperation" when one of her children screamed from downstairs, "Help, mom, there's a fire. There's a fire in the TV room!" She wrote, "To make sure all the children have woken up, I scream at the top of my lungs: 'Everyone has to get out of the house!'" In the minutes that followed, Schols first managed to guide her young children Albin and Oliwe r out the front door, then looked for William, Melwyn and Nellie. After seeing William and showing Melwyn to safety, she made it to her youngest child, Mollie, who was standing in her crib with a full diaper. Schols became unable to move from the flames covering her body. She wrote, "If I have managed to give birth to six children, I will swear to get six children out of this burning house," and that she gathered strength, picked up Mollie and looked to escape. She described William as positioning a ladder they happened to have left out from a long-neglected painting job as their method of escape from the balcony. Once outside, Schols described hearing her dog, Sally, inside making noises and thinking of her cat as well. A neighbor, seeing burns all over Schols' body, told her it was too late to save her pets. Several Swedish outlets published news of the fire on the same day. Following extensive hospital stays for her burns and a period of rehabilitation, Schols returned home. In her book, Schols wrote of Schwartz, the deacon, organizing the fundraiser following the fire. A Facebook post from days after the incident mentions Schwartz by name. Schols said locals helped find clothes for her children, writing, "I am struck by the incredible care that exists in our country." Other examples of that care included "Playing for Emma," a charity hockey match organized in Schols' honor in February 2020. Schols wrote about the match, as well as her family's home insurance situation at the time of the fire: On Sunday, February 2nd, a tribute match will be held for me, where the money raised will go to help me and my family get back on their feet. For all the years we have had home insurance, but just a month or so before the accident, we had, due to our financial situation, fallen behind on that particular bill. This fact is something I am ashamed of today. As I have been mulling this question over here in the hospital. This very month, when the house burns down, we were forced to skip that bill. What are the odds of that? Later in December 2020, the Swedish Heroes Gala awarded Schols the title "Lifesaver of the Year." Near the end of her book, Schols wrote that some companies and people sponsoring the rebuilding of their former home pulled out after she and Anders separated. To close her book, Schols thanked numerous locals and medical personnel, as well as her family, former partner and friends, saving a message for her children for last: My biggest thanks go to William, Nellie, Melwin, Albin, Oliwer and Mollie. I may have saved your lives, but you are the absolute biggest heroes in this whole story. You are my everything and I love you with all my heart. For further reading, we previously reported about other rumors involving Sweden, including investigating whether the country imports trash to fulfill its energy needs , as well as fact-checking whether the city of Södertälje truly trained wild crows to pick up cigarette butts .

title: Did Gloria Steinem work with the CIA? The truth about her past
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: The late feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem once worked with the CIA. Rating: True About this rating Context Steinem led a CIA-backed organization that reportedly recruited young Americans to disrupt Soviet Union-supported festivals and share alternatives to communist ideas. She maintained through her life that her involvement with the CIA was an innocent arrangement and claimed in a 1967 New York Times article that the CIA never asked her to report on other Americans or foreign nationals. After American journalist and feminist activist Gloria Steinem died at age 92 on Sept. 3, 2026, a rumor spread online that she once worked with the CIA. Social media users on X , TikTok and Reddit claimed she was a CIA "asset," "cop" or "operative," or that she led an organization that was actually a front for CIA operations. Steinem repeatedly and publicly acknowledged working with the CIA. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, she ran the Independent Research Service, a CIA-backed organization that recruited young Americans, reportedly to disrupt Soviet Union-supported festivals and promote alternatives to communist ideas. As such, we have rated this claim as true. Whether she actively spied for the CIA is unclear. In 1967 news articles, Steinem insisted she was never asked to pass information to the CIA. Steinem admits involvement after exposé In early 1967, the now-defunct Ramparts magazine revealed that the CIA spent $180,000 financing "an interesting operation known as the Independent Research Service." "This was the organization that made life so miserable for the organizers of the communist-leaning world youth festivals in Vienna in 1959, and in Helsinki in 1962," the article said (Page 32). "The Independent Research Service actively recruited a delegation of hundreds of young Americans to attend the festivals in order to actively oppose the communists." According to a 2016 New York Times article about Steinem, after the Ramparts issue ran, Steinem publicly acknowledged to the Times and The Washington Post that the CIA was a major financial backer of the Independent Research Service. While the Times said the Independent Research Service simply received financial support, the Post said Steinem "worked closely with the Central Intelligence Agency" and "had great praise for the CIA agents whom she collaborated with." "I found them liberal and farsighted and open to an exchange of ideas," Steinem said, according to the Post. "I never felt I was being dictated to at all." Steinem told both newspapers that very few people involved in the Independent Research Service knew of the CIA's involvement. The Post's article also quoted another director of the Independent Research Service, Dennis Shaul, who said, "The Helsinki Festival was a disaster from their (the Communist world's) point of view, and I think we can take a good deal of credit for that." In March 1967, Steinem appeared on a CBS documentary, "In the Pay of the CIA: An American Dilemma," to tell her story about her time taking "secret CIA funds," per a CBS news release archived in the CIA's public records. A clip of her interview in that documentary appears to be available on YouTube. In the clip, she acknowledges working for the CIA and, again, says the CIA did not interfere with her point of view. "I had the conventional liberal's view of the CIA as a right-wing incendiary group, and I was amazed to discover that this was far from the case, that they were enlightened, liberal nonpartisan activists," she said ( at 2:17 ). We reached out to CBS to ask for an official copy of the documentary and await a response. Steinem responds to feminist criticism In 1975, Redstockings, a radical feminist group, attacked Steinem's involvement with the CIA and called Steinem's insistence that she was never asked to gather information for the CIA a "serious lie." " The Report on the Vienna Youth Festival, published with her name on it as Director of the Independent Research Service, contains 13 pages devoted solely to biographies, political affiliations, and even pseudo-political analyses of individuals from all the countries participating in the festival," Redstockings wrote. Redstockings also said it questioned Steinem's motives for entering the women's movement and was "suspicious of her sudden rise to prominence as a 'women's liberation leader' at a time when, unlike other prominent women's liberationists, she was active in no women's group, she had not written a feminist book, won a Congressional seat or played a superb game of tennis." The New York Times reported in 2016 that Steinem said the criticism from other feminists "hurt more than anything." "They never called to ask me what I did," she said. In the same 2016 article, Steinem maintained that her relationship with the CIA was innocent. "It's so interesting now, because the initials C.I.A. will make people believe anything," she said. "It just wasn't like that. It just was so uncontrolled. As I remember saying at the time, if this was our grandmother's money we'd be doing the same thing."

title: White House website's arcade games let players build border wall, deport migrants
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: The White House website has a series of arcade-style games that let players catch and deport migrants and build a border wall, among others. Rating: True About this rating In September 2026, many people online claimed the White House had created its own arcade games and made them available to play on its website, including a game that involved catching migrants. Screenshots of the alleged online game spread on Instagram ( archived ), Facebook and X ( archived ). Snopes readers asked us to verify the claim. The White House has launched an official government arcade featuring games designed to promote Trump administration policies. One has you play as a Border Patrol agent rounding up migrants. Another, called "Build the Wall," asks players to defend the border from what the game literally calls the "coming horde." This is not some random MAGA website or parody. It is official White House messaging on a .gov website, turning immigration enforcement and the detention of human beings into a game. We have officially entered the dystopian arcade portion of the timeline. An X post shared footage from the alleged game: The claim is true. The White House published a series of arcade-style games on its website on or about Sept. 3, including ones in which players are tasked with building a border wall and deporting unauthorized migrants. We found the games at the URLs whitehouse.gov/arcade ( archived ) and arcade.gov . The White House advertised the games in a social media post ( archived ) with the caption: "CAN'T STOP WINNING. 🎮 Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account." A promotional graphic shared by the account appears to copy the logo font of Sega, a video game company, but replaces the company's name with "MAGA," referring to President Donald Trump's campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again": There are several games available in the White House arcade as of this writing, including one called " Flappy Bill " that tells players to keep a piece of legislation in the air as a bald eagle flies past national monuments. Another game, called " Build the Wall " ( archived ), is captioned "Protect the border from the coming horde" and encourages players to stack falling bricks against green zombies running toward a wall. It also has an arrow with a sign saying "Southern Border." The above game's similarities to Tetris, a video game involving falling blocks, prompted a response from that company. Tetris posted on X: " The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of 'Build the Wall'. P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously." A third game, " Rio Run " ( archived ), tells players to "Patrol the line along the river. Pick up every crosser in the lot. Never double back over the line." When we clicked on the game and lost, a label came up saying "0 deported." (arcade.gov) Other games make players "sort the school lunch to Make America Healthy Again" or fill fake Trump savings accounts with money. As of this writing, the games are still available on the White House website. For further reading, Snopes has previously reported on other online PR campaigns from Trump's White House , including when it posted Spider-Man-inspired graphics of immigrants trapped in webs next to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.

title: Why adding a stamp to your ballot won't make it first-class mail
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: Adding a stamp to a postage prepaid ballot will “force” the U.S. Postal Service to handle it as first-class mail instead of bulk. Rating: False About this rating Context The U.S. Postal Service said on its website that it handles prepaid and stamped mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services. In September 2026, a claim ( archived ) circulated online that adding postage to a prepaid mail-in ballot would "force" the U.S. Postal Service to treat it as first-class mail, a service that allows postcards and small envelopes to be delivered in one to five days. The claim circulated as states began sending out mail-in ballots for the 2026 midterm elections, despite the Trump administration's ongoing court battles to enforce an executive order that would restrict voting by mail. One Threads user who shared the claim wrote: By adding a 1st Class Postage Stamp to your postage prepaid ballot, it will then force USPS to handle it as 1st Class Mail, instead of Bulk Mail! SHARE EVERYWHERE! View on Threads The claim also circulated on Facebook ( archived ) and X ( archived ). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true. The claim was false. According to the USPS, the service always handles mail-in ballots as first-class mail unless voters pay for priority or priority express services. In other words, adding additional postage will not expedite the delivery of a standard mail-in ballot. The USPS included the following message on its web page about "Election Mail" (emphasis ours): Mailpieces containing a completed ballot are handled as First-Class Mail® service, regardless of whether they are prepaid by election officials or mailed with a stamp affixed by the voter. The only situation where a completed ballot is not handled as First-Class Mail is when the voter opts to pay for a premium service like Priority Mail® service or Priority Mail Express® service. Who pays postage on a mail-in ballot varies by state. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan, nonprofit organization that represents lawmakers in the 50 U.S. states, 19 states and Washington, D.C. require local election officials to pay postage while voters in other states must pay. In a June 2026 FAQ, the USPS said its policy directs employees to deliver ballots with insufficient postage and attempt to recoup the payment from the local election board. Mail-in ballot return deadlines vary by state. The USPS advises that voters mail their ballots " before Election Day, and at least one week prior to the deadline by which your completed ballot must be received by your election office ." Voters can check deadlines for returning mail-in ballots with their local election office . Some states also allow voters to deliver completed ballots to drop boxes that are emptied by election officials, which eliminates the need to use the postal service to vote. At the time of this writing, the Trump administration sought to implement new federal regulations on mail-in ballots that could require states to submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal and follow a uniform envelope style. In an August 24, 2026, opinion , the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to proceed with implementing the proposed regulations but did not rule on whether they were legal. The Associated Press reported that "legal wrangling" continued over Trump's executive order in lower courts. Therefore, it was unclear at the time of this writing if, or how, the proposed changes to mail voting would affect the 2026 midterm elections. Despite having previously voted by mail himself, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized mail voting, including after he lost the 2020 presidential election. Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

title: Did North Dakota mayor sue Canadian wind farm for using 'American wind'? Claim is full of hot air
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: In August 2026, Steve Clack, the mayor of Walhalla, North Dakota, sued a wind farm in the Canadian province of Manitoba, asking them to pay for using "American wind." Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating A rumor that the mayor of Walhalla , North Dakota, a small town located five miles from the Canadian border, was suing a wind farm in Manitoba, Canada, for using "American wind" spread online in August 2026. For example, a Facebook user shared an image on Aug. 31 with a caption reading "North Dakota Mayor Sues Manitoba Wind Farm for Stealing 'American Wind.'" The story spread amid U.S. President Donald Trump's ongoing trade standoff with Canada , and was seemingly a reflection of the increasing tensions between the neighboring countries. Some users seemed to interpret the rumor about Canada "stealing" America's wind as true. Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy. (Bob Granflaten via Facebook) To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo , Google and Yahoo . If the claim about Walhalla's mayor, supposedly named Steve Clack, were true, journalists with reputable local or national outlets like the The Forum of Fargo-Moorhead, The Grand Forks Herald, The Associated Press or Reuters would have reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case. We didn't find any credible reporting about the alleged lawsuit. We also reviewed local news articles and Walhalla's official city council meetings to determine whether Steve Clack was really the mayor. He was not. The searches did allow us to identify the true source of the rumor — the Canadian news satire radio show "This Is That." The show's Facebook page posted the claim on Aug. 28 , calling it a " classic This Is That clip from our 2nd season." Further research on the show revealed that the satirical segment would have first aired sometime in 2011. The clip posted to the This Is That Facebook page included "#satire" in its description and the accompanying video included an AI content label (presumably, the visuals were AI-generated, as the show aired on radio, not TV). Snopes frequently checks rumors that originate as satirical news stories. For example, in August 2026, we also alerted readers to a fake story describing Trump's behavior in the presidential limousine, including listening to "Dancing Queen" by ABBA. Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective , we use " originated as satire " or " labeled satire " ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

title: French map doesn't prove Lake Ontario was once called 'Lac America.' It's altered
label: Rating: Fake About this rating
text: Claim: An image authentically shows a French map from 1688 that replaced the name "Lac Ontario" with "Lac America." Rating: Fake About this rating In August 2026, during a trade war with Canada, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" for the federal government. Among the social media responses were people who purported to justify the decision. For example, one X post ( archived ) posted an image of what appeared to be an old French map that labeled the body of water "Lac America." Text on the image read, "Wont you take a look at that.. apparently Trump is just correcting what was once called lake America a very long time ago. from an OLD canadia map thats in french." The same image was shared on other social media sites such as Facebook ( archived ), LinkedIn ( archived ) and Threads ( archived ). Snopes readers sent us emails to ask if the image was of a real map. However, the "Lac America" map was an AI-generated edit of a real vintage map that actually labeled the lake "Lac Ontario." Therefore we've rated the edited image as a fake. While some versions of the "Lac America" image crop out parts of the map, full versions of that map have a box in the top left that reads, "Le Lac America avec les lieux circonuoifins & particulierement les cinq nations Iroquoifes. Lannée 1688." The text within the box, plus the map itself, match a real map made by the French Jesuit cartographer Pierre Raffeix in 1688. The difference between the AI-generated edit and the real map, however, is that the real map, as found in the University of Toronto's scan, reads "Lac Ontario" wherever the AI-generated map has "Lac America." BnF, the national library in France, has in its collection what appears to be Raffeix's handwritten version of the University of Toronto map, before he finalized it. Again, on this map the lake is labeled "Lac Ontario" and makes no mention of a "Lac America." Raffeix's "Lac Ontario ou de Saint Lovis" (translated "Lake Ontario or S aint Louis") matches the name given the lake by other French cartographers from the 1600s, as covered by Snopes previously. Even as early as 1641, French Jesuits referred to the lake as "the Ontario or lake of St. Louys." As for the "Lac America" map being AI-generated, there are several clues on that version of the map itself. There is a seal of an anchor flanked by the letters "V" and "C" on the Lac America map that appears directly above the "E" in "America." This appears to be based on a seal above the "T" in "Ontario" in the real map , although that seal appears to have fleurs-de-lis , a symbol associated with French royalty that some Americans might more easily recognize as the logo of the New Orleans Saints football team, on either side of the anchor instead. Additionally, there are certain place names on the fake map that go beyond bad handwriting and into the sort of gibberish commonly associated with AI-generated images, particularly older ones. For example, the label on land immediately above the "Lac" label in "Lac America" does not appear to use real letters, except for an "l" and a "g." While Raffeix's handwriting certainly makes that label hard to read in the real map, zooming in on it reveals the first several letters are "theyag" before the rest becomes illegible. For further reading, Snopes has previously covered claims referencing Trump's federal renaming of Lake Ontario, including a satirical claim about Canadian officials refusing passage to ships bound for "Lake America."

title: HHS report cites inaccurate data to claim more than 5,500 trans minors received 'sex change surgeries'
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: As cited by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, a database from anti-trans group Do No Harm proves that from 2019 to 2023, more than 5,500 minors in the United States had sex change surgeries. Rating: False About this rating An August 2026 U.S. Department of Health and Human Services report claimed that "watchdog analyses tracking" had determined more than 5,500 minors had undergone "sex change surgeries" from 2019 to 2023. The "watchdog analyses tracking" references an anti-LGBTQ+ group that inflated the data by counting a vast number of procedures entirely unrelated to "sex change surgeries," including hair removal, surgical removal of excess eyelid skin and bladder drainage. These procedures were counted in the "sex change surgery" statistic as long as the patient had a gender dysphoria diagnosis or a psychiatric condition related to crossdressing (which is different from being trans). As with any other person's healthcare, there are many reasons why a trans person may need these procedures that have nothing to do with being trans. Credible data indicates that gender-affirming surgeries are rarely performed on minors, and most minors who receive them are not actually trans, but cisgender boys getting chest reductions. A peer-reviewed study from Harvard University researchers in 2024 determined that in 2019, only 85 trans minors received gender-affirming surgery and most of them were age 15 to 17. The Harvard study found no gender-affirming surgeries conducted on children under 12. In August 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services under U.S. President Donald Trump released a report alleging that according to "watchdog analyses tracking," more than 5,500 minors had undergone "sex change surgeries" from 2019 to 2023. Here's what Page 9 of the report says (emphasis ours): Watchdog analyses tracking billed charges for minors from 2019 onward estimate almost $120 million in total hospital and clinic billings nationwide, encompassing over 5,500 surgical procedures and 8,500 courses of hormones or blockers. (14) (14) "What We Found," Stop the Harm Database, accessed March 12, 2026, https://stoptheharmdatabase.com/about/. ($119,791,202 in total submitted charges; 5,747 minors had sex change surgeries ; 8,579 minors received hormones and puberty blockers). Social media users across Facebook repeated the supposed statistic and cited the report, including Republican U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger, a pharmacist from Tennessee ( screenshot ). Similar posts included a video of Adm. Brian Christine, assistant secretary for health at HHS, who claimed that there were more than "5,500 sex-rejecting procedures" performed on minors ( screenshot ). Snopes readers searched the website to investigate the legitimacy of this statistic. The HHS report pulled this number from a database of supposed surgeries created by Do No Harm, an advocacy group that opposes gender-affirming care for trans minors and diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in medicine. The Southern Poverty Law Center, a civil rights organization that tracks extremist organizations, has designated Do No Harm as an anti-LGBTQ+ hate group. Do No Harm's methodology report lists insurance codes — standardized codes insurance companies use to describe various health care procedures and treatments — that the organization used to come up with the statistic. However, a Snopes review of the report found that many of these codes are entirely unrelated to "sex change surgeries," thus contradicting Do No Harm's claims . Furthermore, both a peer-reviewed study from Harvard University researchers and a Reuters analysis found far lower rates of gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors. In truth, for minors, these surgeries are exceedingly rare and occur only among older teenagers. As such, we have rated this claim as false. A spokesperson for Do No Harm, Caroline Anderegg, said in an email that answers to our questions could be found on Do No Harm's methodology page and report. Anderegg did not return a follow-up inquiry noting that the methodology report and page did not answer our questions about what insurance database the group used and how the group filtered the insurance codes to ensure the data included only "sex change surgeries." Methodology doesn't hold up to scrutiny Do No Harm's website for its "Stop the Harm Database" claimed that between 2019 and 2023, "5,747 minors had sex change surgeries." However, its methodology report said Do No Harm included insurance procedure codes for treatments that do not change a person's sex, including electrolysis for hair removal, bladder drainage, "removal of excessive skin of upper eyelid" and more (pages 17 through 20). These procedures are also not necessarily for gender-affirming care more broadly and can happen for many different reasons. Do No Harm said it included these procedure codes only when connected to a patient with a gender dysphoria diagnosis or transvestic disorder, a psychiatric condition where a patient experiences clinically significant distress or impairment due to sexual arousal while crossdressing (Page 17). However, the codes used are outdated, said Dr. Morissa Ladinsky, a pediatrician with Stanford University who once co-led a clinic in Alabama for trans youth. Furthermore, a gender dysphoria code merely indicates that the patient is transgender, not that the procedure was done specifically to alleviate gender dysphoria, said Kellan Baker, senior adviser for health policy at the Movement Advancement Project, a nonprofit think tank known for tracking LGBTQ-related laws and policies. " I really cannot underscore to you how irregular the Do No Harm analysis is," Baker , whose work as a health services researcher involves identifying trans people in insurance claim databases, said in a phone call. There are many reasons why a trans patient might receive any number of these procedures that are unrelated to being trans. For example, a trans child could have a urine obstruction and need bladder drainage, or require excess skin removal for droopy eyelids impairing their ability to function. Furthermore, some of the codes, such as codes for intersex surgery, are used for intersex people, not transgender people. Intersex people are born with a variety of different sex characteristics that do not fit typical binary ideas of male or female bodies. Intersex infants and children in the United States sometimes receive surgeries, either for medical necessity or, more controversially, to align their bodies with more "typical" traits. Ladinsky said that the procedure codes listed " nearly never have relevance in gender affirming surgery" for minors, calling the report "one crazy white paper." Baker also pointed out that Do No Harm claims to use "an all-payer claims database" — a database with every open and shut insurance case — but did not reveal which database it used to find this information. He said that such a database with all insurance claim information does not actually exist. Gender-affirming surgeries rarely performed on minors There are very few studies on the number of gender-affirming surgeries done on minors, largely because the surgeries themselves are so rare, Baker said. However, Harvard researchers published a peer-reviewed study in 2024 that analyzed 2019 insurance claim data and found no incidences of a child under 12 receiving a gender-affirming surgery. Out of a total of about 22 million minors sampled, the study found only 85 instances of a minor undergoing a gender-affirming surgical procedure in 2019, with 82 of those instances involving chest-related procedures, presumably either a chest reduction or breast tissue removal, commonly known as top surgery. The vast majority of those instances involved teenagers ages 15 to 17. The study also found that far more cisgender boys — those who align with their gender assigned at birth — received gender-affirming chest reductions than transgender boys. Cisgender boys often receive these chest reductions because of gynecomastia , or physically harmless enlarged chest tissue that can affect their self-esteem and mental health. Snopes reached out to the Harvard researchers involved in the study for their thoughts on the Do No Harm database and did not immediately hear back. In 2022, Reuters, a credible news source, analyzed data from Komodo Health — considered the most complete health insurance database available — and found 238 mastectomies, or top surgeries, in 2019, 256 in 2020 and 282 in 2021 among trans minors. The analysis also found 56 genital surgeries among patients ages 13 to 17 with a prior gender dysphoria diagnosis from 2019 to 2021. However, the Reuters analysis did not appear to separate out trans youth who received these surgeries due to health issues unrelated to gender identity, unlike the peer-reviewed study from Harvard researchers. Furthermore, any increase in gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors has likely reversed due to the rise in anti-trans health care policies across the country and on the federal level, Baker said. The bottom line The data HHS cited in its report comes from an anti-LGBTQ+ group that used faulty analysis to inflate data on gender-affirming surgeries among trans minors. It's more accurate to say that from 2019 to 2023, more than 5,500 minors, many of whom had a gender dysphoria diagnosis at one point in time, received various procedures for any number of medical reasons, the vast majority of which were unrelated to being trans. Peer-reviewed research suggests that gender-affirming surgeries among minors are incredibly rare and usually involve cisgender boys undergoing chest reductions.

title: Did Trump say US has 'too many non-working holidays' that cost country 'billions'?
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: A screenshot authentically shows a post U.S. President Donald Trump made to Truth Social saying that there were "too many non-working holidays in America" that cost the country "billions of dollars" to keep businesses closed. Rating: True About this rating Context Trump made the post on June 19, 2025 — it was not a 2026 "Labor Day message," as some people claimed. Rumors spread in early September 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump posted a message to social media claiming that it costs America "billions of dollars" to keep businesses closed on federal holidays. People on social media platforms and Reddit shared a screenshot of the alleged post and added comments like, "a president notorious for spending weekends at Mar-a-Lago to golf and ham it up at sycophantic dinner parties, thinks American workers get too many non-working holidays." The screenshot circulated as the United States approached the annual Labor Day holiday on Sept. 7. Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., wrote a lengthy criticism of what she called Trump's "Labor Day message" on her X account on Sept. 2. Trump shared the post on Truth Social, but it wasn't a Labor Day message, nor was it posted in 2026. Trump posted the message at 7:03 p.m. on June 19, 2025. It can also be viewed on Trump's Truth , an archive of all of Trump's Truth Social posts. The full post read: Too many non-working holidays in America. It is costing our Country $BILLIONS OF DOLLARS to keep all of these businesses closed. The workers don't want it either! Soon we'll end up having a holiday for every once working day of the year. It must change if we are going to, MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! A search revealed 29 Truth Social posts from Trump on June 19, 2025, including the post in question, but none of the others appeared to be related to that post. While it was unclear what specifically Trump was posting about at the time, June 19 is recognized as Juneteenth , a holiday commemorating the end of slavery in the U.S. Juneteenth became a federally recognized holiday under then-President Joe Biden in 2021. Given Trump's track record at criticizing Biden in speeches , online posts , debates and in interviews , it's possible this post was another attempt at diminishing his predecessor's accomplishments. We reached out to the White House to clarify whether Trump's post from June 19, 2025, was indeed meant as commentary on Juneteenth and/or Biden and will update this article if we receive a response.

title: Talarico voted against bill meant to protect Texas land from Chinese interests. Here's why
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: Texas state Rep. James Talarico, a Democrat, voted against SB 17, a bill meant to prevent China from buying land in Texas. Rating: True About this rating Context It's true that Talarico voted nay on the bill in question, SB 17, even though he had previously voted in favor of continuing to amend its language. The final version of SB 17 included amendments that its opponents said would broaden it beyond its intended scope. A spokesperson for Talarico said he voted nay on the final version to prevent giving the governor more power. The bill ultimately passed and became law in September 2025. Rumors that Texas state Rep. James Talarico voted against a bill that would prevent the Chinese Communist Party from buying land in the state circulated on the internet in early September 2026 as Talarico, a Democrat, campaigned for a U.S. Senate seat. People on social media claimed Talarico voted against a bill called SB 17, some accusing him of rejecting "the basic responsibility to protect the state's soil and food system." (X user @EricLDaugh) Supporters of Talarico's Republican opponent in the November 2026 election, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, unleashed a campaign ad amplifying the claim. It's true that Talarico voted against SB 17 , a bill aimed at preventing foreign interests from purchasing land in Texas. However, as Talarico and others pointed out, the bill had been amended such that it was likely to have effects beyond the scope of its original intent. The legislation was initially aimed to prohibit real estate deals involving Texas land by countries identified by U.S. intelligence officials as national security threats: primarily China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. The bill eventually passed by the Texas House in May 2025 was amended so that the governor, rather than federal intelligence officials, could ultimately "determine the countries whose residents, governments and other entities could be banned from buying property here," according to reporting by The Texas Tribune . In the Texas House Journal from May 8, 2025, which also recorded Talarico's nay vote, a fellow critic, Democratic Rep. Mihaela Plesa, explained, "While the intent to safeguard critical infrastructure and land interests is valid, CSSB17, as amended, became too broad and open-ended. The bill now permits the governor and state agencies to unilaterally add entire countries to its prohibitive list, restricting land ownership by nationals of those countries without requiring future legislative approval or public oversight."
