title: Did Florida weatherman say he feared he could no longer predict hurricanes because of funding cuts?
label: Rating: Correct Attribution About this rating
text: Claim: During a weather broadcast, meteorologist John Morales said of his ability to predict hurricanes in Florida, "I am not sure I can do that this year because of the cuts, the gutting, the sledgehammer attack on science in general." Rating: Correct Attribution About this rating Context Morales said these words in June 2025, not in the summer of 2026, as some posts implied. Snopes reached out to him, asking if he felt the same way a year on, and awaits a response. In August 2026, a rumor spread that Florida weatherman John Morales , of NBC 6 South Florida, had gone off-script during a weather broadcast saying he feared he could no longer accurately predict hurricanes due to government funding cuts enacted by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump. As Snopes readers emailed and searched the website seeking to confirm this was true, the claim spread on social media. One Facebook post showed an image of Morales and said he had "suddenly shifted gear" during a broadcast to tell the audience he was no longer certain he could predict the weather "this year" due to "the cuts, the gutting, the sledgehammer attack on science in general" ( archived ): Morales did say these words, and as a result we've rated the quote correctly attributed. However, he did not say it in the summer of 2026, but in June 2025. We reached out to Morales to ask if he still felt he could no longer confidently predict the path of hurricanes. We will update this report should he respond. Snopes identified the video clip in which Morales said he feared he could no longer predict hurricanes due to government funding cuts. It was posted to the YouTube channel of NBC 6 South Florida, a local NBC affiliate, on June 3, 2025: After re-airing a clip from 2019 in which he discussed Hurricane Dorian , a violent hurricane that had devastated the Bahamas and was moving up the east coast of the U.S., Morales said (at the 00:50 mark): Lots of people in Florida were concerned the hurricane was heading here. And as you've grown accustomed to my presentations over my 34 years in South Florida newscasts, confidently I went on TV and I told you, it's going to turn. You don't need to worry. It is going to turn. And I am here to tell you that I am not sure I can do that this year because of the cuts, the gutting, the sledgehammer attack on science in general. And I could talk about that for a long, long time and how that is affecting the U.S. leadership in science over many years and how we're losing that leadership. And this is a multigenerational impact on science in this country. All right. But specifically, let's talk about the federal government cuts to the National Weather Service and to NOAA . Did you know that Central and South Florida National Weather Service offices are currently basically 20 to 40% understaffed from Tampa to Key West, including the Miami office? Twenty to 40% understaffed. Now, this type of staffing shortage is having impacts across the nation because there's been a nearly 20% reduction in weather balloon releases, launches that carry those radio signs. And what we're starting to see is that the quality of the forecasts is becoming degraded. There's also a chance, because of some of these cuts, that NOAA hurricane Hunter aircraft will not be able to fly this year, and with less reconnaissance missions, we may be flying blind, and we may not exactly know how strong a hurricane is before it reaches the coastline, like happened a couple of years ago in Hurricane Otis in Acapulco, Mexico. At the time, reputable news outlets such as The Independent and The New York Times reported on Morales' broadcast. For further reading, Snopes covered several claims related to Trump administration government funding cuts, including the rumor that such cuts caused a screwworm outbreak in the U.S.

title: RFK Jr. repeats false claim that MMR vaccine contains fetal tissue
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: The vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella contains tissue from aborted fetuses, as U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. claimed in August 2026. Rating: False About this rating In August 2026, U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed in an X post that the vaccine used to prevent measles, mumps and rubella contained "fetal tissue." Kennedy was responding to Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, who accused him of peddling conspiracy theories about vaccines . In his X post on Aug. 25, Kennedy defended his claim ( archived ). He said, in part: The rubella virus used in MMR-II is grown on the cultured cell line composed of lung tissue from an aborted three-month-old female embryo and listed as "WI-38 human diploid lung fibroblasts" in the ingredients of MMR-II as portions of these cells end up in each vial of MMR II. This was not the first time Kennedy made this claim. On April 30, 2025, he claimed during a NewsNation townhall with television presenter Chris Cuomo that the MMR vaccine "contains a lot of aborted fetus debris" (starting at the 1:08 mark). However, the health secretary's claim that the vaccine contains fetal material from abortions was incorrect. Therefore, we have rated the claim false. The 2025 measles outbreak It is true that, in 2025 and 2026, the U.S. was seeing its worst outbreak of measles since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with 2,777 cases from the beginning of 2026 to Aug. 20, 7% of which required hospitalization. As of this writing, the CDC has also reported three deaths in 2025 and none in 2026. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) (CDC) Measles is a highly contagious disease that requires 95% of the population to be immunized to prevent its spread, according to Harvard Medical School. For years, the country was able to prevent new cases by keeping the vaccination rates at or above 95%. However, in more recent years, the vaccination rate began to fall. It was at 92% in 2023 and at 82% in the area where the 2025 outbreak started in West Texas, also according to Harvard Medical School. Experts have long identified disinformation and misinformation as key forces causing fears about the safety of the MMR vaccine and others, and, as Snopes reported in February 2024 and in May 2017 , Kennedy has been a prominent voice in promulgating false claims about vaccines. For full immunization, the schedule calls for two doses of the MMR vaccine , according to the CDC. Most people who were infected in the 2025 and 2026 measles outbreak were either unvaccinated, had an unknown vaccination status or had received only one of the two doses, according to Harvard Medical School. False claims about the MMR vaccine The MMR vaccine has long been the target of false claims. For example, a now-debunked article, reported on by Snopes in January 2019, succeeded in convincing many concerned parents that a mercury-based preservative known as thimerosal, which some vaccines and other injections used to contain , was responsible for an increase in autism rates. While it is true that autism diagnoses have continued to increase in the U.S., it is not for this reason. In fact, childhood vaccines no longer contain thimerosal. The combined MMR jab contains three live attenuated viruses. These versions of the viruses are too weak to cause an infection but are strong enough to provoke an immune reaction in which the body produces specific antibodies to fight the viruses if the person is exposed to them later. The claim that the MMR vaccine contains fetal material stems from a misunderstanding of how the rubella attenuated virus is produced. According to an article that appeared in the Jan. 29, 2020, issue of the medical journal Vaccine, the most common rubella strain used in vaccines is attenuated in a cell culture that uses the specific cell line WI-38 : The most commonly used vaccine strain for the rubella virus is attenuated strain RA27/3, which was extracted using explant liver culture and attenuated by passaging in human diploid fibroblasts (WI-38), at temperatures of 30 °C and 35 °C. The cell line WI-38 was isolated "from the lung tissue of a 3-month-old, female, embryo," according to the description of a website that commercializes the cells for use in vaccine development. eonard Hayflick, a U.S. scientist, isolated the cells from the embryo of a legal abortion in Sweden in the early 1960s . The cell line is credited with preserving countless lives, according to a 2024 obituary for Hayflick in the journal NPJ Aging (emphasis ours): The 'Hayflick cells', WI-38, have been the basis for producing vaccines for poliomyelitis, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, adenovirus, rabies, and hepatitis A. Over the last 50 years, the number of people benefiting from these vaccines has been estimated to be several billion worldwide. However, vaccine development has not needed to take new cells from more recent abortions. Further, while vaccine developers do attenuate the virus in the cells, they later extract it and purify it , removing all trace of WI-38 cells. In sum, no trace of the cells appears in the vaccine.

title: Does photo show Hakeem Jeffries with Epstein?
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: An image shared online in August 2026 authentically shows U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., with the late financier and sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein. Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating In August 2026, an image appeared online claiming to show ( archived , archived ) U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., with the late financier and sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein. According to some posts, the photograph was supposedly taken at an event in 2013. Snopes readers wrote in asking whether the image was real. (David J Harris Jr. via Facebook) We found that the photo not real, and was generated with artificial intelligence tools. The post was a good example of AI slop — low quality content produced using AI aiming to play the algorithm to go viral and make money. August 2026 wasn't the first time t he image went viral. Snopes debunked it months earlier . Performing a reverse image search on Google showed the earliest example of the image was dated Feb. 11 and originated from the X account @DumbFckFinder — a finding supported by the "DFF" watermark to the right of Jeffries' head. We reached out to the owner of that account hoping to confirm they created the photo, but had not heard back at time of publication. That account describes its output as parody and satire. When Snopes first investigated the image, the account's bio said it is "an AI-powered meme engine that turns stupidity into content ," reading: We use AI to create memes, songs, stories, and visuals that call things exactly how they are — fast, loud, and impossible to ignore. If something looks dumb, sounds dumb, or feels off, we turn it into something shareable. (The account's bio has changed since then.) A reverse image search revealed the image had been posted only to social media, and never by prominent news media outlets. Given the scale of the Epstein case, prominent news media outlets would have widely reported this rumor, if true. Finally, we ran the image in the post through Google's Gemini AI . Any image generated by Gemini contains a watermark called a SynthID . Gemini found that " most or all of this image was edited or generated with Google AI." To avoid errors, we recommend checking for other signs of AI on top of using SynthID screening tools since they can show false positives. In this case, our primary evidence was the X account's original disclaimer that its output is "AI-powered." For further reading, Snopes previously reported on another story from the same account of a fake photo with Epstein and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer . For background, here is why we alert readers to rumors created by sources that call their output humorous or satirical.

title: Faroe Islands woman used sheep to map country. Here's how and why
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: In 2016, a woman used sheep to map the Faroe Islands after Google left the islands off of Google Street View. Rating: True About this rating In mid-2026, some people on social media celebrated a story from the Faroe Islands , a self-governing archipelago north of Scotland. Apparently, 2026 marked the 10-year anniversary of the time a Faroese woman allegedly strapped cameras on sheep to map the country when Google wouldn't, according to a post on X ( archived ). The opening of the post read: Google would not send a Street View car to the Faroe Islands, so in 2016 a Faroese woman strapped a camera to a sheep and mapped the country herself. The grievance was legitimate. Eighteen islands in the North Atlantic, some of the most spectacular road in Europe, causeways and tunnels and single track cut along the edge of a cliff face, and none of it on Street View. Google had been up Mont Blanc. Google had been to Greenland. Google had been above the Arctic Circle in half a dozen countries. The Faroes had about fifty thousand people and a coastline, and they were simply not on the list. Durita Dahl Andreassen worked for the tourist board in Tórshavn. Her reasoning was straightforward and, in its way, unanswerable. There are more sheep on the islands than people. They walk freely. They go everywhere. They have no schedule and no other commitments. So a fellow islander built a harness. Onto it went a 360 degree camera, a mobile phone and a lightweight solar panel to keep the batteries up, the whole rig weighing under a kilo. The camera was set to fire every minute. Five sheep in five locations were fitted out and released to do what they were going to do anyway, which was walk about eating grass on the edge of some of the most photogenic drops in the North Atlantic. The images came back tagged with GPS coordinates, over a mobile signal, from a sheep. Andreassen uploaded them to Google Maps. They called it Sheep View 360. Her job title, for a period, was Sheep View 360 Project Manager, which remains one of the finest lines ever printed on a business card. The one technical hitch, reported by the tourist board with total sincerity, was motivation. The sheep had to be encouraged to go to the interesting bits, which meant somebody standing behind them doing the thing you do to move sheep. The technology worked perfectly. The talent needed direction. The claim also spread on social media websites such as Facebook ( archived ) and Instagram ( archived ). The claim is true. Visit Faroe Islands ( archived ), the island territory's official tourism board, celebrated the 10-year anniversary of its "Sheep View 360" campaign on July 12, 2016. Leading the campaign for Visit Faroe Islands was Durita Andreassen, who explained the project in a video on the Visit Faroe Islands Sheep View 360 webpage . The day Visit Faroe Islands launched the campaign, it released a video showing the sheep walking around with the cameras on their backs. A map from the campaign shows Andreassen's sheep captured images of the Hosvik area. There are three spots near Hosvik on Google Street View in which the Sheep View 360 can still be seen today . The campaign worked. On Aug. 11, 2016, Google announced it had started working with the Faroe Islands to bring Google Street View coverage to the area. Just over a year later, Visit Faroe Islands proudly announced that the territory now had Google Street View coverage . For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about sheep, including a miscaptioned photo that incorrectly asserted sheep went through a fence gate that wasn't there.

title: Judge ruled certain AI-generated child sex abuse material is protected by First Amendment. Here's context
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: A federal judge rule certain AI-generated child sex abuse material is protected by First Amendment. Rating: True About this rating Context In his decision, Judge John Z. Lee of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit, referred to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions from 1969 and 2002. The first says people have the right to keep obscenity in the privacy of their homes and the second says child sex abuse material that does not depict real children is not child pornography and is protected by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. The judge also said that while he is bound by precedent, he is concerned by "the lines these cases draw." In August 2026, a rumor spread that a federal judge ruled certain child sex abuse material generated by artificial intelligence was protected by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which establishes the right to free speech. Several Snopes readers emailed to share an Instagram post relaying the story. "A federal judge has ruled that the First Amendment protects an individual's right to privately possess child sexual abuse content created using Al if it does not depict a real person and remains in the home," the image in the post read. On X, several people amplified the claim, with one calling it "disgusting" ( archived ): In sum, the claim was true, but it lacked crucial context. In his Aug. 25, 2026, decision , Judge John Z. Lee of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit, said precedent forced him to make this ruling, pointing to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions. He added that the current state of technological advance meant the court had "concerns" about the "lines" set by these two Supreme Court decisions. The U.S. Department of Justice declined to comment on whether the agency intends to take the case to the Supreme Court. Law hasn't caught up with AI, judge suggested In 2024, a man named Steven Anderegg was arrested on charges of fabricating, possessing and distributing AI-generated child sex abuse material, as well as sending some of this material to a minor. Anderegg asked for the charges of production and possession to be dismissed, which a federal district court in Wisconsin granted on grounds that these counts ran against decided caselaw. The prosecutors then appealed this decision, but Lee agreed with the lower court, citing two decisions the Supreme Court rendered in 1969 and 2002. The first decision , Stanley v. Georgia, said the First Amendment protects people who privately keep obscenity. "The First Amendment does not allow a state to criminalize the private possession of obscene matter," read the summary of the case on the Justia website, a free online collection of all U.S. Supreme Court decisions. The second decision — Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition — came six years after the Child Pornography Prevention Act of 1996 . It ruled that child sex abuse material that does not depict real children is not child pornography, and that it is protected by the First Amendment. This decision explicitly covered digital images. "T he statute sought to outlaw all speech that was related to the possibility of child pornography, including images of adults who look like children and computer-generated images," the case's Justia page reads. While Lee said he was compelled by judicial precedent to make this ruling, he also expressed "concerns about the lines these cases draw," given how quickly AI technology is evolving. The judge also said that fabricated child sex abuse material that does not depict real persons was becoming more and more difficult to distinguish from such material that showed real children, making law enforcement more difficult. "Recent data suggests that the influx of AI-generated images reported to the NCMEC [National Center for Missing and Exploited Children] CyberTipline imposes increasing burdens on law enforcement," the judge wrote in his decision. A paragraph in Lee's decision summarized his rationale (Page 3 of this document ): We now live in an age where GenAI [generative AI] models can render images depicting the abuse of virtual children that are virtually indistinguishable from those depicting the abuse of actual children. This case illuminates how this evolving technology complicates the lines drawn by the Supreme Court in Stanley , Osborne , and Free Speech Coalition . Indeed, in Free Speech Coalition , the Supreme Court addressed the scope of First Amendment protections for virtual CSAM, but that was nearly twenty-five years ago, and the image-generation technology available today was likely unimaginable back then. Given the relentless advancement in artificial intelligence models, we have some concerns about the lines these cases draw, but we are not free to redraw them ourselves. In other words, Lee said he could not on his own change a precedent set by the Supreme Court. It would therefore fall upon the Supreme Court to change the interpretation of the law to account for current technology and its consequences. For further reading, Snopes examined the claim that 17 Republican Colorado lawmakers voted against banning AI-generated child sex abuse material .

title: Did Disney buy Dollywood? Claim is pure fantasy
label: Rating: Labeled Satire About this rating
text: Claim: Disney bought country singer Dolly Parton’s Dollywood theme park. Rating: Labeled Satire About this rating A rumor ( archived ) that Disney bought Dolly Parton's Dollywood theme park circulated online after the beloved star's death in August 2026. The Mouse Trap News Instagram account shared news of the alleged takeover, writing , "What do you think of Disney taking over Dollywood?!" (@mousetrapnews, accessed via Instagram) The story also appeared on Mouse Trap News' Facebook ( archived ) and TikTok ( archived ) accounts. Commenters across the platforms appeared to question whether the rumor was true. Snopes readers also contacted us to investigate its legitimacy. The rumor about Disney buying Dollywood is not real. Mouse Trap News is a satirical news outlet covering the Disney parks. Profile descriptions on Facebook , Instagram and TikTok described the accounts' output as " 100% Fake." The outlet also posted a written story on its website, which describes its content as " 100% made-up parody and satire stories about Disney Parks." Therefore, we find this claim was labeled satire. Search engines such as DuckDuckGo , Google and Yahoo did not find any credible reporting to suggest Disney had bought Dollywood ( archived , archived , archived ). Because of both Disney and Parton's worldwide fame, reputable sources would have reported on such a takeover, if true. Mouse Trap News shared the rumor on or around Aug. 28, 2026, three days after Parton's death. The video that Mouse Trap News posted on its social media profiles used a combination of footage of Dollywood and Disney parks, as well as unrelated clips from two authentic videos. Some clips came from a video of Parton speaking about the " My Life of Many Colors Museum," which was set to open in the fall of 2026. Other clips came from a video of Dollywood Parks & Resorts President Eugene Naughton speaking about how the park would honor Parton's legacy after her death. Remembering Parton as the park's "dreamer-in-chief," Naughton told viewers: I know a lot of people are concerned that things are going to change without Dolly being present here and I want to assure you that it's not. Just know that we're all going to keep her alive here. For further reading, Snopes has previously debunked stories from Mouse Trap News. For example, in June 2025, we alerted readers to another satirical story about Disney banning MAGA hats . Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective , we use " originated as satire " or " labeled satire " ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

title: Lake Ontario isn't named after Canadian province
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: Lake Ontario was named by Indigenous people, not after the Canadian province of Ontario. Rating: True About this rating In late August 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered that Lake Ontario, the easternmost of the Great Lakes, be renamed "Lake America" in government publications. Trump signed that executive order while he feuded with Canadian leaders over failed trade negotiations. Some people on social media immediately claimed Trump wasn't even targeting a Canadian name in his apparent attempt at retaliation. One X user wrote ( archived ) that Lake Ontario was named by Indigenous tribes hundreds of years ago, and Canada's province of Ontario adopted the name later. People made the same claim on Facebook ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ) and elsewhere on X ( archived ). Preserved maps from early explorers show the name "Ontario" for the lake long before the province was labeled with the same name, which aligns with the lake's and province's histories as described by museums and historians. Therefore, we've rated this claim true. According to the Canadian Encyclopedia , "Ontario" is thought to have come from an Iroquois word meaning "beautiful lake" or "sparkling water." Ontario's provincial government says the Iroquois word is "kanadario." Other sources transliterate the word differently. The National Museum of the Great Lakes , says "Ontario" derived from the Huron (also known as the Wendat, who spoke an Iroquois language) word "Ontarí'io," meaning "great lake" or "beautiful water." Either way, "Ontario" was an indigenous word referring to a body of water, not a piece of land. "Ontario" was first applied to the lake by Europeans in 1641, according to the Canadian Encyclopedia, and appears on maps of North America as early as 1656. The lake's name in the 1650 was in flux, at least for French cartographers exploring the area. Maps from 1653 and 1656 refer to the lake as, translated into English, Lake St. Louis or Lake Ontario. Notably, the 1656 map referred to the lake as Ontario first and Lake St. Louis second. Similarly, a map from 1657 called it Ontario Lake with a mention of the St. Louis name beneath it. None of those maps labeled the land north of the lake, the present-day province of Ontario, as Ontario. In fact, this holds true even in a 1775 French map and a 1777 English map , both of which refer to the lake simply as "Lake Ontario." The province of Ontario came into being in 1867, according to the Canadian Encyclopedia , when Britain's North American colonies joined together to become the Dominion of Canada. Before then, the land that's now Ontario was known as Upper Canada and Canada West . Prior to 1791, it was part of a singular province of Quebec that included both today's Ontario and Quebec. While neither the Canadian Encyclopedia nor Canadian government webpages explicitly state that the province got its name from the lake, it at the very least used the name after the lake had long been called Ontario by the people around its shores. For further reading, we previously investigated a claim that Trump demanded changes to Canada's French-language rules as part of a trade deal.

title: Did Dolly Parton's Imagination Library donate books to children in Israel?
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: Country singer Dolly Parton's Imagination Library donated books to children in Israel. Rating: False About this rating Context The organization PJ Library, which provides free books for Jewish children — including children in Israel – was inspired by Parton's Imagination Library but did not have a formal relationship with it. The Imagination Library operated in the U.S., U.K., Canada, Ireland and Australia. Parton expressed support for PJ Library's efforts in an 2023 interview. Amid news of singer Dolly Parton's death at age 80 in August 2026, many people looked back at her charitable work through the Imagination Library, an organization she founded that has provided millions of free books to children in the U.S. and other countries. An online debate ensued on X about whether Parton had donated books to Israeli children, part of a broader discourse about her alleged views on the state of Israel. Some posts claimed Parton worked with PJ Library ( archived ), an organization that sends free books to Jewish children worldwide, including children in Israel. One X user wrote : "People accusing Dolly of being evil because she MAYBE donated books to some Israeli children?" (X user @K1TKATCLUBS) There is no evidence the Imagination Library has ever operated in Israel. According to its website , the organization operates only in the U.S., U.K., Canada, Ireland and Australia. In 2022, the Library announced it would provide free books each month to 200 refugee children in London until they turn 5. We reached out to the Library for a response to claims about its ties to Israel. Tracy Long, a director with the Dollywood Foundation, which funds Imagination Library, directed us to its website where it states its operations are limited to the U.S., U.K., Canada, Ireland and Australia. PJ Library is a program run by The Harold Grinspoon Foundation, a Jewish philanthropic organization. It operates in Israel through a Hebrew-language counterpart, Sifriyat Pijama, and Arabic-language companion program, Maktabat al-Fanoos. While PJ Library was inspired by Imagination Library, the two organizations were not formal partners. Parton expressed support for PJ Library's work in an interview, but according to a PJ Library spokesperson she did not support it financially. As such, we rate this claim as false. Snopes reached out to PJ Library and the Harold Grinspoon Foundation to ask about the rumor. Spokesperson Mark Gold told Snopes over email that Parton was never formally involved in the group's work (emphasis ours): No, there was never a formal partnership between PJ Library and the Imagination Library, nor did Ms. Parton donate books or funds to PJ Library or PJ Library initiatives in Israel. Mr. Grinspoon was inspired by the Imagination Library, but the PJ Library program was developed independently of the Imagination Library. PJ Library is funded by the Harold Grinspoon Foundation and other partners who contribute directly to the PJ Library program. Sifriyat Pijama in Israel is a program of Keren Grinspoon (the Harold Grinspoon Foundation in Israel) and is funded by that foundation. The ministry of education for the State of Israel is also a partner in Sifriyat Pijama as well as in the related program "Maktabot al Fanoos" that provides free books to Arabic speaking children in Israel. PJ Library also acknowledged that it was inspired by the Imagination Library shortly after Parton died, when the library posted a picture of Parton with Grinspoon on Instagram : PJ Library and the Harold Grinspoon Foundation team are sad to learn of the passing of musician, philanthropist, and American legend Dolly Parton. Dolly's Imagination Library helped inspire Harold Grinspoon to found PJ Library in 2005.⁠ ⁠When Harold had the privilege of chatting with Dolly in 2023, she shared the following with him: "I am honored to get to help inspire a love of reading in children. They truly are our future."⁠ ⁠Parton's 2023 interview with PJ Library is archived here . She expressed support for the library's work, saying: PARTON: Well, I'm always honored when my Imagination Library inspires others, like Harold Grinspoon and PJ Library. That is so very special to me — especially because the Imagination Library comes from a very personal place for me … PJ LIBRARY: We love keeping up with the Imagination Library and its many accomplishments! In 2023, you celebrated the incredible milestone of gifting 200 million books to children. PJ Library is also celebrating: Last year we sent our 50 millionth book, and this year is our 18th birthday. What is most important to you about continuing to do this work? PARTON: First of all, congratulations, PJ Library! I'm thrilled to celebrate milestones with you! Of course, I am very, very proud of how far we've come with the Imagination Library. We were thrilled to celebrate our 100 millionth book in 2018, and here we are just five years later celebrating 200 million books worldwide. Isn't that amazing? Separately, the Grinspoon Foundation sponsors some of the Imagination Library's activities in Massachusetts. Gold told Snopes over email: The Harold Grinspoon Charitable Foundation is still the sponsoring organization for Imagination Library in Springfield and West Springfield Massachusetts. Approximately 675 children in this region receive a monthly mailing to their home of a book at no charge as a gift from the Harold Grinspoon Charitable Foundation as part of the Imagination Library program. In sum, Parton expressed broad support for PJ Library's work, but she did not specifically send books or funds to Israel through her Imagination Library. The Harold Grinspoon Foundation, which runs PJ Library, has separately sponsored branches of The Imagination Library in Massachusetts. Parton often shied away from discussing her political views in public. Snopes has covered numerous rumors and false claims about Parton.

title: CCTV footage shows deadly flood destroying Nepal-China border crossing
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: CCTV footage from Aug. 26, 2026, authentically shows a deadly flood destroying the Gyirong Port, a Nepal-China border crossing. Rating: True About this rating Context Snopes found no evidence the footage was artificially generated or doctored, and reputable news outlets such as The Associated Press also deemed the footage authentic. Drone footage taken in the aftermath confirmed the structure was pulverized. Our search for the exact source of the original CCTV footage remains in progress as of this writing. Editor's note: Some of the videos linked and embedded in this article contain imagery that may be upsetting to readers. As rescuers raced to find survivors of a deadly landslide and flash flood in Nepal on Aug. 26, 2026, that according to CBS News killed almost 600 people and left roughly 2,500 missing as of this report, footage emerged online purportedly showing the moment floodwaters destroyed a Nepal-China border crossing. The clip spread across multiple social media sites, including X , Facebook and Reddit . It showed the flood cascading down a valley as dozens of people attempted to flee, eventually crashing onto the border port — a large gate over the road passage — before obliterating the entire scene as mud flooded the screen. As climate change intensifies , melting glaciers — such as those found in the Himalayas — can cause this scale of catastrophic flooding. Several commenters on one X post ( archived ) that had more than 13 million views claimed the footage was AI-generated, and dozens of Snopes readers searched the site for information related to videos of the flooding. (X user @iNikhilsaini.) As reported by The Associated Press and other reputable news outlets , the clip was authentic CCTV footage.The structure pictured was Tibet's Gyirong Port , a land crossing between Nepal and China that was pulverized in the flooding. Therefore we've rated this claim true. The footage the AP published featured a watermark in the upper right corner for the Annapurna Post, a Nepali news outlet that posted the footage on Aug. 26 ( archived ). It was captioned (translation via DeepL): How terrible was the flood? CCTV footage from the immigration office on the Chinese side of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing. The time shown in the footage is Chinese time. At that time, it was around 9 o'clock in Nepal. Our search for the exact source of the original CCTV footage remains in progress. We contacted the Annapurna Post seeking further information and will update this story if we receive a response. The Annapurna Post's footage showed no evidence of AI generation or digital editing. The border crossing had only recently reopened in January 2026 after flood damage in 2025. Though images of the port before the 2025 flooding appear slightly different from the CCTV footage, an April 2026 image of the structure uploaded by a Flickr user appears the same, indicating the CCTV footage is authentic. If it were AI-generated, it would likely contain visual inconsistencies. (Photos courtesy of the Annapurna Post and Flickr user @findingtodd) As several social media users pointed out, flooding of the severity seen in the CCTV footage likely left little of the structure behind. Post-flood aerial footage captured by Chinese state news agency Xinhua and other images on social media show the valley where the flood swept the structure away is almost devoid of any sign the gate once stood there. The angle of the camera that captured the CCTV footage appears to approximately be at the coordinates 28°16'51.2"N 85°22'40.6"E on Google Maps.

title: USDA recalled 30K pounds of beef from Argentina. Trump's import plan wasn't to blame
label: Rating: Mixture About this rating
text: Claim: The U.S. Department of Agriculture recalled 30,000 pounds of Argentine beef that the administration of President Donald Trump had imported to bring down domestic beef prices. Rating: Mixture About this rating What's True The USDA recalled 29,628 pounds of raw beef products imported from Argentina on Aug. 7, 2026, because the Food Safety and Inspection Service had not reinspected it upon entry to the U.S. What's False The recalled beef was not part of the Trump administration's announced plan to import 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef." An Aug. 26 presidential proclamation said imports under that plan would start on Sept. 1, 2026. In August 2026, a claim ( archived ) circulated online that the U.S. Department of Agriculture recalled 30,000 pounds of Argentine beef that the Trump administration had imported to bring down domestic beef prices. Around a week before claims circulated, on Aug. 21, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump announced ( archived ) on Truth Social that his administration would allow the import of 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef" to lower domestic beef prices. One Threads user who appeared to connect the recalled beef with the Trump administration's import plan wrote : This was predictable, but the Trump administration is now frantically recalling 30,000 lbs. of foreign beef they brought into the country. Here's an idea — maybe we just buy from American ranchers for a while. View on Threads Similar claims also circulated on Facebook ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ), X ( archived ), Bluesky ( archived ) and Reddit ( archived ). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim. The claim was a mixture of true and false elements. It was true that the USDA recalled approximately 29,628 pounds of raw beef products imported from Argentina on Aug. 7, 2026. The department said the imported product had not been reinspected when it entered the U.S., meaning the Food Safety and Inspection Service could not ensure it met U.S. safety standards. However, the beef the USDA recalled was not part of the Trump administration's plan to import 300,000 metric tons of "product for ground beef." According to an Aug. 26 presidential proclamation , the Trump administration would start those planned beef imports on Sept. 1, 2026. The recall According to the USDA's recall, a Florida-based company called Corte Argentino USA LLC had imported the Argentine beef products, which were produced between May 15, 2026, and May 20, 2026, and carried use-by or freeze-by dates between Sept. 15, 2026, and Sept. 20, 2026. The USDA listed the following products for recall: Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Top Sirloin Butt" ("Cuadril Sin Tapa") Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Eye Round" ("Peceto") Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Topside Cap Off" ("Nalga AD S/Tapa") Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Flat" ("Carnaza Cuadrada") Various weight cardboard boxes containing "FrigorIfico Gorina SAIC" boneless beef "Knuckle" ("Bola de Lomo") The FSIS recalled the beef because it had not been " reinspected " upon entry to the United States. Imported meat must pass this inspection before it can be sold in the U.S. The reinspection process allows the FSIS to check that products are " safe, wholesome, and accurately labeled" according to domestic standards. Speculation swirls about Trump beef import plan Trump signed a proclamation about the import plan on Aug. 26 that said the additional imports would take place in three 30-day windows, starting on Sept. 1. Neither the proclamation nor members of the Trump administration had confirmed where the imported beef would come from at the time of this writing. On Aug. 25, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, whose department would inspect the incoming beef under the new plan, told (video time code 07:19) reporters at the White House she was "not privy" to discuss where the imported beef came from. Despite, or perhaps because of the lack of information about the plan, online speculation swirled that Trump would import Argentine beef that China had rejected because it found an antibiotic in a shipment of meat that was banned in both countries. Snopes' reporting found that China did suspend imports of beef from a single facility owned by the Argentine meatpacker ArreBeef after inspection found one shipment from the facility contained the antibiotic chloramphenicol . The beef that the USDA recalled on Aug. 7, 2026, did not come from this supplier. For further reading, Snopes previously investigated a rumor that the Trump administration's imported beef would come from slaughtered wild horses. Snopes reporter Emery Winter contributed to this report.

title: Did Ron Howard write letter about being liberal? Here's the truth
label: Rating: Incorrect Attribution About this rating
text: Claim: Director Ron Howard authored a letter starting, "I'm a liberal, but that doesn't mean what a lot of you apparently think it does." Rating: Incorrect Attribution About this rating In summer 2026, an old claim that director Ron Howard wrote an open letter about what it supposedly means to be a liberal resurfaced. The letter, which is around 1,300 words, began as follows: I'm a liberal, but that doesn't mean what a lot of you apparently think it does. Let's break it down, shall we? Because quite frankly, I'm getting a little tired of being told what I believe and what I stand for. Spoiler alert: not every liberal is the same, though the majority of liberals I know think along roughly these same lines: The remainder of the letter consists of 16 numbered points describing the author's beliefs. In August 2026, the claim appeared in multiple posts on Facebook and numerous Snopes readers searched our site for information about it. (Facebook user Christina Tann) As we reported when we first looked into the text's origins in 2020, Howard was not the real author of the letter. Instead, the words were the work of novelist Lori Gallagher Witt . As a result, we rated the letter as misattributed. Witt first posted the letter on her Facebook ( archived ) and Tumblr ( archived ) accounts on Jan. 7, 2018. A screenshot of her original Facebook post is below. (Due to the letter's length, we split the screenshot into two roughly equal halves that appear side by side.) (Lori Gallagher Witt) Witt's original letter included a longer introduction than the version that circulated in 2025. The original version opened as follows: An open letter to friends and family who are/were shocked to discover I'm a liberal… This is going to be VERY long, so: TL;DR: I'm a liberal, I've always been a liberal, but that doesn't mean what a lot of you apparently think it does. Some of you suspected. Some of you were shocked. Many of you have known me for years, even the majority of my life. We either steadfastly avoided political topics, or I carefully steered conversations away from the more incendiary subjects in the name of keeping the peace. "I'm a liberal" isn't really something you broadcast in social circles where "the liberals" can't be said without wrinkling one's nose. But then the 2016 election happened, and staying quiet wasn't an option anymore. Since then, I've received no shortage of emails and comments from people who were shocked, horrified, disappointed, disgusted, or otherwise displeased to realize I am *wrinkles nose* a liberal. Yep. I'm one of those bleeding heart commies who hates anyone who's white, straight, or conservative, and who wants the government to dictate everything you do while taking your money and giving it to people who don't work. Or am I? Let's break it down, shall we? Because quite frankly, I'm getting a little tired of being told what I believe and what I stand for. Spoiler alert: Not every liberal is the same, though the majority of liberals I know think along roughly these same lines. The Facebook post's edit history showed that on Feb. 2, 2018, around a month after she originally published the letter, Witt added a notice reading "(c) 2018 Lori Gallagher Witt. Feel free to share, but please give me credit, and if you add or change anything, please note accordingly." A similar notice also appeared at the bottom of her Tumblr post. In an email to Snopes in February 2025, Witt said she was inspired to write the letter not because of a single event but because she believed her social circle did not understand her beliefs. She said: It had been brewing in my head for a while, especially because I have/had a lot of conservative friends and relatives who would often parrot things about "those liberals." There was a lot of comments about how we "hate America," we're communists, we want to destroy everything, etc. It was this really vile and disingenuous picture of who and what we are, and I felt the need to set the record straight. I genuinely had no idea it would resonate with that many people or that it would go viral. How the misattribution spread The letter's misattribution to Howard began in 2020, when, as Witt explained in a Facebook post , someone named Ron Howard — no relation to the director — shared her post without attribution. That person eventually corrected his post to note Witt as the text's author after she reached out to him. But by that point, other internet users had already begun sharing the letter with the name "Ron Howard" attached. Since then, Witt has posted numerous times about her frustration with the persistence of the misattribution, which she has dubbed "the Howarding." In 2025, Witt posted a photo of Howard holding a poster with images of social media posts containing the letter and a line reading "I didn't write this" with a checkmark and Howard's signature next to it. Witt said over email that the photo was from Howard's April 2025 appearance at Pittsburgh's Steel City Con, and that her husband had brought the poster for Howard to sign and pose with. As of this writing, readers have shared Witt's original 2018 Facebook post around 30,000 times. By contrast, a Feb. 9, 2025, post that incorrectly attributed the words to Howard amassed more than 100,000 shares — more than three times as many as Witt's original post — in just a few days. Witt said although Howard was by far the person she's most frequently seen miscredited with the letter's authorship, she's experienced other people attempting to take credit for — and even make money off — her words in the past. "I could live with a post going viral and getting separated from my name, but I draw the line when people try to monetize it or otherwise use it to elevate themselves," she said. Witt also said she believed a connection between Howard and U.S. Vice President JD Vance may have spurred renewed interest in the misattributed letter. In 2020, Howard directed and produced the film adaptation of "Hillbilly Elegy," Vance's 2016 memoir . We've previously looked into other claims involving Howard. They included a rumor that a clip from the television show "Arrested Development" in which he appeared was proof the 1969 moon landing was fake.

title: Video claiming to show McConnell barely moving for 20 hours on Senate floor is heavily edited
label: Rating: Mostly False About this rating
text: Claim: A time-lapse video authentically shows Sen. Mitch McConnell sitting in the U.S. Senate chamber, barely moving, for 20 hours straight. Rating: Mostly False About this rating What's True Video provided by C-SPAN shows McConnell attended the 19-hour, 45-minute session and remained seated continuously for stretches as long as six hours. Periodically over the first few hours of the session, he can be seen standing up, moving around and walking in and out of the chamber, albeit leaning on desks for support. During the session, he was visibly slow and weak. At the end, an aide helped him out of the chamber. What's False It's false that time-lapse video authentically shows McConnell sat on the floor of the Senate, barely moving, for 20 hours straight. As U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., remained absent from the Senate floor due to his health issues in August 2026, a video taken June 4, when he was still able to attend, purportedly showed him remaining seated, nearly motionless, throughout a 20-hour Senate voting session. According to several posts on X and Reddit , the footage was condensed into a time-lapse video of the entire 20-hour session. A post on Instagram claimed McConnell was in a wheelchair. A post on X claimed he was "in the Senate for nearly 20 hours and barely moved." The full 19 hours and 45 minutes of C-SPAN footage recorded that day proves otherwise. It also proves that the time-lapse video was heavily edited and only covered select parts of the session. McConnell didn't sit near-motionless on the Senate floor for 20 hours. The C-SPAN video shows he walked in and out of the chamber several times on his own, though he was visibly weak and leaning on desks. He also sat for brief periods during the early part of the session. McConnell only remained continuously seated for around six hours toward the end of the session, after which he was escorted out by an aide. As such, we rate this claim as mostly false. Photographs on image repository site Getty Images show McConnell standing but being physically supported by aides on the day of the session. Contrary to some social media posts, he wasn't in a wheelchair that day but was often photographed in a wheelchair in prior months. Ten days after this session, McConnell was hospitalized after he reportedly fell in his home. Snopes received several health updates from the senator's office in the subsequent weeks. As of this writing, McConnell has still not returned to the Senate and is recovering at home. For further reading, Snopes has kept track of McConnell's health based on public information and debunked numerous false claims of his death.

title: Did Costco pull Callaway golf products due to ad backlash?
label: Rating: Mixture About this rating
text: Previous Article Next Article Article 1 of 21 in Collection Claim: In August 2026, Costco removed Callaway golf products from its inventory online and in stores because of backlash over advertisement released by Callaway partner Good Good Golf that featured a man shoving a woman to the ground. Rating: Mixture About this rating What's True Google searches for Callaway products on Costco's website resulted in dead links, and searching Costco's website directly also displayed no Callaway products, suggesting that the products had been unlisted. What's Undetermined Snopes was unable to confirm whether Callaway products were also taken off the shelves at Costco warehouses. Furthermore, there was no public information available from Costco explaining why Callaway products had been delisted, meaning it's possible that Callaway products would be put back on the shelves. On Aug. 21, 2026, Good Good Golf , a golfing YouTube channel that runs a golf apparel store of the same name, shared a new advertisement for a driver produced by the golf manufacturing giant Callaway. The advertisement shows a woman — former NCAA golfer and Good Good partner Alexis Mietkowski — reaching for a golf club before a man — Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark — runs over and pushes her to the ground. "Do not touch my new driver," he says in a menacing voice while standing over her. The advertisement sparked immediate backlash online and was quickly deleted. Good Good Golf and Callaway both issued apologies in the following days. Claims quickly appeared online that the warehouse chain Costco had pulled all Callaway products from its stores and website in response to the advertisement. Some versions of the claim also suggested that Costco refused to stock meat U.S. President Donald Trump imported from Argentina . Snopes readers searched the site looking for more information about the claim. We contacted Costco, Callaway and Good Good Golf as part of researching this story, but had not heard back from any of them. We rate the claim a mixture of true and unproven information. Searching Google for Callaway products available at Costco returned dozens of results that all led to pages that said "product not found" on the retailer's website, suggesting that Costco had recently unlisted the products. Meanwhile, a similar search directly on Costco's website showed several golf products, but none from Callaway. Therefore, we concluded that Costco had unlisted Callaway products. A Google search for Callaway products listed on Costco's website returned dozens of results, all of which led to pages saying "product not found." However, Costco did not release any information explaining why Callaway products had been removed from its website, and whether the change was permanent. Similarly, we weren't able to confirm that Callaway products had been removed from shelves in Costco stores across the country (for instance, one post on the r/golf subreddit claimed Callaway clubs weren't on shelves in Cincinnati, Ohio, while commenters said in replies that Callaway clubs were still available at their local stores). ESPN reported on Aug. 26 that Dick's Sporting Goods and its subsidiary Golf Galaxy would pull Good Good Golf products — not Callaway products — from its stores. According to The Athletic , the brand also reportedly lost a reality TV show on the Golf Channel. Meanwhile, Callaway announced on Aug. 27 that it had officially severed ties with Good Good Golf because of the advertisement, and the PGA said it would remove Good Good's name from an upcoming event in Austin, Texas, where it was set to be the title sponsor.
