For instance, one Instagram post ( archived ) read: Apparently, lemons aren't naturally occurring Lemons are a hybrid fruit created by crossbreeding a bitter orange and a citron, meaning the fruit we know today was cultivated through centuries of selective breeding rather than existing as a naturally occurring wild species (Instagram user @davidattenborough_fandom) For years , the claim spread across various platforms including Instagram , Reddit , Facebook , Threads , X and TikTok . In short, as we found when we looked into the topic in 2024, the claim that lemons are not "naturally occurring" because they are a manmade hybrid is false. Lemons are indeed hybrids of citron and sour orange, but there is no evidence humans deliberately crossbred those species to create the first lemon. Researchers told Snopes the hybridization most likely occurred naturally thousands of years ago, potentially through insect pollination. Humans later selected and propagated lemon trees through horticultural techniques such as grafting and cuttings . Where did lemons come from? Citrus fruits have a complicated history. As National Geographic explained in a 2017 article ( archived ), citrus species can easily mutate and cross with each other, which allowed their genes to mix naturally over thousands of years, and later through human breeding. A 2016 study titled "Phylogenetic origin of limes and lemons revealed by cytoplasmic and nuclear markers" noted that the origins of "most lemons and limes" remained "controversial or unknown." However, a 2018 study published in the scientific journal Nature confirmed lemons originated as a hybrid of citron and sour orange (see image below). (www.nature.com) A later 2023 study sequencing the lemon genome reached the same conclusion. Patrick Ollitrault , a citrus genetics researcher at the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development, told us via email that phylogenomic research shows lemons resulted from sexual hybridization between citron and sour orange. Did humans create lemons? Ollitrault said the hybridization of sour orange and citron, that created lemons, happened naturally, and not through human breeding, as social media users suggested. For example, a bee could have carried pollen from a citron flower to a sour orange flower, causing the two species to cross. After the hybrid appeared, humans selected lemons for their desirable characteristics and propagated them using methods such as grafting and cuttings . He added that many modern citrus fruits ultimately descend from four ancestral species: citron ( Citrus medica ), mandarin ( C. reticulata ), pummelo ( C. maxima ), and a wild Philippine species ( C. micrantha ). In a follow-up email, he said social media posts claiming lemons do not occur naturally are false. Professor Emeritus Mikeal L. Roose , a specialist in citrus genetics, genomics and breeding at the University of California, Riverside, added some more context via email. Roose told us that lemons could have originated through natural hybridization, but the exact circumstances are not known because this happened a very long time — probably at least 2,000 years — ago. This timeline is also supported by archaeological evidence. A 2017 study on the spread of citrus found that the earliest known remains of lemon were discovered in Rome's Forum Romanum and dated to the late first century B.C. or early first century A.D. Roose said humans may still have played an indirect role. The parent varieties of lemon may have originally grown in different areas, but early humans carried the fruits with them during migrations. This may have brought the plants closer to each other and made natural hybridization possible, likely with the help of bees. Therefore, humans may have helped bring the parent varieties into contact, but there is no evidence they were deliberately crossbreeding citron and sour orange to create lemons. Fred Gmitter , a professor of horticultural sciences at the University of Florida's Citrus Research and Education Center who specializes in citrus breeding, genetics and genomics, similarly told Snopes there was no evidence that deliberate human breeding produced the first lemon. According to Gmitter, the most likely explanation is that a "natural hybridization event that took place several thousand years ago" produced the first lemon tree. He said "true lemons we know today," including Eureka, Lisbon and Femminello, later appeared through chance mutations from the "ancestral first lemon." Human role in the lemon's history Although there is no evidence humans created the first lemon, they later played an important role in finding, selecting and propagating lemons. Gmitter explained that lemons can clone themselves through seeds, meaning they can produce genetically identical trees. Therefore, the first lemon tree could have produced many genetically identical descendants as its seeds spread naturally. Early humans therefore did not necessarily have to find one single, rare lemon tree and may have come across groups of very similar or identical lemon trees. "Naturally occurring hybridization, not involving deliberate human activity, is how these forms originated," Gmitter told us, explaining that human involvement came later, when people encountered naturally occurring lemons and began making use of them. As he summarized, "life really did give us lemons" — but through naturally occurring hybridization rather than deliberate breeding by humans. For further reading, in April 2011 we investigated whether lemons "kill cancer cells" and are "10,000 times stronger than chemotherapy." Moreover, in March 2020, we debunked a false rumor that hot water with lemons would cure or prevent COVID-19. Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

title: Did Trump demand sails on US Navy ships and consider adding cannons? Here's the truth
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: U.S. President Donald Trump demanded to equip all Navy ships with sails and considered adding cannons. Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating In August 2026, people shared a rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump demanded to equip all Navy ships with sails and considered adding cannons. For example, on Aug. 16, an X user posted ( archived ) a graphic showing a very large ship with masts and sails. The image displayed the word "Live" and a "Breaking News" chyron. The image lacked a news media outlet name, reading, "Trump Demands All Navy Ships Equipped With Sails, Cannons Also Being Considered." The user added a bit of apparent humor in their post, writing, "And Wood Burning Stoves!" (@JamesTate121 accessed via X) The story spread in the days after Trump, in an Aug. 13 presidential memorandum, ordered the Navy to return to an older system of aircraft carriers using steam catapults for launching fighter jets. Other users shared the same graphic on Facebook ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ) and X ( archived ). To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as Bing , DuckDuckGo and Google . If Trump truly had publicly demanded or considered adding sails and cannons, journalists with reputable news media outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting about Trump talking about sails and cannons. We concluded this claim originated as satire after taking into account the false and comedic nature of the rumor, the "Breaking News" image graphic's inauthenticity and lack of a news media outlet affiliation, and the fact that a Facebook user mentioned later in this story who may have posted the earliest available record of the image graphic also previously published false or humorous content . Researching the rumor In an attempt to find the original source, we performed a reverse image search , a type of search that seeks to find other websites where the same image has appeared online. To do that, we visited the Google Images website, clicked on the camera icon on the right side of the search bar and uploaded the image. That upload and search found the aforementioned social media post examples, as well as the apparent ship illustration source , but did not locate the image graphic's source. Text searches on social media platforms for "Trump Demands All Navy Ships Equipped With Sails," both with and without quotation marks, also failed to locate a source. We then attempted more reverse image searches, using Google Images' tool to crop the search area to only look at small parts of the image graphic, as opposed to selecting the entire image. One of those searches found what could have been the earliest post featuring the image. Facebook user and group admin Joe Kleinschmidt shared ( archived ) the image in his Anti-QAnon Memes group just before midnight Pacific time Aug. 15. (Joe Kleinschmidt accessed via Facebook) We reached out to Kleinschmidt and another group admin on Messenger to confirm whether he created the graphic and ask for information about the generator or tool used to make it. After attempting to join the group, we received a general message declining the join request, reading, "that's not a generator - that's photoshop work - look up 'Meme War Veteran' on facebook to know where it came from." We will update this article if Kleinschmidt provides further details. We emailed Facebook's The Meme War Veteran to inquire whether the user created the image graphic and "Breaking News" template. The user, displaying a bio about parody and satire, has shared other posts using the same template. The user confirmed creating a similar-looking template but denied involvement in making the image about Trump, sails and cannons. The image did not appear on that user's page. For further reading, we previously reported the facts about a rumor claiming Trump posted on Truth Social, "Only suckers and losers would enlist, go to sea on an aircraft carrier, and then complain and send their family nasty notes about our military. They weren't at sea long enough."

title: Real shirt that confuses Flock cameras, other surveillance tech hasn't been sold for years
label: Rating: Mixture About this rating
text: Claim: A fashion designer is creating shirts made to confuse automated license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, in mid-2026. Rating: Mixture About this rating What's True It is true that in 2019, digital security expert and novelty fabric designer Kate Bertash launched a line of shirts and sweaters named Adversarial Fashion. The garments, which displayed many fake license plates, were designed to confuse surveillance camera systems by overloading them with "junk data." However … What's False … the sale of these clothes ended in 2023. As of this writing, he website suggested the clothing would be re-released, though it did not indicate when this would happen. In August 2026, a rumor spread that a fashion designer was creating shirts designed to confuse automated license plate readers, such as Flock cameras. Several posts on social media shared the claim, including on Facebook , Instagram and X . One post on X said a designer and "cybersecurity professional" named Kate Rose had created the shirts ( archived ): The posts all included an image of a man in a covered parking lot with his back to the camera. He wore a black shirt with fake license plate numbers and letters, some of which were framed in purple rectangles. Words in yellow at the bottom of the image read "A fashion designer is feeding Flock cameras junk data using clothes covered in fake plates." In short, it was true that a designer and digital security expert named Kate Bertash had created these clothes as part of a line named Adversarial Fashion, which she first presented in 2019. However, the website said they had not been for sale since 2023, though it said to "stay tuned for re-release" without providing a date. For this reason, we rated the claim a mixture of true and false information. We reached out to Bertash to ask if and when the line would go back on sale. We will update this report should she respond. Bertash first presented the line at the DEF CON27 hacking conference in 2019. In a session posted on YouTube , she said she "to help organizations that do social good work to get the kind of technology and security resources that they need day to day" (at 0:36): Bertash added that she also liked to design and sell "novelty fabrics," in part for children. The session was dedicated in part to teaching viewers to create and print novelty fabrics to counter mass surveillance systems. After outlining some of the surveillance systems to counter (including facial recognition, thermal cameras and automated license plate readers), Bertash presented examples, including blankets designed to block the heat signature recognizable on thermal cameras, or makeup designed to confound facial recognition systems. At the 11:58 mark in the video, Bertash presented some of her ideas to counter ALPRs, including the shirt in the photo that was widely shared in August 2026, as well as a dress. The slide included a website address, AdversarialFashion.com. Bertash then shared a video from an ALPR camera as it attempted to register some of the fake license plates on the shirt and the dress. The website showed that the clothing line had received wide media coverage between 2019 and 2021, including from Vice , The New Yorker and The Financial Times, but that it had not been on sale since 2023. " Stay tuned for a re-release!" the page read. For further reading, Snopes has examined several claims about Flock cameras, including the rumor that a Texas sheriff's deputy had used data from 83,000 Flock cameras to try to find a woman who had an abortion.

title: Trump said he 'probably' wouldn't have rescued 10-year-old from drowning
label: Rating: Correct Attribution About this rating
text: Claim: In August 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump said of 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai's ocean rescue, "I don't know if I'd do it. I wouldn't, probably." Rating: Correct Attribution About this rating Context Some users misrepresented Trump's remarks by claiming the president said he would have outright refused to rescue Rai. That was not the case. Trump also told Rai he was "lucky" the president was not on shift as a lifeguard during the rescue. It was unclear exactly what Trump meant by his remarks. In August 2026, a claim ( archived ) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump said of 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai's ocean rescue , "I don't know if I'd do it. I wouldn't, probably." Trump allegedly made the remark while hosting Rai and Ryder Williams, the 16-year-old lifeguard who rescued Rai, at the White House on Aug. 17, 2026. The Facebook page Occupy Democrats, which shared Trump's alleged statement, wrote : This afternoon, at the White House, Trump hosted a life guard, 16-year-old lifeguard, who saved 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai, looking to get a little good PR with a feel-good event to honor a real hero. Of course, he then immediately ruined it by telling the kid he wouldn't have saved him. "I don't know if I'd do it," the president said. "I wouldn't, probably. You're lucky I wasn't on the service that day." Claims about Trump's purported remarks also circulated on Instagram ( archived ), Bluesky ( archived ) and Reddit ( archived ). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim. Trump made the above statement. As such, we've rated this claim as correctly attributed, with an important caveat: some users ( archived , archived ) misrepresented Trump's remarks by claiming he told Rai that he would have outright refused to rescue him. That was not the case. According to a recorded livestream of the interaction between Trump, Williams and Rai, Trump said of Williams, discussing the rescue (time code 7:40), "He's a real hero. You know, when you see that — I don't know if I'd do it. I wouldn't, probably." Trump appeared to direct this comment to people in the audience rather than Rai himself. Several people in the room laughed. Trump then turned to Rai and continued, "You're lucky I wasn't on the service that day." When viewed in their full context, Trump's remarks show he appeared to consider the idea of carrying out such a rescue, concluding that he "probably" would not have rather than outright refusing the idea. Trump also told Rai he was "lucky" the president was not on shift as a lifeguard the day he needed rescue. This suggests the president may believe he would either be unwilling or unable to carry out the rescue. It was unclear exactly what Trump meant by his remarks or whether he meant them as a joke. We contacted the White House to ask for context about Trump's comments and await a reply. According to The Associated Press , Rai had been in the water at Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz, California, on July 25, 2026, when he lost his footing in the waves. Williams told California Parks in an interview after the rescue that he had seen Rai fall and ran to him, but was unable to recover the child alone due to strong waves. Williams said: After the first wave, I was unable to pull him out because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard. There were two to three more waves before lifeguard Aaron Bohnen entered the water to help me. Bystanders jumped in to try to help, and I yelled at them all to get back to shore. Footage from the rescue showed Bohnen helping Williams bring Rai back to shore. Rai later told The Associated Press he did not remember the rescue because he lost consciousness. Rai's father, Sumit Rai, said his son had been "two seconds" away from death and that another wave could have swept him further out to sea. Trump's son, Eric Trump, shared the viral video of Williams and Bohnen rescuing Rai on X on July 27 and wrote ( archived ), "Give this 16-year-old lifeguard the highest civilian honor. This is truly the best of America! Well done!" Williams told media at the White House on Aug. 17, "In those dangerous moments that we have, we always try to fall back on our training. We are trained so well by many to handle that situation as best we can." For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump said " grass is like human beings" or that part of the late Senator Lindsey Graham's body "literally blew up."

title: Unraveling claim Hakeem Jeffries took $300K from healthcare PACs before opposing Medicare for All
label: Rating: Mixture About this rating
text: Claim: Hakeem Jeffries took more than $300,000 of PAC money from healthcare companies during the 2026 midterm election cycle before coming out against Medicare for All. Rating: Mixture About this rating What's True Jeffries received more than $300,000 from PACs in the healthcare industry, some of which are connected to insurance companies. Jeffries also said during an August 2026 interview that he does not currently support Medicare for All legislation. What's False Contrary to the claim's implication, many of the organizations tied to healthcare PACs that provided funding to Jeffries either support Medicare for All — or some form of universal healthcare — or haven't publicly declared a stance against it. In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, social media users spread a rumor about the influence of the healthcare industry on U.S. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. According to the claim — which circulated on Facebook and Threads — Jeffries allegedly took more than $300,000 in PAC money from healthcare companies during the 2025-26 election cycle before saying he would not support Medicare for All, or a national health insurance program for all Americans. Here's how one Facebook post ( archived ) framed the claim: It's no surprise Hakeem Jeffries came out against Medicare for All. Jeffries took over $300,000 in PAC money from healthcare companies this cycle alone — and he wasn't even facing a primary challenger. Jeffries did, in fact, say that as of August 2026, he does not support current Medicare for All legislation, despite co-sponsoring similar proposals from 2014 to 2021 as a rank-and-file member. Jeffries stopped sponsoring Medicare for All proposals after House Democrats elected him as their leader in November 2022 . Furthermore, donations to Jeffries from the 2025-2026 midterms cycle did include over $300,000 in PAC money tied to the healthcare industry. However, not all of the healthcare PACs that supported Jeffries are against Medicare for All, as the claim implies. These PACs represent a wide range of interests , including health insurance companies, hospitals, nursing homes, healthcare professionals and research companies. Thus, we have rated this claim a mixture of truth and falsehood. A spokesperson for Jeffries, Justin Chermol, called the idea that Jeffries took money to change his position on Medicare for All a "misguided conspiracy theory" that is "blatantly false." "Leader Hakeem Jeffries serves a House Democratic Caucus of 215 members that is racially, ideologically and geographically diverse," Chermol said in a direct message . "He does not sponsor or endorse major pieces of legislation until there is broad consensus, consistent with the past practices of his predecessors who served as Speaker or Leader." (As of this writing, 114 of 212 House Democrats, or about 54%, have co-sponsored Medicare for All legislation for the 2025-26 legislative session.) Chermol's message also said the Democratic Caucus has a "shared goal of universal healthcare" and that House Democrats are committed to expanding healthcare access through existing programs. Jeffries doesn't support Medicare for All legislation Jeffries' comments about Medicare for All came from a filmed "Meet the Press" interview with NBC journalist Kristen Welker on August 16, 2026. A clip of the full exchange is available on NBC's YouTube page. At 1:39 , Jeffries states his position: Reporter: Just to be very clear though, as a Democratic leader in the House, would you vote for or against Medicare for All? Jeffries: I think as you've indicated in your question to me, it's not legislation that I currently am co-sponsoring or that I support. But we do support the notion that we've got to find a path forward to fix our broken healthcare system and make healthcare affordable for every single American. It is worth noting that "Medicare for All," as a concept, represents many different proposals for a national health insurance program. Jeffries' team did not directly respond on the record to an inquiry about whether he might support alternative versions of the Medicare for All proposal that are not currently being discussed in Congress. OpenSecrets data on PAC donations misrepresented The rumor about the amount of money Jeffries took from healthcare PACs appeared to originate with Notice News, which bills itself as a progressive independent news outlet. Notice News' reporting misrepresented data shared on OpenSecrets, a credible source that uses Federal Election Commission data to track campaign finance and lobbying. We reached out to Notice News to ask for more information about the outlet's reporting process and will update this story if we hear back. In a video posted by Notice News that spread the claim, the news outlet points to a screenshot of Jeffries' OpenSecrets page as its source for the PAC donation information. It appears that Notice News shared an accurate screenshot of a chart on Jeffries' OpenSecrets page under "Industries," which showed that Jeffries received about $321,250 from health-related PACs, which are labeled "Health." The chart shows PAC contributions by sector and industry: (OpenSecrets) However, a closer look of the "Health" data on the "PACs" page indicated that these organizations represent a wide range of interests with varying views on and interest in Medicare for All. Only $52,500 of the $321,520 came from "HMOs," or "Health Maintenance Organizations," which provide a certain kind of private health insurance plan. That category includes companies like UnitedHealth Group, which oversees UnitedHealthcare. (Private health insurance companies represent the obvious opposition to a Medicare for All proposal, given that they would largely be replaced if the United States moved to a national health insurance system.) (OpenSecrets, illustrated by Snopes) Meanwhile, the American College of Physicians Services, which contributed $7,500 to Jeffries, is the advocacy arm of the American College of Physicians, which supports Medicare for All. In contrast, the American Hospital Association's PAC, which contributed $10,000 to Jeffries, opposes Medicare for All. Several of the PACs represent organizations that support universal healthcare but don't have specific positions on Medicare for All, such as the American Academy of Family Physicians and the American College of Nurse-Midwives . Other PACs listed under "Health," like the American Seniors Housing Association , are more focused on other parts of the health industry, like Alzheimer's research or workforce shortages. It's also worth noting the "Health" category that Notice News used to back up its claim does not even include most PACs representing private health insurance. Health insurance companies that are not HMOs are included under the " Insurance " category, instead. Per OpenSecrets' Insurance category for Jeffries, the House minority leader received $37,000 from non-HMO health and accident insurance companies' PACs like Blue Cross Blue Shield. That means that as of this writing, according to OpenSecrets, Jeffries has received $89,000 from private health and accident insurance companies during the 2025-26 midterm cycle. OpenSecrets also categorizes some contributions under "Ideology/Single-Issue," which includes a section for "Health & welfare policy." Jeffries received an additional $15,000 in PAC contributions under the Health & welfare policy section. It was unclear, however, whether any of those contributors held a strong position for or against Medicare for All. The bottom line There's no evidence that Jeffries changed his position on Medicare for All in 2026 as a result of funding from the healthcare industry. Jeffries has not co-sponsored or actively supported Medicare for All legislation since House Democrats elected him to lead their caucus. Furthermore, social media posts stating that Jeffries received over $300,000 from the healthcare industry don't accurately represent how much money Jeffries has actually taken from PACs related to healthcare, nor do they accurately represent how much money Jeffries has taken from entities that oppose Medicare for All.

title: Posts claim Eric Clapton brought deaf teen onstage in 1992. Tune out the noise
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Previous Article Next Article Article 1 of 15 in Collection Claim: In September 1992, musician Eric Clapton invited 16-year-old Sarah Mitchell, who was deaf, onstage at a concert in Birmingham, England, and performed for her. Rating: False About this rating In August 2026, a story recirculated on social media claiming musician Eric Clapton once stopped a concert to bring a deaf teenager onstage. One Facebook post spreading the story started: Eric Clapton was lost in a guitar solo when something in the front row broke through his concentration. Twelve thousand people were standing, shouting, moving with the music. And right in the center of it all, a teenage girl sat completely still. September 23, 1992. The National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham, England. Clapton was in the middle of his Journeyman tour, playing to a packed arena. He had already powered through "Bad Love," "Pretending," and "Before You Accuse Me." The crowd was electric. But in the third row, center section, one person wasn't reacting at all. Her name was Sarah Mitchell. She was sixteen years old. And she had been profoundly deaf since birth. (Facebook user Amila K Madige) The posts further claimed that during a show in Birmingham, England, on Sept. 23, 1992, Clapton stopped midsong and brought a "profoundly deaf" 16-year-old named Sarah Mitchell onto the stage. Clapton supposedly positioned an amplifier behind her chair so she could feel the music's vibrations and then played a song for her as the arena fell silent. Over the months , the story spread on numerous social media platforms, including X , LinkedIn and YouTube . Some posts featured links leading to articles on advertisement-filled websites. Snopes readers also searched our website for information about whether the claim was true. However, the story about Clapton amounted to fiction. Searches of Bing , DuckDuckGo , and Yahoo found no credible media outlets reporting about such an event, and several key details in the story conflicted with well-documented information about Clapton's tours and Birmingham performances in 1992. The fabricated story resembled glurge , which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." It was one of hundreds of similarly fake stories about celebrities on Facebook that aim to generate views and advertising revenue via websites linked in posts. Timeline doesn't match tour records The story placed the alleged moment on Sept. 23, 1992, at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham. However, Clapton's official timeline shows the Journeyman World Tour opened at the NEC on Jan. 14, 1990 — not September 1992 — and ran for three consecutive nights. Fan-compiled tour listings corroborated the dates and location. Moreover, the posts framed the alleged moment as part of Clapton's Journeyman tour, which ended in March 1991 and did not extend into September 1992. Clapton did play in Birmingham in early February 1992 , but those shows were at the National Indoor Arena, not the NEC. He later returned to the NEC for a series of benefit concerts in October 1992 — dates that don't match the rumored Sept. 23 appearance. The story also isn't mentioned in " Eric Clapton: The Autobiography ," first published in the United Kingdom in 2007. Because the book covers key moments from Clapton's career and touring life, the encounter described in the social media posts would likely have been included if it had actually happened. AI-generated content helped spread story The claim frequently circulated alongside an image showing Clapton with a teenage girl that appeared to have been generated using artificial intelligence. Hive Moderation , an online AI detector, determined that the image was highly likely to be AI-generated. (Facebook user Dena Wells) In August 2026, a nearly-identical image spread with the story, but this time with a black-and-white filter and a "Curiously Unusual Wonders" watermark : (Facebook user Amila K Madige) Similarly, most of the accompanying text was likely AI-generated, according to the AI detector ZeroGPT . ( Research shows AI-detection software is imperfect. Readers should consider the tools' results with skepticism.) (ZeroGPT) The text's tone, structure and emotional language further pointed to AI authorship. Finally, the story appears to have originated from a YouTube channel presenting itself as a source of "true stories About Eric Clapton that will restore your faith in humanity," but the video provided no verifiable evidence of the event. The channel's other content follows the same clickbait pattern, with sensational, vague titles and attention-grabbing thumbnails designed to generate clicks. Many of the thumbnails also appear to be AI-generated or heavily manipulated, which is consistent with a channel producing content that's primarily focused on generating views: (YouTube channel @EricClaptonTheUntoldLegacy) The false rumor about Clapton fits a familiar pattern of shareable, feel-good celebrity stories that spread quickly online because they appeal to emotion and usually rely on little more than reposts. We have debunked similar claims before, including posts alleging U.S. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump spent New Year's Day 2026 at a Pennsylvania orphanage and that Stephen Colbert launched a multimillion-dollar "Evergreen Sanctuary" for abused dogs . title: UNICEF report didn't disprove famine in Gaza, contrary to claims
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: A summer 2026 UNICEF report "dismantled" the "lie" that there is or was a famine in Gaza. Rating: False About this rating Context A July 2026 UNICEF report found the acute child malnutrition rate had recently dropped in Gaza, but largely because of humanitarian aid assistance. UNICEF said food insecurity remains high in Gaza and that malnutrition rates could rise again without sustained peace and humanitarian aid. This report does not contradict an August 2025 determination by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, of which UNICEF is a technical partner, that Gaza was officially suffering a famine at that time. In August 2026, a rumor circulated online that new acute child malnutrition data from UNICEF — the United Nations' agency that provides humanitarian and developmental aid for children — "dismantled" the "narrative" that a famine had occurred, or was occurring, in Gaza. Various U.N. agencies , including UNICEF, reported in August 2025 that famine had been confirmed in Gaza for more than half a million people in and around Gaza City. The agencies said famine is declared when thresholds for extreme food deprivation, acute malnutrition and starvation-related deaths are surpassed. A year later, some social media users questioned those findings based on alleged new data. For example, one Instagram account wrote , in part ( archived ), "The World Called It a Famine in Gaza. UNICEF's Own Data Says Otherwise." The post includes an image of an incorrectly drawn map of the Middle East that purportedly shows each country's acute malnutrition rate for children under age 5. The full text of the post reads: The World Called It a Famine in Gaza. UNICEF's Own Data Says Otherwise: A new survey shows Gaza has one of the lowest acute child malnutrition rates in the world: A UNICEF-coordinated survey found that acute malnutrition rates among children in Gaza range from just 0.2% to 0.8% - lower than Egypt (3.3%), Jordan (2.3%), Syria (12.2%), and even some European countries. These are not Israeli government figures. This is the UN's own data, collected using standard WHO methodology. The famine narrative was one of the most damaging lies spread against Israel. UNICEF just dismantled it. It should be noted that the caption and the image list different percentages for Gaza. The post's caption says Gaza's acute malnutrition rate is between 0.2% and 0.8%, while the map graphics say it's 1.3%. Other posts on Facebook ( archived ) and Instagram ( archived ) make the same claim that new UNICEF child malnutrition data refutes the existence of a famine in Gaza. In short, the referenced UNICEF data does not contradict previous declarations by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification — commonly referred to as the IPC — that there was a famine in Gaza. Therefore, we've rated the claim false. The "new" UNICEF data refers to an authentic July 2026 snapshot of data a UNICEF-led team is continuously collecting and updating. The Instagram post's caption accurately describes the data for various Gaza Strip governorates in that snapshot, although it lacks the context of the data's purpose as a reference for on-the-ground humanitarian aid providers and ignores separate food insecurity data. This authentic data does not show that there is currently a famine in Gaza as of this writing, but it also does not disprove that there was previously a famine in Gaza — which is consistent with the U.N.'s position. "The bottom line is, both findings stand: Famine was confirmed in August 2025, and acute malnutrition among children has fallen since," Kurtis Cooper, chief of media at UNICEF, told Snopes over email. "That improvement is a product of the assistance delivered in between, post-ceasefire, and not evidence that it was unnecessary." Source of the data referenced in claim The referenced data appears to originate from a slideshow presented at the U.N.-led State of Palestine Nutrition Cluster coordination meeting on July 22, 2026 . Snopes first became aware of the slideshow through this Reddit comment . We were able to verify its legitimacy by going to the State of Palestine Nutrition Cluster's page on ReliefWeb — a digital service of the U.N.'s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — and clicking on the "National Level Cluster Coordination Meeting minutes" link . The slideshow can be found within the July 22, 2026, meeting folder ( archived ). It is titled "SoP Nutrition Cluster Coordination Meeting 22 July 2026 … Gaza Nutrition SMART Survey Result." The cluster team is staffed by UNICEF employees, which explains why the data is being attributed to the agency. Cooper confirmed that the details of the recent nutrition survey were shared online via a PowerPoint presentation for the members of the nutrition cluster, which he said is a U.N.-led group that coordinates organizations providing nutrition assistance. The survey, Cooper said, measured conditions in mid-2026, more than nine months after the IPC confirmed famine in Gaza in August 2025. The survey "does not tell us what conditions were in August 2025, and it was never designed to," Cooper said. What the slideshow, survey say The slideshow includes a survey, of which the stated goal was, "To assess the nutritional status of children aged 0–59 months and women of reproductive age (15–49 years) and identify key contributing factors to malnutrition across the Gaza Strip to inform the humanitarian response" (Page 6). The findings applied to the 83% of the Gaza population (roughly 1.72 million people) living in areas aid workers could access roughly up to the date of publication: July 22, 2026. The remaining 17% of the population (roughly 358,000 people) were still within either buffer zones or a militarized zone that were inaccessible to the aid workers who conducted the survey (Page 9). The data from the Instagram post's caption claims acute child malnutrition rates in Gaza range from 0.2% to 0.8%. This aligns with a range for one measure from the slideshow's survey data: wasting by Weight-for-Height Z-score (the graph on the left on Page 12). That graph shows the range of GAM rates (meaning total acute malnutrition rates) among the governorates is from 0.2% in Khan Yunis and Rafah to 0.8% in Gaza and North Gaza. However, the data from the most "programmatically useful indicator," as described by the slideshow on Page 13, places the rates between 0.7% and 2%, depending on the governorate that aid workers had access to. This indicator includes both WHZ data and another measure for acute malnutrition in children, Mid-Upper Arm Circumference. The rates for stunting (Page 14) — which the slideshow says "points to longer-term nutritional stress and repeated deprivation beyond immediate wasting" and identifies as the "main child nutrition concern" in Gaza" — are between 11% and 13.5%, again depending on the governorate. This data matches a July 23, 2026 analysis by the IPC, a global initiative with numerous stakeholders, including U.N. agencies such as UNICEF, that seeks to inform decisions through greater food security and nutrition analysis — which found that acute malnutrition across the Gaza Strip is low or "acceptable" (see the right-most map, Page 1). The IPC is the same international partnership that on Aug. 22, 2025, declared a part of Gaza was officially experiencing a famine (see "Key highlights," PDF Page 4). What UNICEF says On July 23, one day after the slideshow was, per Relief Web , presented at the meeting, UNICEF reported that IPC's analysis from the same day "shows improvements in food security and child nutrition across the Gaza Strip," but warned that this improvement "remains fragile" because that progress is "driven largely by expanded access to humanitarian food, nutrition, agricultural and health assistance." According to UNICEF, the majority of Gaza's population is dependent on humanitarian aid. UNICEF wrote that while the analysis highlights how quickly conditions can improve when humanitarian aid is ramped up, sustained peace, aid funding and access are necessary to prevent the improvement from reversing. Both UNICEF and IPC highlighted that food insecurity remains high across the Gaza Strip. UNICEF made no reference to prior famine declarations, nor did it suggest in any way that these current conditions are incompatible with the famine it had previously declared. Cooper, the spokesperson for UNICEF, told Snopes that the situation in Gaza has improved because of the expansion in humanitarian assistance between August 2025, when there were severe access constraints and supply disruptions for humanitarian aid groups in Gaza, and mid-2026. "It reflects improvements in conditions rather than evidence that the assistance or the earlier famine classification was unwarranted," Cooper said. Gaza famine In August 2025 , UNICEF said more than half a million people in Gaza were experiencing famine, again referencing an IPC analysis. That analysis refers to a snapshot similar to the above July 23 IPC analysis , as well as a report on the Famine Review Committee's review of IPC's findings at that time. (The IPC calls upon the FRC to independently review its analyses, finding potential or ongoing famine conditions wherever they may occur.) At that time, the IPC and FRC agreed that famine was actively occurring in Gaza Governorate, which is largely made up of Gaza City, and could occur in two other governorates aid workers could access within the following few weeks (see "Key highlights," PDF Page 4 ). While the IPC and FRC did not extend the famine label to North Gaza Governorate due to limited evidence at the time, it did note that conditions there were likely equal to or worse than the conditions in Gaza Governorate (see the bold sections at the bottom of PDF Page 4). Later in August, the IPC released another report , seeking to answer questions about its decision to declare famine conditions in Gaza Governorate. In that follow-up report, the IPC noted that it used a dataset provided by the Nutrition Cluster — the same UNICEF-led group that is the source of the data in the above social media posts — as evidence for famine in the territory (Section 3, PDF Page 2). It noted that the cluster's data found one measure of acute child malnutrition — GAM by Mid-Upper Arm Circumference, which differs from the measure (GAM by Weight-for-Height Z-score) suggested in the social media posts — increased from 10.1% to 16.4% in Gaza Governorate within three weeks (PDF Page 3). At that time, the amount of humanitarian aid that was making it into Gaza was limited by Israel's offensive military operation in the territory. The first phase of a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas began on Oct. 10, 2025 . However, hostilities have continued since, which UNICEF has condemned . In December 2025 , the FRC released another report reviewing IPC's August analysis that Gaza Governorate was experiencing famine. In that report (PDF Page 2), the FRC reiterated that famine conditions existed in Gaza Governorate "during the July to mid-August period." It did not state that it or the IPC believed famine conditions lasted beyond then and past the date of the ceasefire. Snopes could find no evidence of the IPC and UNICEF claiming that the current conditions in Gaza equate to a famine. That report also highlights the distinction between IPC analyses and the Nutrition Cluster's surveillance system (see Paragraph beginning " Fifth, " PDF Page 4). While the IPC's analyses are designed to be consensus-building processes that consider a wide range of evidence and contributing factors, the Nutrition Cluster's surveillance system continuously monitors the outcomes of ongoing responses and reporting data as it becomes available in order to meet the needs of aid partners. Data entry and cleaning of the Nutrition Cluster system, which the IPC and FRC both use for their analyses, happens in an ongoing, rolling basis. The Nutrition Cluster may retrospectively add and process data for a given time period as information becomes available to it. AI-generated map Many of the posts featuring the claim in question include a map apparently showing the data referenced in the posts' captions. There are a few issues with the map that are immediately noticeable. As noted near the top of this article, one is that the data from the captions does not match the data on the map. The captions claim Gaza's acute child malnutrition rate is between 0.2 and 0.8%, whereas the map says Gaza's rate is 1.3%. The other glaring error is that the map is not geographically accurate. In reality, Gaza has a border with Egypt . In the map , Egypt is detached from Gaza in a southeasterly direction. The West Bank has also been moved north to have a border with Lebanon that does not exist in real life . Kuwait, which sits between Iraq and Saudi Arabia , does not appear at all on the incorrect map, while the portion of Iran does not match the actual shape of that part of the country. These nonsensical mistakes are usually made by generative artificial intelligence tools. The data shown in the map graphic appears to be based on the primary data tab of the "Joint data set including survey estimates ( 2025 edition )" spreadsheet downloadable on this UNICEF page , titled, "Child Malnutrition," which lists historical data not representative of the present situation in 2026. There is no entry solely for Gaza in the spreadsheet, but there is joint data for the Palestinian territories (both Gaza and the West Bank) from 2020 that found their combined wasting rate was at 1.3% at the time. (This data can be found by searching for the ISO code "PSE" and highlighting Row 2,639, Column W, to see the combined "Wasting" percentage for men and women). Not all of the data perfectly matches entries from that spreadsheet, but some do. The 2.3% rate for Jordan (ISO code "JOR") matches the spreadsheet's wasting entry for the country from 2023. Iraq's (ISO code IRQ) 3.9% rate appears to match the spreadsheet's 2018 underweight data (Column Z) for the country. Many of the countries' rates on the map ( Egypt , Iran , Iraq , Jordan , Lebanon , Saudi Arabia , Sudan , Syria and Yemen ) match Global Hunger Index data measuring wasting rates by WHZ for children under age 5. Global Hunger Index is a multi-stakeholder, peer-reviewed annual report that aims to measure and track hunger across the globe. For further reading, Snopes wrote about the famine in Gaza in August 2025, shortly after the FRC officially classified the conditions in Gaza Governorate as such.

title: What CNN's Pamela Brown said about going aboard USS Lincoln
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: CNN's Pamela Brown went aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln in summer 2026. Rating: True About this rating Context Brown went aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln for several days starting in early July, as confirmed by the Department of Defense, Brown and videos of her broadcasts from the ship. Following reports in August of deteriorating conditions aboard the Lincoln in August, Brown summarized her experience on the Lincoln as "something messier than a single narrative" where sailors reported "genuine hardship alongside genuine resilience." In August 2026, national attention turned to the USS Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier deployed to the waters around Iran since January , after reporting came out about deteriorating conditions and concerns about sailors' mental health as the ship's deployment continued to drag on. Following the reports, the U.S. Department of Defense sent the USS George Washington to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln and relieve it from duty. As the reports emerged, critics of President Donald Trump's administration highlighted the conditions the sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln reportedly suffered as a result of the aircraft carrier's long deployment. As part of a desire to bring more attention to these reports, some social media posts praised CNN's Pamela Brown for allegedly visiting the vessel and telling "the truth Trump doesn't want you to hear," as one Facebook post ( archived ) described it. According to the post, what Brown found on the USS Abraham Lincoln "was more human and more damning than any single headline." The post read: Sailors dealing with black mold, food so bad that crew members were losing weight, and no idea when they were going home. The ship has been deployed for nearly nine months. Multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard. And the number one issue crushing morale wasn't the mold or the food. It was the silence. No end date. No clarity. No honesty from the people who sent them there. One sailor put it plainly in a message to Brown. What started as a two-week combat operation became seven months with a shifting justification every few weeks. First it was to help Iranian protesters. Then to denuclearize Iran. Then to support a blockade. Nobody could tell them why they were still there or when they were coming home, while their families had their lives on hold waiting for them. Hegseth called coverage of the Lincoln "completely misrepresented." Brown wrote that sentiment "did not go over well" with the sailors she's been talking to. That is as politely as a journalist can call a defense secretary a liar. Thank you, Pamela Brown, for getting on that ship and letting those sailors be heard. (Facebook) Similar claims about Brown going on board the USS Abraham Lincoln also appeared on Instagram ( archived ) and Threads ( archived ), and Snopes readers searched our site for information about whether she really visited the aircraft carrier. The claim that Brown went aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln and reported on sailors' conditions from the ship is true — a lthough the visit took place in July 2026, around a month before the above posts about the visit circulated. There is video of Brown reporting to CNN live from on board the aircraft carrier, and the Department of Defense confirmed her stay on the ship on social media. Brown's own account of the conditions aboard the Lincoln during her time on it was also more nuanced than the social media posts suggested, and she did not paint an entirely negative picture. Confirming Brown's time aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln According to an article by Brown that CNN published in August about her time on the USS Abraham Lincoln , she boarded the aircraft carrier on July 7. On July 9, she reported live from on board the ship on a CNN broadcast. By July 13, video available on CNN's website shows she was back in the studio at CNN reporting about her experience on the Lincoln. In that segment, Brown talked about how the sailors said they went months without fresh fruit and vegetables during a time when rations were low . She recorded that report from in front of the fresh produce the ship had acquired since that time. While on board the Lincoln in July, Brown posted additional video of her time there to her Instagram account ( archived ). In August, the Department of Defense confirmed over X ( archived ) Brown was on the Lincoln "last month." In an apparent attempt to refute reports of deteriorating conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, the Defense Department highlighted ( archived ) that Brown and her crew ate ice cream while on the ship. Immediately after her return from the Lincoln, CNN ran a segment of Brown's interviews with sailors highlighting the mental toll the long deployment had on the ship's crew, as well as what the ship's leadership was doing to support their mental health. Brown wrote about these experiences in her written account of her time on the Lincoln in August. That account was the same one referenced in the above social media posts. What Brown wrote about her time aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln According to Brown, sailors described losing "significant weight" because meals at one point were "reduced to tuna mixed with noodles, or corn dogs." By the time she arrived, she wrote in the August CNN article, food was plentiful and there were morale-boosting events like ice cream socials, but sailors still had to wait in line for up to an hour for each meal. Brown wrote that she didn't personally notice widespread black mold, but a sailor aboard the ship had messaged her that there had been "black mold around the ship for awhile." Some sailors told Brown of low morale, while others said it felt better than past deployments simply because it had Wi-Fi. Others spoke of camaraderie between the ship's crew, Brown wrote. The hardest part for sailors, Brown wrote, was the open-ended extension of the ship's deployment. For further reading, Snopes has recently investigated a number of claims about the USS Abraham Lincoln.

title: Someone tweeted 'Stop chat gpt' in 2012, but it likely wasn't a prophecy
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: In 2012, a Twitter user posted “Stop chat gpt!!” even though ChatGPT would not be released until 2022. Rating: True About this rating Context The post was authentic, posted to Twitter (now X) on Oct. 5, 2012. However, conclusions about the post's actual meaning or intent are purely speculative and it was unlikely to be related to OpenAI's ChatGPT platform or time travel. A rumor that a social media post from 2012 called for users to stop using ChatGPT, a generative AI chatbot released by OpenAI in 2022, circulated online in August 2026. Social media users allegedly unearthed a post on Twitter (now called X) that purportedly read, "Stop chat gpt!!" The screenshot shared online depicted a post dated Oct. 5, 2012. The seemingly prophetic tweet spread quickly across social media, with some claiming it was simply common Indonesian slang that looks like ChatGPT in retrospect, while another person responded , "I'm indonesian, don't listen to this guy she is a time traveller 100%." The post was authentic. A Twitter account called "Marieanne" with a handle of @Meytrullers17 posted on Oct. 5, 2012 ( archived ): "Stop chat gpt!!" As users offering "time travel" as an explanation for the perceived anachronism in the post pointed out, ChatGPT did not launch until 2022. The Twitter account in question is inactive as of this writing. The user managing the account last posted on June 22, 2013. According to the public account information, it was based in Indonesia. Some people replying to the post speculated it was possible the "Stop chat gpt" message referenced the Indonesian term "ga penting," meaning "not important," which they claimed is often abbreviated as "gpt." Indonesian culture is known for its extensive use of abbreviations. Southeast Asian marketing firm Illuminate chalked this up to a multitude of reasons , including Indonesia's general love of wordplay, the rise of social media, and its history operating under "a military-led government for 32 years," whose "efficient" and "structured language" affected its widespread adoption of acronyms and abbreviations. There are numerous travel blogs dedicated to cataloging various abbreviations used in Indonesia to help visitors navigate the country. Snopes' search for "gpt" on those sites yielded no results. A search of Marieanne's other tweets revealed other uses of "gpt," including a post from 2012 that said "Stop BC sg gpt tah." In addition, the account also posted about receiving spam messages, suggesting that the use of "stop chat gpt" could mean something along the lines of "stop sending unimportant messages." While the other posts did not shed light on the viral post's intended meaning, it did show that it was not an isolated usage of "gpt" as an abbreviation. Snopes attempted to contact the owner of the account for comment but we have thus far been unable to get in touch.

title: Fox News aired graphic falsely suggesting gas prices fell since August 2025
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: A video authentically showed a Fox News graphic that falsely suggested national average gas prices fell between August 2025 and August 2026. Rating: True About this rating Context The graphic inaccurately suggested that the national average gas price was $4.13 in August 2025 compared to $4.06 on the day it aired in August 2026. A Fox News spokesperson confirmed to Snopes that the network aired a correction during its "America Reports" program and on the FOX Business Network on Aug. 18. In August 2026, social media posts claimed ( archived ) a video authentically showed a Fox News graphic that falsely suggested national average gas prices fell between August 2025 and August 2026. The alleged graphic, which aired on Aug. 17, 2026, compared national average gas prices "today," "a week ago" and "a year ago." According to the graphic, the national average gas price on the day the graphic aired was supposedly $4.06 compared to $4.13 one year ago, suggesting prices had fallen between August 2025 and August 2026. Independent journalist Aaron Rupar, who posted a video including the graphic on Aug. 17, wrote , "Fox News graphic claims falsely that the average price of gas one year ago was $4.13, lower than it is right now. It was actually $3.14!" (It's worth noting that the graphic allegedly showed gas prices were higher — not lower — in August 2025 compared to August 2026, contrary to Rupar's statement.) Other social media users also shared the alleged graphic on Facebook ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ), Threads ( archived ) and Reddit ( archived ). A spokesperson from Fox News confirmed to Snopes via email on Aug. 18, 2026, that the graphic had aired during its "America Reports" program and on the FOX Business Network on Aug. 17. The spokesperson sent clips that showed an on-air correction during "America Reports" and on the FOX Business Network on Aug. 18. Rupar's post showed the graphic on "America Reports." Given this confirmation, it was true that Fox News broadcast the graphic in question. It was also true that the $4.13 figure for national average gas prices in August 2025 was incorrect. According to the American Automobile Association and the Bureau of Transportation Statistics , the national average price for regular gas in August 2025 was $3.14 or $3.13, respectively, meaning prices had risen — not fallen — compared to the price on Aug. 17, 2026. The Fox News spokesperson did not reply to a question about why the graphic aired with an incorrect figure. What we know about graphic The graphic appeared on "America Reports" during a live shot with Fox Business reporter Edward Lawrence right before the program's host John Roberts interviewed U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright on Aug. 17, 2026. A clip of Wright's interview included a frame of Lawrence and "America Reports" co-host Jacqui Heinrich at the start. Rupar's clip , which the Fox News spokesperson confirmed displayed the graphic that aired during "America Reports," showed a short frame of Lawrence and Heinrich at the end, suggesting the two events occurred in immediate succession. The graphic listed its source as "AAA," likely referring to the American Automobile Association, which runs a website that tracks average fuel prices. According to that website , the national average price for regular gas on Aug. 17, 2026, was approximately $4.06. The Fox News graphic used the same figure. On Aug. 18, the "week ago" national average gas price on AAA's website was approximately $4 — the same figure Fox News used in its graphic. However, the "year ago" national average gas price on AAA's website was $3.1376, or approximately $3.14. The Fox News graphic incorrectly listed this figure as $4.13. Despite promises, gas prices soared after Iran war Some social media users who shared the Fox News graphic appeared to suggest that the network purposely misled its viewers on behalf of U.S. President Donald Trump's administration. A Fox News spokesperson did not reply to a question about why the network aired the graphic with an incorrect figure. Though Trump ran on promises to cut energy costs for Americans, the war in Iran and resulting stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz instead caused national average gas prices to rise above $4 per gallon in early April 2026 for the first time since August 2022. By August 2026, instead of promising lower energy prices, Trump instead asked voters to forgive paying "a tiny little bit more for your gasoline" to keep Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, one of the chief goals of the war that began in late February 2026. As of this writing, there had been no significant progress toward a peace deal to end the conflict. Trump said during an Aug. 14, 2026, speech that Iran was being "very badly defeated" and that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz "a territory of the United States." Meanwhile, Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in an X post ( archived ) aimed at Trump that the Strait : ...will be closed and opened only under Iran's command, and as long as you do not accept the reality of your defeat and abandon your illusions, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade. For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated various claims involving Fox News and the Iran war .

title: Does photo show Trump and White House aide Natalie Harp looking out helicopter window?
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: A photograph authentically shows U.S. President Donald Trump looking through the window of the Marine One helicopter with his aide Natalie Harp. Rating: True About this rating In August 2026, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., criticized U.S. President Donald Trump, saying the president "wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace" — referring to White House aide Natalie Harp. His statement resulted in widespread speculation about the relationship between Trump and Harp, along with the online dissemination of a purported photograph of the two looking out an aircraft window. The image, which spread on X and Facebook , showed Trump and Harp seated close together in a lit-up cabin looking out the window of an aircraft. Many users questioned whether the photograph was real. (Facebook user Meidas Touch) The above image is authentic. It is a zoomed-in version of a photograph taken by Washington-based photojournalist Al Drago . As such, we rate this claim true. Drago took the photo capturing the moment between Trump and Harp on April 10, 2026. Several photographs on Getty Images , a reputable photo repository, show Trump's son Eric Trump was seated across from them in Marine One, the presidential helicopter. The caption states : President Donald Trump looks out the window with Eric Trump, executive vice president of Trump Organization Inc., left, and Natalie Harp, executive assistant to US President Donald Trump, center, aboard Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House, on Friday, April 10, 2026 in Washington, DC. US President Donald Trump traveled to Trump Winery in Charlottesville, Virginia for a fundraiser. (Al Drago, accessed via Getty Images) Ossoff, who is up for re-election in November, named Harp while claiming Trump was not able to perform the job of president, also making references to the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier and a new Air Force One given to the Trump administration by Qatar. Ossoff said: While the sailors on the Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings, he golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn't want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar. Asked about Ossoff's comments, Trump called the senator a "Pee-wee Herman look-alike" and said he would "much rather do other things." Harp is reportedly very close to Trump and is often photographed at his side. She is responsible for typing his posts on Truth Social. For further reading, Snopes has previously covered unproven rumors of an affair between Trump and Harp.

title: Did Secret Service agent share private details about how Trump acts in presidential limousine?
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: A U.S. Secret Service agent who has served seven presidents said Donald Trump is weirder than all of them put together and provided behind-the-scenes details about what he's like in his presidential limousine. Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating In August 2026, people shared a rumor alleging a U.S. Secret Service agent who has served seven presidents said President Donald Trump is weirder than all of them put together and provided private, behind-the-scenes details about what he's like in the presidential limousine. For example, on Aug. 12, a Facebook user posted ( archived ) the lengthy rumor, which told of a purported "stash of Secret Service memos" revealing secrets about Trump. The post featured an image with a headline reading, "A Secret Service Agent Explains What Trump Is Like Behind The Scenes." The image displayed the publication name The Halfway Cafe and the date Nov. 17, 2025, as well as a photo of Trump walking the White House grounds. (Scott Shamblin accessed via Facebook) Among the many claims about Trump's car rides, the post said Trump enjoys listening to Abba's "Dancing Queen," watches pornography without muting the volume, farts and then accuses the driver of flatulence, throws Big Macs at the windshield when he hears bad news and talks with an exaggerated Asian accent after meeting with an Asian diplomat or leader. Other users reposted the rumor on Facebook ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ) and Threads ( archived ). Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy. In short, this was not true. The rumor a Secret Service agent called Trump weirder than numerous other presidents combined and provided private information about his motorcade ride activities originated from The Halfway Cafe and The Halfway Post , related publications whose content is labeled as satirical in nature. If a Secret Service agent truly had spoken out, news media outlets would have covered it, and their coverage would have appeared in searches of Bing , DuckDuckGo , Google and Yahoo . That was not the case. A writer named Dash MacIntyre owns the two Halfway blogs. He, or another person managing the publication's accounts, reported the made-up story in an article on The Halfway Cafe's Medium.com blog and The Halfway Post's Substack blog in November 2025, as well as in an X post ( archived ). The Halfway Cafe's bio reads, "Dadaist graffiti news. Halfway true comedy and satire for your doomscrolling by Dash MacIntyre. I don't report the facts, I improve them." Snopes emailed MacIntyre to ask about his inspiration for the made-up story, in the case he wished to share more information about his writing. We will update this article if we receive further information. In previous reporting, MacIntyre pointed us to an article he wrote about his "Dada News" content. That story labeled his writing as "absurd for absurdity's sake," as well as the following: Dada News is most politically effective when it compels conservative critics to waste their free time crafting long, laborious responses attacking the integrity, intelligence, and sense of humor of Dada journalists that those Dada journalists do not read and ignore completely. For further reading, we previously investigated another MacIntyre satire story about Grindr threatening to share identities of Republican politicians who "secretly" used the gay dating app to protest Florida legislation.

title: Did Trump admin declare brass instruments a national security threat?
label: Rating: Mostly True About this rating
text: Claim: In August 2026, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump declared brass instruments a national security threat and imposed tariffs on them. Rating: Mostly True About this rating What's True The U.S. Department of Commerce included brass instruments on a list of products that faced proposed tariffs for alleged national security reasons. What's False The government agency did not say brass instruments themselves posed a threat. Rather, the issue was the copper-containing metal alloy these instruments are made of. The cited for this inclusion was Presidential Proclamation 10962, of July 30, 2025, in which Trump said copper "in all forms" (including copper alloys) "is being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States." In August 2026, a rumor spread that the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump had declared brass musical instruments to be a national security threat to justify imposing tariffs on them. One Facebook post about the claim read: Trump vs trumpets! This week, the Trump administration declared tubas, trombones, trumpets, and French horns a national security threat. Brass instruments could soon face a 25% tariff on imports, parts, and accessories, as part of a wider push to expand tariffs on aluminium, steel, and copper. The six-page proposal, published by the Department of Commerce, uses the words "national security" nine times. (Facebook page Classic FM) Variants of the claim also spread on Reddit and on X . The social media posts echoed reports in blog posts and news outlets, including the website of Classic FM , a radio station dedicated to classical music, and HuffPost . Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed and searched the website seeking to verify the information. It is true that on Aug. 6, 2026, the Department of Commerce published a request for comment on the Federal Register for a proposed rule to impose tariffs on brass instruments, among other products. The publication cited national security concerns. However, it was not the instruments themselves the government department appeared to focus on, but the material from which they are made — a copper alloy. The request for comment cited Presidential Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025, in which Trump said copper "in all forms" — including its alloys — " is being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States." As a result, we've rated the claim mostly true. "Reshoring steel, aluminum, and copper production back to the United States is a national security prerogative, given that America cannot be reliant on foreign countries for metals that are critical for military hardware, key infrastructure, technology, etc," a spokesperson for the White House told Snopes in an email. "If we only tariff the raw slabs of these metals being dumped onto the U.S. market, U.S. producers would still get undermined by foreign metal production flowing instead into the foreign production of derivative products like instruments that then get dumped onto our market instead." We have also reached out to the Commerce Department to ask if it could made a direct link between brass instruments and national security concerns. We will update this report should we receive a response. Background of the proposed tariffs The request for comment featured a list of several products on which the Commerce Department proposed to impose tariffs. Besides "brass-wind musical instruments and parts and accessories thereof," the list included fire extinguishers and oxygen tanks. These imported products needed to be subjected to tariffs because they contained aluminum, steel or copper, the Commerce Department said. All three metals were the target of three separate presidential proclamations in which Trump deemed their importation excessive and a national security threat. Proclamation 10962 specifically concerned copper "in all forms," including alloys. The material for brass instruments is an alloy of copper and zinc, which presumably justified their inclusion in the list of imported products worthy of tariffs. The Commerce Department's request for comment appeared to argue that imposing such tariffs helped protect domestic industries: As explained in the reports submitted by the Secretary to the President and cited in Proclamations 9704, 9705, and 10962, steel, aluminum, and copper are being imported into the United States in such quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States. Therefore the President ordered adjustments of imports to protect U.S. national security interests by identifying derivative products on which tariffs must be imposed in order to protect the U.S. defense industrial base. The U.S. defense industrial base is critical to protecting U.S. national security interests. The request for comment also said the Commerce Department would seek to impose 25% tariffs on these products, except for those deemed to be "agricultural equipment," which would be subject to 15% duties. By law, the Commerce Department cannot impose this rule before a period ending on Aug. 27, during which it will receive comments on its proposal. For further reading, Snopes has covered Trump's tariffs extensively, including the claim that Trump had imposed a 2,000% tariff on Belgian chocolate .

title: Don't fall for claim Trump said 'only suckers and losers would enlist' in US Navy and then complain
label: Rating: Fake About this rating
text: Claim: A screenshot authentically shows an August 2026 Truth Social post in which U.S. President Donald Trump said, "Only suckers and losers would enlist, go to sea on an aircraft carrier, and then complain and send their family nasty notes about our military. They weren't at sea long enough." Rating: Fake About this rating A rumor that U.S. President Trump posted a degrading message on social media about service members aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln circulated online in mid-August 2026. People on social media shared a purported screenshot of a Truth Social post in which Trump allegedly wrote, "Only suckers and losers would enlist, go to sea on an aircraft carrier, and then complain and send their family nasty notes about our military. They weren't at sea long enough." The screenshot also appeared to include text added by a user that read, "not the first time he called them suckered or losers." (Twitter user @Charlie22825276) The rumor spread online as reports spread of sailors trying to jump overboard due to mental health hardships and strain caused by a lengthy deployment, which Trump reportedly said on Aug. 14, 2026, was "not nearly long enough." The widespread sharing of the purported screenshot led to numerous Snopes readers contacting us for more information on its authenticity. The post was fake. A search of the president's X and Truth Social accounts and an online archive of Trump's social media posts revealed no such post. Additionally, the purported screenshot does not visually match Trump's actual Truth Social page. The screenshot featured no icon signifying Trump's account as part of "Truth+," the platform's premium service, and the font didn't match what is used on Truth Social. Further, it was clear from the fake screenshot that the post text was overlaying the icons displayed on the platform, which would not occur if the screenshot was legitimate. Rather, it appeared the originator of the fake post used a screenshot of an old Truth Social post and added their own text on top of it. A reverse image search on Google using the screenshot of the alleged post returned only other instances of users sharing the fake post. A reverse image search on TinEye of the same screenshot returned no results. The screenshot circulated amid reports of poor conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which had been deployed for nine months as of this writing, setting a record for uninterrupted time at sea, according to The Associated Press. Trump reportedly downplayed reports of supply issues and mental health struggles aboard the vessel. On Aug. 17, Adm. Brad Cooper, the U.S. Central Command commander, published an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal about visiting the ship, writing, "Issues related to food, hot water and other concerns raised months ago were addressed by leadership and resolved." The White House's website posted about Cooper's visit and linked to the op-ed. The additional claim that Trump had previously called service members "suckers" and "losers" referred to a rumor that began circulating in 2020, stemming from a piece in The Atlantic citing anonymous sources. Snopes investigated that rumor , but we found no credible evidence the president had ever said as much publicly and couldn't say for certain whether he had or hadn't said it in private.

title: Did Trump order USS Abraham Lincoln sailors to sign NDAs before they can leave ship?
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: In August 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln to sign NDAs before they were allowed to leave the aircraft carrier. Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating In mid-August 2026, social media users circulated a claim that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln to sign nondisclosure agreements before they were allowed to leave the aircraft carrier. One Facebook post spreading the rumor was captioned, "Trump is making USS Lincoln sailors sign an NDA before they can get off the ship. #navy #ussabrahamlincoln #military #nda #fascism." (Facebook user Politics Girl Official) Variations of the claim also spread on social media platforms, including Threads , X and Instagram . We also received emails from readers asking whether the claim was true. In short, it was not. We found no evidence Trump ordered sailors to sign NDAs before coming ashore, and the rumor originated from a Facebook post with a "satire" label. The earliest version of the claim we found came from a Facebook post by Karl E. Rominger. Its headline read " TRUMP ORDERS USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN SAILORS TO SIGN NDAs BEFORE COMING ASHORE." The post's text stated: Donald Trump announced today that sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln will not be permitted to leave the ship until they sign legally binding nondisclosure agreements promising never to say anything "negative, nasty or insufficiently beautiful" about their deployment. Especially off-limits: the mysterious laundry-room fire. Sailors are specifically forbidden from suggesting the fire was anything other than a completely ordinary laundry-room fire that absolutely, positively had nothing whatsoever to do with Iran. They are also forbidden from wondering aloud whether the carrier remained at sea while repairs were completed so nobody standing on a dock with a cellphone could photograph whatever definitely did not happen. "Nothing happened," Trump explained. "And anybody saying something happened will spend the remainder of their natural life at Fort Leavenworth for talking about the thing that never happened." Pete Hegseth, Marco Rubio and J.D. Vance immediately described requiring thousands of returning sailors to sign secrecy agreements on the gangway as "totally normal military procedure." Hegseth added that anyone asking why such an agreement would be necessary if nothing happened clearly hates the troops.
