Trump initially claimed the NDA was his idea before explaining that Susie Wiles developed it, Hegseth approved it, Rubio translated it into diplomatic language, and Vance volunteered to explain on television why Americans should never believe anything sailors tell their own families. Because nothing says nothing happened quite like threatening everybody who was there if they talk about it. (Facebook user Karl E. Rominger) The post explicitly labeled its content as satirical. It ended: "Follow Karl E. Rominger for more news, satire and uncomfortable questions. #KarlTalks #Satire #USSAbrahamLincoln #Trump #Politics." Moreover, the Facebook profile page describes its content as "Political parody, sharp commentary" and it features numerous other fictional stories written in a similar style. Story inspired by real-life fire on another carrier? There was a real laundry-room fire aboard a U.S. aircraft carrier during the Iran conflict. It happened on the USS Gerald R. Ford, when a fire broke out in the ship's laundry room on March 12, 2026, which U.S. Central Command said was not related to combat. The Ford later stopped in Greece for repairs, and more than 200 sailors were treated for smoke inhalation. The satirical Facebook post may have been referencing this incident when mentioning a "mysterious laundry-room fire," but we found no evidence confirming that. In any case, the fire happened on a different carrier months before August 2026. Abraham Lincoln deployment context The rumor spread while the USS Abraham Lincoln already was drawing attention over its unusually long deployment. As of this writing, the aircraft carrier had spent about nine months at sea, and reports described food and supply shortages and low morale among its crew. Other claims about conditions aboard the carrier also circulated online. For instance, in August 2026, we investigated reports that sailors tried to go overboard during the extended deployment. All in all, certain concerns about the USS Abraham Lincoln's extended deployment and its conditions in August 2026 were well-documented. However, the allegation that Trump ordered its sailors to sign NDAs before being allowed ashore originated from an account that labels its content as satire. For further reading, we have previously investigated other fabricated posts from the same account. For instance, in June 2026, we fact-checked a fabricated screenshot claiming Trump said he walked out of an NBC "Meet the Press" interview because reporter Kristen Welker kept staring at his ear. Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective , we use " originated as satire " or " labeled satire " ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

title: Does Nancy Mace have arm tattoos?
label: Rating: True About this rating
text: Claim: An image authentically showed South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace with tattoos on her arms. Rating: True About this rating In August 2026, an image circulated online that social media users claimed showed South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace with tattoos on her arms. One X user who shared ( archived ) the image wrote, "Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) reveals new tattoos in recent appearance." Similar images of Mace wearing a sleeveless blue top that revealed multiple tattoos on both arms also circulated on Facebook ( archived ), Threads ( archived ), Instagram ( archived ), Reddit ( archived ) and Bluesky ( archived ). Snopes readers contacted us about the image, asking whether it was real. The images of Mace with tattoos on her arms appeared to be screenshots from episodes of her podcast, "Get MACED," on YouTube. An Aug. 13, 2026, episode titled "The CALL is Coming From INSIDE the House: Nancy Mace EXPOSES Radical Election Results" included two clips of Mace wearing the sleeveless blue top in the introduction (at 0:09 and 0:25) and one of her wearing a black denim top that also exposed her arms and tattoos (at 0:30). The day before, a separate podcast episode was the first in the series to feature an intro sequence that included several pictures and videos of Mace that showed her tattoos. The Aug. 12 episode did not include the clip of Mace wearing the sleeveless blue top. Given that Mace published the videos showing her arm tattoos on her own YouTube channel that social media users later shared screenshots from, we find claims that those screenshots authentically showed the South Carolina legislator true. We contacted representatives for Mace to ask what her arm tattoos showed, when she got them and why and await a reply. Mace's arm tattoos appeared consistent across the images and videos she posted on YouTube on Aug. 12 and 13 and also appeared in Mace's Instagram account profile picture and in a video ( archived ) on the platform posted Aug. 13. We found no reason to suspect Mace edited her videos or images to add arm tattoos that she did not have in real life. From the available videos and photos, it appeared Mace's arm tattoos included various bird, flower and religious motifs as well as the word "Justice." Mace had tattoos before August 2026 reveal In a February 2026 profile of Mace, Politico's Michael Kruse reported that the three-term representative got her first nine tattoos "in the midst of losing or firing every one of her staffers" in 2023 or 2024. These did not appear to be the same tattoos Mace revealed in her August 2026 podcast episodes. Images from Mace's podcast intro in August 2026 showed her arm tattoos extended almost down to her elbows on the inside and outside of both arms. Photos of Mace from the reputable picture agency Getty Images in November 2024 and March 2025 showed her bare arms without tattoos, suggesting Mace got the arm tattoos after these dates, though it was unclear exactly when. At the time of Kruse's profile, Mace reportedly described the tattoos she got in 2023 or 2024 like something akin to a coping mechanism. Kruse wrote that she said she got her tattoos "not just to feel 'the pain that I need to feel' but to 'reclaim' her body." Since then, Mace lost South Carolina's Republican primary for governor on June 9, 2026. She announced ( archived ) the next day that she would not seek a fourth term as a representative for South Carolina and would instead return to work in the private sector. For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other rumors surrounding Mace .

title: Did Muslims in Dearborn try to silence church bells? There's no proof
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: In July 2026, Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanded that churches stop ringing bells on Sundays. Rating: False About this rating Context Dearborn had a documented local dispute over mosque loudspeakers used for the Islamic call to prayer in 2025. But local reporting described complaints about those broadcasts, not Muslims demanding that churches stop ringing bells. In August 2026, a rumor recirculated on social media that Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanded that churches stop ringing bells on Sundays. One X post ( archived ) spreading the claim started: In Dearborn Michigan: Muslims DEMAND submission!! In Dearborn Michigan, Muslims are now demanding that CHRISTIAN CHURCHES stop ringing their bells on Sundays. This is real and their reasoning should terrify every Christian American. Muslims are saying "According to Sharia Law, church bells cannot be louder than our Islamic call to prayer. We are the majority in this city and you HAVE TO respect us, our laws, and our religion." Versions of the rumor spread across multiple social media platforms, including X , LinkedIn and Threads . However, the rumor appeared to spread only through social media posts, which did not identify who allegedly made the demand, which church or churches were targeted, when it happened or where the quoted statement came from. We found no credible local news report , city code provision or public statement supporting the claim. Local reporting instead pointed to a different controversy — residents' complaints about mosque loudspeakers. As such, we rated the claim false. We contacted the city of Dearborn for comment and asked whether it was aware of any incident matching the claim. We will update this article if we receive a response. Complaints about mosque loudspeakers The rumor may have grown out of a real, but different, noise dispute in Dearborn. Local reporting showed the city had recently dealt with complaints from some residents about mosque loudspeakers used to broadcast the Islamic call to prayer. In October 2025, Detroit-area news outlet WXYZ reported that some Dearborn residents had complained about outdoor calls to prayer that could be heard on loudspeakers throughout the city. According to WXYZ, the Islamic Institute of Knowledge on Schaefer Road broadcast the call to prayer by loudspeaker twice a day for about two minutes. The outlet reported that Dearborn resident Andrea Unger had raised concerns at City Council meetings, saying she did not want to hear the loudspeakers in her yard or home. The same report quoted Fouad Berry, a board member at the Islamic Institute of Knowledge, saying the mosque had stopped broadcasting the early-morning prayer after complaints came in "just to be respectful to the community." Also according to the report, Dearborn police Chief Issa Shahin said at an Oct. 7, 2025, City Council meeting that mosques could be cited if they used loudspeakers before 7 a.m. or exceeded permitted decibel levels. Detroit news station WKBD also reported on the mosque loudspeaker complaints. According to that report, Unger presented a signed petition at a City Council meeting concerning the use of an outdoor loudspeaker at the Dearborn Community Center, one of several mosques in Dearborn that had received noise complaints. WKBD reported that Dearborn officials conducted decibel tests at some mosques and found instances of a mosque violating the city ordinance. The outlet also reported that Nabeel Bahalwan, director of the Dearborn Community Center, said the mosque was within allowable noise limits and did not want to bother neighbors. None of that reporting described Muslims demanding that church bells be silenced. Rather, it described residents' complaints about mosque loudspeakers and city officials' efforts to enforce Dearborn's secular noise rules. Dearborn's noise rules Dearborn's code also does not support the post's framing. The city's general noise regulation prohibits "unreasonably loud, disturbing, unusual or unnecessary noise" that disturbs or endangers the comfort, peace, health or safety of others. The provision does not mention Shariah, Islam, mosques, churches or church bells. A separate section restricts the use of loudspeakers or similar devices between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. when the sound creates a noise disturbance across a residential property line. That rule applies to loudspeakers "for any purpose," rather than to one religion or type of house of worship. What we know about Dearborn's demographics The post's description of Dearborn as a "Muslim-majority town" was not supported by an official religious count. Dearborn is known for its large Muslim and Arab American communities. However, the census-related figure often cited in coverage of the city concerns ancestry, not religion. Detroit news station WDIV reported that U.S. Census Bureau data showed people of Middle Eastern or North African ancestry made up 54.5% of the city's population. In other words, the 54.5% figure measured Middle Eastern or North African ancestry, not Muslim identity. The federal government does not have an official count of Dearborn residents by religion. Pew Research Center has reported that U.S. census forms do not ask about religion, and that the decennial census has never directly asked Americans about their religion. The Census Bureau also has said (Page 22) it does not collect data on religious affiliation in its demographic surveys or the decennial census. Some nongovernmental groups compile religious-demographic estimates. For example, the Association of Religion Data Archives' 2020 U.S. Religion Census includes data for the Detroit-Warren-Dearborn metropolitan area, but not a city-level count for Dearborn itself. Snopes has previously fact-checked similar false claims tying Dearborn or Michigan communities to Islamic law, which is commonly referred to as Shariah. In 2017, we found that a viral image did not show a KFC in Dearborn using separate lines for men and women, but the photo was actually taken at a KFC in Saudi Arabia. In 2018, we investigated a claim from a satirical website that a so-called Shariah zone in Michigan had banned bacon and required women to wear burqas in public.

title: Heritage Foundation committee chair said it's 'not a failure' to have all male Nobel Prize winners
label: Rating: Correct Attribution About this rating
text: Claim: Scott Yenor, chairman of a Heritage Foundation initiative, said in 2021: "Every effort must be made not to recruit women into engineering but rather to recruit and demand more of men who become engineers. Ditto for med school and the law and every trade. If every Nobel Prize winner is a man, that's not a failure." Rating: Correct Attribution About this rating Context Popular posts on Facebook and Threads correctly attribute to Yenor most of an excerpt of a speech given by him, though the final few sentences of the quote meme actually consist of someone else's commentary on Yenor's remarks. In August 2026, an old quote from a Heritage Foundation committee chair spread online, in which he allegedly expressed regressive views about women. The quote spread months after Snopes investigated the connections between U.S. President Donald Trump's second administration and the Project 2025 initiative — a blueprint for reshaping the federal government promoted by The Heritage Foundation , a conservative think tank. Many online claimed Scott Yenor, a Heritage Foundation initiative chairperson, had once expressed negative views about women in engineering and other fields traditionally thought of as "male." According to posts on Threads ( archived ) and Facebook , Yenor allegedly said : Every effort must be made not to recruit women into engineering but rather to recruit and demand more of men who become engineers. Ditto for med school and the law and every trade. Efforts should be redoubled to encourage more men to enter the medical field, space exploration, mining endeavors and every other high-end and even low-end profession. If every Nobel Prize winner is a man, that's not a failure. It's kind of a cause for celebration. Why can't our celebration of male excellence in sports be translated into all facets of life? More successful men will mean more happy citizenry and a stronger nation. Such medicated, quarrelsome and meddlesome women gain their meaning through the seeming participation in the global project. They are agents of the new world, but not new life. Such women are now the backbone of every left-wing cosmopolitan party in the western world, from the Greens in Germany to the Democratic Party in America. And if our ideal woman is a childless media scold or a barren bureaucratic apparatchik, there is no question whether we can have a future. We can't. There is a question of whether we deserve one. But women have fewer options, the thinking goes, they'll have more children, they'll be bound more tightly to the men in their lives with fewer ways out. This is about dragging the country back to a time when women had only one choice. To submit to men. (Threads user @tracifairheart) Yenor did indeed make most of the above statement in 2021, excluding the last few sentences of commentary and not in the order in which it is presented. We rate this claim as a correct attribution on the whole, with the caveat that the last paragraph shared in quote memes was actually part of a commentary on Yenor's opinions by MS NOW host Ali Velshi. As of this writing, Yenor is listed on The Heritage Foundation's website as the chairman of the "American Citizenship Initiative," which appears to focus on promoting so-called traditional family values. Other commentary by Yenor published on the Heritage Foundation includes " Married Women Reap More From the Festive Season Than Singles " and " Porn is Poisoning Our Culture ." Yenor is not, however, listed as a contributor to Project 2025's " Mandate for Leadership ," The Heritage Foundation's report detailing proposals to cut or reduce federal departments, as well as its overall agenda for a conservative government. Yenor's appointment to the Heritage Foundation committee took place in December 2025, long after the "Mandate for Leadership" was published. We reached out to The Heritage Foundation for comment and to learn whether Yenor still ascribes to the views he expressed in the video, outlined below. We will update this report accordingly. 'The Family Form That Nations Need' In November 2021, Yenor gave a speech titled, "The Family Form That Nations Need," at the National Conservatism Conference held by The Claremont Institute, a conservative think tank. The full video of his speech can be accessed on YouTube: At the 11:00 mark, Yenor speaks the words quoted in social media posts (emphasis ours): Our feminist culture leads us to want less male achievement. Their excellence, after all, creates inequities. That's a shame. That denial of reality has to stop. Every effort must be made not to recruit women into engineering but rather to recruit and demand more of men who become engineers. Ditto for med school and the law and every trade. Efforts should be redoubled to encourage more men to enter the medical field, space exploration, mining endeavors and every other high-end and even low-end profession. If every Nobel Prize winner is a man, that's not a failure. It's kind of a cause for celebration. Why can't our celebration of male excellence in sports be translated into all facets of life. More successful men will mean more happy citizenry and a stronger nation. Perhaps mandatory gun training should — I'm from Idaho so I'm required to say that — the promotion of wrestling and other acts of physical courage are necessary in our age of "soy boys." Our celebration of diversity is just the opposite of the strength that we need as a country. So much in our culture and in our politics complicates the male-female dance in addition to that. The continuation of the passage actually came earlier in Yenor's speech, at the 2:32 mark (emphasis ours): But what does this independent woman really mean? Our independent women seek their purpose in life in mid-level bureaucratic jobs like human resource management, environmental protection and marketing. They're more medicated, meddlesome and quarrelsome than women need to be. Without connections to eternity delivered through their family, such medicated, quarrelsome and meddlesome women gain their meaning through the seeming participation in the global project. They are agents of the new world, but not new life. Such women are now the backbone of every left-wing cosmopolitan party in the western world, from the Greens in Germany to the Democratic Party in America. And if our ideal woman is a childless media scold or a barren bureaucratic apparatchik, there is no question whether we can have a future. We can't. There is a question of whether we deserve one. Misattributed addendum Yenor's speech did not contain the following paragraph, which was tacked onto the bottom of the passage in some image memes sharing the quote: Snopes searched for evidence that Yenor actually said or wrote any part of the above words and found none, but we did find a Facebook post in which Yenor's statements were paired with a March 2026 episode of MS NOW host Ali Velshi's show . In that show, as part of a commentary on Yenor's opinions, it was Velshi who uttered the final sentences of the quote meme (at 11:29 in the MS NOW video, emphasis ours): So their answer is to push women back in their place, to strip away their autonomy, to push them out of public life, to narrow the futures available to them. Ultimately, this agenda is not really about solving demographic decline. […] If women have fewer options, the thinking goes, they'll have more children. They'll be bound more tightly to the men in their lives with fewer ways out. This is about dragging the country back to a time when women had only one choice: to submit to men. In December 2021 , Yenor posted a follow-up statement on X ( archived ), denying he wanted to prevent women from being in such professions, instead saying "special efforts to recruit women into fields where they don't seem to want to be" should be stopped. In December 2025, a Heritage Foundation employee responded on X ( archived ) to an Atlantic article criticizing Yenor's appointment and labeling it as Heritage supporting discrimination against women: Heritage is fortunate to have amazingly talented teammates, where scholars and staff at all levels (and both sexes) are free to discuss and debate ideas on a wide range of topics without it being cast as a "Heritage policy." People know a Heritage policy when they see it, and we will continue to advance common sense conservative solutions for the American people. Snopes has reported on Project 2025 extensively , including how the Trump administration's policies are overlapping with the ideas put forth by the conservative think tank.

title: Massachusetts Democrats didn't unveil Molech statue at state Capitol, despite claims
label: Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating
text: Claim: In August 2026, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey unveiled a statue of Molech (also spelled Moloch), a pagan god who the Bible associates with child sacrifice, in front of the state Capitol. Rating: Originated as Satire About this rating A rumor spread online in August 2026 that Massachusetts Democrats had installed a demonic statue in front of the state Capitol building. According to the claim, the statue was of Molech ( also spelled Moloch , which is how we'll refer to the figure from here on), an ancient god who, according to multiple passages in the Old Testament, was related to child sacrifice. (X user @Howodd69) The story spread after Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat, signed a bill into law that makes it possible for all women to receive an abortion after 24 weeks of pregnancy, based on a physician's "professional medical judgment." (Anti-abortion advocates online suggested the state had legalized "abortion until birth," a claim Snopes separately fact-checked .) Readers wrote in looking for more information on the supposed statue. To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo , Google and Yahoo . If the statue were real, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or The Boston Globe, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case. We didn't find any credible reporting about the Moloch statue. The story originated with The Babylon Bee, a satirical news site that describes itself as a "Trusted Source for Christian News Satire." The Babylon Bee originally posted the story on Aug. 13, 2026. Snopes has alerted readers to several instances of rumors originating from satirical articles published by The Babylon Bee, including a fictitious story suggesting that new government-run grocery stores in New York City would require shoppers to have a "special mark" on their hand or forehead — the number 666, often associated with Satan or the Antichrist. Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective , we use " originated as satire " or " labeled satire " ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

title: Did Jill Biden babysit for Joe Biden before they dated? Here's the real story
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: Jill Biden was a teenager working as the Biden family babysitter when she started dating then-Sen. Joe Biden. Rating: False About this rating In August 2026, a long-standing rumor recirculated on social media, claiming that former U.S. first lady Jill Biden was a teenager working as a babysitter for former President Joe Biden's children when they met. "Working class Joe. The only thing he worked over was the underage babysitter," one X post ( archived ) read. The post featured an image purportedly showing Jill and Joe Biden alongside text that read: This is Joe Biden at age 30 with his then 15 year old babysitter (while stil[l] married to his first wife) The babysitter became his 2nd wife when she turned 18 three years later Her name is JILL BIDEN In short, the claim that Jill Biden was a teenage babysitter for Joe Biden's children when they started dating is false. The couple met in 1975, after the death of Joe Biden's first wife, when Jill was in her 20s. We previously fact-checked this claim in 2021 and 2025 when similar false rumors spread on social media. How and when the Bidens first met Jill Biden was born on June 3, 1951 , and Joe Biden on Nov. 20, 1942 , making them nearly nine years apart in age. Given this age difference, it would have been impossible for Joe Biden to be in his 30s while Jill Biden was still a teenager. According to the White House website , Jill Biden met then-Senator Joe Biden in 1975. They married in 1977. In a 2016 Vogue interview , Jill stated that when she met Joe, she was a college senior. This means she was in her 20s at the time, not a teenager. A Delaware Morning News article from July 17, 1977, detailed the origins of their relationship, stating that Joe Biden's brother, Frank, set them up on a blind date: Son told Joe to marry Jill Jul 17, 1977 The Morning News (Wilmington, Delaware) Newspapers.com In a 2012 CNN interview , when asked whether it was true that Joe Biden "set his eyes" on her after seeing a picture of her, Jill Biden recalled: "I had met him once before, and but we were in a crowd and it was at a fundraiser. So then I guess he saw my picture somewhere and he said 'oh, that's the kind of girl I'd like to date.' And I knew his brother, so his brother said 'oh, I know her.' Cause I was in college at the time and his brother was there. So Frank called me and, or got my number, and Joe called me. He said 'this is Joe Biden' and 'would you like to go out?'" A 2020 campaign video titled "Get to Know Jill Biden" further corroborates this timeline. In it, Joe Biden recounts: Joe Biden: My brother said, "There's this woman. You'll really like her, Joe." So I gave her a call. And she had a date that night. Jill Biden: You said "Do you think you could break your date?" Joe Biden: Oh, that's right. What did you do? Jill Biden: "Well, I called and told the guy that I had a friend in from out of town and went out with Joe. Joe Biden: I was 30. I was a senator. And I was a widower. Several years earlier, a tractor-trailer broadsided my wife and three children. My wife and daughter were killed. I wasn't big on the whole dating scene. But when I met Jill, I fell in love with her when I saw her. Photographs that spread with the claim Posts spreading the rumor have used authentic photographs of Jill and Joe Biden, but paired them with false descriptions of Jill Biden's age and how the couple met. Jill Biden originally posted one of the photographs used to spread the rumor on her Instagram and X accounts in August 2020, stating it was taken after she met Joe Biden in 1975, when she was in her 20s. "Those were the first words I spoke to Joe when he called me out of the blue on a Saturday in 1975," Jill wrote. The Philadelphia Inquirer also published the photo with a caption credited to the Biden campaign, dating it to 1976. At the time, Jill would have been about 24, and Joe about 33. Joe Biden's first wife, Neilia Hunter Biden, had died in a car crash three years earlier. When the claim recirculated in 2026, some posts used another old photograph of the couple alongside the false claim that Jill Biden was Joe Biden's teenage babysitter. That photograph was also authentic and seemed to have been taken in the same setting. Joe Biden's granddaughter Naomi Biden shared the image on X in November 2020, captioning it: "They've come a long, long, way together." However, at least one version of the rumor circulating in August 2026 used what appeared to be a digitally distorted version of the same photograph. Other rumors about Jill Biden that we have fact-checked in the past include the claim that she is not a medical doctor and is therefore wrongly using the title "Dr." and a rumor that she did not agree to marry Joe Biden until his fifth proposal .

title: Did Trump-linked oil company set up drilling operation in Greenland without permission?
label: Rating: Mixture About this rating
text: Claim: A company linked to U.S. President Donald Trump began setting up an oil drilling operation in Greenland without the government's permission. Rating: Mixture About this rating What's True In August 2026, equipment for the Jameson Land oil project was moved without the necessary government approval, which led Greenlandic authorities to issue a warning. What's False As of August 2026, Greenland Energy had not begun drilling, and there was no evidence that Trump owned or controlled the company. What's Undetermined It remains unclear whether or to what extent Trump or members of his administration had any direct contact with the company about its activities in Greenland. In early August 2026, social media users circulated claims that a company connected to U.S. President Donald Trump had moved into Greenland and started setting up an oil drilling operation without permission. For instance, one Facebook post ( archived ) began: 🚨 TRUMP-LINKED OIL COMPANY LANDS DRILLING EQUIPMENT IN GREENLAND WITHOUT PERMISSION AS TRUMP THREATENS TAKEOVER 🚨 […] A Texas oil company with ties to Donald Trump just landed a dozen shipping containers of drilling equipment on Greenland's remote eastern coast. They never got permission. Greenland's government issued a "strong warning" that no approval had been granted. But Greenland Energy, a company set up last year with chairman Larry Swets enjoying access to Trump's inner circle, pushed forward anyway. A company representative named Robert Price told residents at a community meeting in June that they had permission to bring equipment ashore. That was false. Greenland's resources ministry confirmed there are "no actually active permissions for any exploration activity." When caught, the company blamed "enthusiasm" for the confusion. Then the next month, locals watched a tug pull a barge to shore and unload containers. (Facebook user Jim Heath﻿) "An American company lands equipment on foreign soil without permission, lies about having approval, and the sitting president posts memes threatening to take the whole island. Trump is making the USA a villain in real time," the post ended. Similar versions of the claim spread elsewhere . One Instagram video alleged Trump was "having an oil company that he is linked to go and start drilling in Greenland" and that "experts are saying across the Internet that this is what looks to be essentially an invasion without an invasion." One article's headline went further, claiming that "Trump's oil company begins drilling in Greenland without consulting authorities." Snopes readers also contacted us about the story and searched our website for information about it. In short, there was some truth to the claims. However, they often made both the company's actions and its ties to Trump sound stronger than the evidence showed. It was true that in late July 2026, the equipment connected to the planned oil project was moved without the required authorization, which led Greenland's government to issue a warning. But, as of this writing, the drilling had not started and the exploration licenses were still valid. Also, we found no evidence that Trump owned or controlled Greenland Energy. For those reasons, we rated this claim a mixture of true, false and undetermined information. Snopes reached out to Greenland Energy, Greenlandic authorities and the White House for comment and will update this story if we receive responses. Origin of the rumor and what actually happened Social media claims stemmed from genuine reporting about a planned oil exploration project in Jameson Land in eastern Greenland. Questions about the project already surfaced in July 2026, when The Guardian reported that Greenland Energy representative Robert Price told residents the company had permission to bring equipment ashore, while Greenland's resources ministry said there were no active permissions for exploration activities or preparations. At the end of July, Danish news outlet Danwatch reported that equipment linked to the project was moved to Nerlerit Inaat without the required authorization. Greenland's government confirmed the move and issued a "strong warning," saying future logistical activities had to be approved in advance. Later, The Guardian reported on Aug. 8 that a "Trump-linked" oil firm was preparing to drill. Importantly, the article said the company was preparing for drilling, and not that drilling had already started. Did the company start drilling without permission? The incident that prompted Greenland's warning was not unauthorized drilling, but the movement of equipment connected to the project without the necessary approval. Greenland's Ministry of Trade and Mineral Resources said the license holder "did not have the necessary approvals from the mineral resources authority in place before initiating this operation," according to a Google translation of its statement. The project's actual drilling rig did not arrive in Greenland. Stampede Drilling, the Canadian contractor hired for the project, said it would not take the rig ashore unless all required regulatory approvals were in place. But that does not mean the entire project lacks a legal basis. Greenland stopped issuing new oil and gas licenses in 2021, but the three licenses covering the Jameson Land project were issued in 2015 and 2018 and remain valid through the end of 2028. Those licenses do not automatically authorize drilling, which still requires separate approvals from the authorities. Moreover, Greenland Energy does not itself currently hold those licenses. Greenland's government said the company "incorrectly informed the public" that it was the license holder. The licenses are in fact held by White Flame Energy A/S, while Greenland Energy is involved as an investor and operator of the project. As of August 2026, drilling had not started. On Aug. 12, Greenlandic authorities said the required regulatory process could not be completed in time for the planned drilling campaign, including the assessment of its environmental and social impact. The government and company said drilling could now begin no earlier than winter 2027. How is the company connected to Trump? We found no evidence that Trump owns, controls or has directly invested in the company. Therefore, c alling Greenland Energy "Trump's oil company" is unsupported. The "Trump-linked" description appears to come mainly from connections between people involved with the company and Trump or his administration. For instance, as The Guardian reported , Greenland Energy hired Envoy Media — a company founded by television personality Phil McGraw. McGraw supported Trump during the 2024 election and Trump later appointed him to his Religious Liberty Commission. The company also appointed Carol Craig to its board. Craig leads Sidus Space, which has received work connected to the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense initiative. The Guardian pointed to investor Kenneth Griffin, a major Republican donor who voted for Trump in 2024 and contributed to his inauguration. The outlet also reported that some Greenland Energy shareholders discussed hoping for a public endorsement from Trump that could boost the company's stock price. Snopes was unable to independently verify the posts from the shareholder Telegram group cited by the newspaper. There was also some direct contact with the Trump administration. Greenland Energy CEO Robert Price told Greenlandic broadcaster KNR that he and company chairman Larry Swets met Trump's special envoy to Greenland, Jeff Landry, at a conference in Nuuk in May and discussed the project. However, Price said the company did not receive any promises of political support from the administration and denied having any broader relationship with Landry or Trump's circle. Still, none of those connections showed that Trump was behind the project. The Guardian reported Greenland Energy representative Robert Price, when asked whether Swets had close relations with Trump, replied, "Not that I know of." Swets also said the oil project was not connected to the prospect of U.S. annexation of Greenland. Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark and is strategically important because of its Arctic location and natural resources. Trump has repeatedly said he wants the United States to acquire Greenland and has at times floated the possibility of using military force. Bottom line All in all, it was true that in late July 2026, equipment connected to the Jameson Land oil project was moved without the required authorization, and Greenland's government issued a warning over it. The company also had some indirect connections to Trump and his administration. However, as of this writing, it had not yet started drilling. Also, Trump does not own the company, and we found no evidence that he directly instructed it to carry out its activities in Greenland. The project itself is based on legally valid exploration licenses, although separate activities still need approval. For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated numerous rumors surrounding Trump's interest in Greenland.

title: Fauci didn't cover up data supposedly showing COVID-19 vaccine had 82% miscarriage rate
label: Rating: False About this rating
text: Claim: Texts prove Dr. Anthony Fauci, who helped lead the United States' COVID-19 response, covered up data indicating that 82% of pregnant women who received an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine in their first trimester miscarried. Rating: False About this rating Context The rate of miscarriage among pregnant women who received the COVID-19 vaccine is not 82% — that figure comes from a misinterpretation of a 2021 study. Studies have consistently shown the rate of miscarriage among vaccinated women is in line with rates among the broader population. In August 2026, anti-vaccine advocates claimed online that Dr. Anthony Fauci, the former presidential medical adviser, covered up credible data showing a miscarriage rate of more than 80% among pregnant women who received the COVID-19 vaccine in their first trimester. The claim circulated on X , Facebook ( screenshott ) and Instagram after Sens. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Ron Johnson, R-Wis., both prominent Fauci critics, released an apparent text message from Fauci that said the second COVID-19 shot "theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester." "They said the Covid vaccine had a 12.6% miscarriage rate for pregnant women but it was actually 82%," one X post said . "Fauci and his co-conspirators need to be thrown in jail." (X users DC_Draino, KatiePavlich) Posts called for Fauci's imprisonment, alleging the above text showed that Fauci, who helped lead the nation's COVID-19 pandemic response, knew the COVID-19 vaccine could harm pregnancies but still told pregnant people to get vaccinated. We have rated this claim as false. These posts have drawn an incorrect conclusion that relies on flawed data. Multiple studies have shown that pregnant people who receive a COVID-19 vaccine are not at an increased risk of miscarriage or pregnancy complications. As numerous fact-checking organizations determined in 2021 — and as we have independently verified — the 82% statistic is a gross misrepresentation of data released in an April 2021 study. Meanwhile, the apparent text from Fauci at the center of the claim was dated January 2021, before researchers were done collecting data for the study. That means Fauci could not have been referring to its supposed findings. In fact, Fauci's text, if legitimate, did not cite any data about miscarriages at all. It said that theoretically the vaccine could cause symptoms that may be associated with miscarriage — in other words, the text refers to a possibility Fauci thought was worth further investigation before the vaccines became available to the public. Thus, the texts do not show that Fauci "covered up" any data. There's also no evidence he ignored, covered up or downplayed data showing that COVID-19 vaccines increase miscarriage rates, because that data doesn't exist. Later texts from the same set of messages Paul and Johnson released indicate that, as the body of data grew more robust, Fauci said he believed it indicated "no issues" with vaccinating pregnant women. There's no evidence Fauci believed otherwise while telling pregnant people to get vaccinated during the pandemic. Snopes has not independently verified the legitimacy of these apparent texts, which Paul and Johnson said came from Fauci's government-issued cellphone. There's no evidence the texts are fake. We reached out to Fauci to confirm he sent these texts and await a response. Origin of '82% miscarriage rate' claim In April 2021, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention researchers published a study titled "Preliminary Findings of mRNA Covid-19 Vaccine Safety in Pregnant Persons." The report used data taken from Dec. 14, 2020, to Feb. 28, 2021, in the CDC's v-safe pregnancy registry , a self-reported database of pregnant people who received one of the two mRNA COVID-19 vaccines available at the time. The report determined that of 827 women who had a "completed pregnancy" by March 2021, 104 had a miscarriage, which is called a "spontaneous abortion" in the study ( see Table 4 ). Thus, of completed pregnancies available in the study, there was a 12.6% rate of miscarriage, which is in line with estimates for miscarriage rates across all pregnancies, which range from about 9% to 22%, with higher rates among older women. Even this 12.6% datapoint, however, is incomplete — as the CDC later acknowledged — because the agency lacked follow-up data for the vast majority of women who were vaccinated early in their pregnancies. Later studies with more-complete data found miscarriage rates at 9% to 10.9%, equivalent to or lower than the rate of miscarriage among the broader population. Anti-vaccine advocates claimed in 2021 that the rate of miscarriage should be calculated using only completed pregnancies among women who were vaccinated in the first or second trimester, because the loss of a fetus after 20 weeks — halfway through the second trimester — is considered a stillbirth , not a miscarriage. Of the 827 women with a completed pregnancy, 700 received the vaccine in their third trimester ( see Table 4 ). Thus, the 82% rate of miscarriage comes from determining that 104 of 127 of the remaining women in the "completed pregnancy" group had a miscarriage. However , because the study only spanned a few months, women who had healthy pregnancies and were vaccinated within the first or second trimester did not have time to finish their pregnancies by the end of the study, and therefore they were not included in the "completed pregnancy" data. Meanwhile, if any pregnancy ends — or is "completed" — within the first or second trimester, it's probably because it was a miscarriage. (Other reasons listed in the study included deliberate abortions and ectopic pregnancies .) Most of the 3,958 total participants in the study were still pregnant by the time researchers followed up with them in March 30, 2021, which means they could not have been included in the 82% rate of miscarriage calculation. Consider two hypothetical pregnant study participants who received the vaccine during their first trimesters in January 2021. One woman went on to have a healthy pregnancy lasting nine months, meaning by March, she was still pregnant — and would therefore not be included in the "completed pregnancy" data used to calculate the supposed 82% rate of miscarriage. The second woman had a miscarriage in February that ended her pregnancy, so she would have ended up as part of the "completed pregnancy" data. Thus, the "completed pregnancy" data for people who were vaccinated in the first or second trimester is skewed toward participants who had miscarriages. Fact-checkers also have debunked a related claim that a study showed an 81% rate of miscarriage among pregnant women who received the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine. They determined the calculation was a math error and relied on a similar misrepresentation of the facts. Fauci texts don't show 'cover-up' The texts Johnson and Paul released of Fauci appearing to discuss vaccines for pregnant women don't show Fauci attempting to cover up any data. According to the messages, in January 2021, Dr. Vivek Murthy, then the U.S. surgeon general, had asked Fauci and Rochelle Walensky, the CDC director at the time, whether there was "any data or theoretical reason why vaccinating early vs late in pregnancy would be preferred?" In response, Fauci said, "There are no data or theoretical reason to believe that vaccinating early versus later in pregnancy would be preferred" ( see Page 2 ). About two hours later, he sent a text that said (emphasis ours): I asked around a bit more and another issue came up that you need to be aware of. Since many people have significant cytokines storm and fever after the 2nd dose, this theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester But there's no evidence this theorized concern from Fauci showed up in the data available at the time. On Page 4, a text attributed to Fauci said "no issues have arisen" among pregnant women who received the vaccine (emphasis ours): I would say that in any vaccine in which data are lacking in pregnant women one must weigh the potential risks against the benefits. COVID-19 can be a serious disease especially in pregnancy. In the vaccine trials, pregnant women were not allowed but following the EUA, a large number (more than 10,000) pregnant women have been vaccinated. No issues have arisen . The FDA and the ACIP and the ACOG are all permissive for pregnant women to have a choice. Animal tox studies did not raise any red flags. In a February 2021 interview with the medical journal JAMA Network, Fauci said publicly that "we've got to be careful," but at that time, the FDA had found "thus far, no red flags" among pregnant women who had received the vaccine ( at 18:03 ). Thus, his apparent private texts aligned with his public messaging. The CDC officially began recommending the vaccine to pregnant women in August 2021 . In sum … The claim that texts prove Fauci covered up data showing a miscarriage rate of 82% for pregnant women who received the COVID-19 vaccine doesn't pass a basic sniff test. Regardless of vaccination status, most pregnancies that end in the first or second trimesters do so because of miscarriage. That's the only thing the "82% rate of miscarriage" points to. The actual study showed no link between miscarriages and the COVID-19 vaccine, and later studies corroborated those results. Fauci's texts, if legitimate, show him expressing preliminary concern about a possible effect of the new vaccines. The same texts show Fauci's confidence in the safety of the vaccine for pregnancies growing as more and better data emerged.

title: Ad Attacking N.C. Republican Senate Candidate Uses His Own (Dated) Words Against Him
summary: In his campaign’s latest TV ad, Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper of North Carolina highlights the issue of affordability using direct quotes from his Republican opponent. They are, in fact, direct quotes from Michael Whatley — but they are a bit dated, and some of the comments were more defensible or true at the time when Whatley made them.
text: In his campaign’s latest TV ad, Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper of North Carolina highlights the issue of affordability using direct quotes from his Republican opponent — “No AI, no special effects, just Michael Whatley in his own words.” They are, in fact, direct quotes from Whatley — but they are a bit dated, and some of the comments were more defensible or true at the time when Whatley made them. The ad starts with a quote from Whatley: “Grocery prices are down, gasoline prices are down, housing prices are down, inflation is down,” he says. “Unbelievable,” Cooper comments. Judged by today’s metrics, Whatley’s statements are wrong. Grocery prices between January 2025, when Trump took office, and July have increased 3.35%. That’s larger than the 2.58% increase in the year and a half before Trump took office. Gasoline prices are up almost $1 from the price the week before Trump took office. Housing prices have risen 1.6% between 2024 and 2025. And the Consumer Price Index — the most commonly cited measure of inflation — increased 3.4% over the 12 months ending in July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That’s up from the annualized 3.0% that Trump inherited. But Whatley, then chair of the Republican National Committee, made those comments in a NewsMax interview in July 2025. Things were a little different then. That’s before the war with Iran and before the effect of Trump’s tariffs had kicked in, among other things. Gasoline. At that time, gasoline prices were almost exactly what they were when Trump took office, according to the Energy Information Administration — the national average for regular gas was $3.11 per gallon when Trump was sworn in versus $3.12 for the week ending July 21, 2025. Gasoline prices would gradually decline from there, dipping to $2.78 per gallon in January 2026. The Cooper campaign noted to us that Whatley continued to claim gasoline prices were down in an interview in mid-November 2025. At that point, gasoline prices were down slightly, about 5 cents a gallon from the price Trump inherited. Then the war with Iran, which began in late February, caused prices to soar. The price per gallon reached $4.50 in May and was $4.07 for the week ending Aug. 31 (nearly 31% higher than when Trump took office). Whatley has been supportive of Trump’s war with Iran, saying it is necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Inflation. As we said, inflation has continued to rise in Trump’s second term. But when Whatley made his statement in July 2025 that “inflation is down,” the annualized rate of inflation , as measured by the Consumer Price Index, was 2.7%. That was down from 3.0% in the 12 months before Trump took office. So prices were still rising, but the annualized rate of inflation was lower. (We’ve pointed this out repeatedly when Trump has claimed that prices are “plummeting downward.”) Less defensible was Whatley’s claim from an interview with Real America’s Voice in January — highlighted in the Cooper ad — that “there is no inflation.” Whatley added (not in the Cooper commercial), “Inflation has fallen off a cliff since President Trump came in.” The annualized rate of inflation at the time was 2.7%. That’s not “no inflation” but it is lower than the rate Trump inherited. As we noted earlier, since then the CPI has risen, and is higher than the annualized rate when Trump took office. Home prices. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis , the average sales price of homes in the U.S. dropped from $514,200 in the first quarter of 2025 to $502,700 in the second quarter of 2026. The median price of new homes also fell from $423,100 in the first quarter of 2025 to $410,700 in the second quarter of 2026, per the bank. The median price of an existing single family home has continued to rise in Trump’s second term, according to sales figures from the National Association of Realtors , albeit at a much slower rate than during Biden’s presidency, and, for that matter, during Trump’s first term. According to NAR, the seasonally adjusted annual median price rose from $412,500 in 2024 to $419,300 in 2025. That’s a 1.6% increase. But it’s slower than the overall rate of inflation. “It is welcoming to see incomes rising faster than home prices, which has helped boost affordability—but the big short-term challenge to affordability is coming from rising mortgage rates,” NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun said in August. During Biden’s presidency, the median sales price of existing single family homes rose 37.4%. The median price also rose 27.5% during Trump’s first term. Both of those increases well outpaced overall inflation growth during their presidencies. Groceries . It was not true then nor is it now, that grocery prices “are down.” The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI for “food-at-home” — products bought at a grocery store or supermarket — overall grew by 0.7% between January and July 2025, when Whatley made his comment. So grocery prices were not lower. But the rate of growth was slower than in the previous six months, 1.48%. Grocery prices have continued to climb since then, and have risen a total of 3.35% from when Trump took office and July of this year. As we wrote around the time Whatley made his comment in July 2025, there were some exceptions to the overall rising prices. The price of energy, airfare, new and used vehicles and eggs and were all down. But overall, prices continued to climb, and many experts cautioned that the president’s tariffs were likely to cause further price increases. “DC insider Michael Whatley has been insisting for months that prices are down and there is no inflation while hardworking North Carolinians are getting crushed by high prices,” a spokesperson for the Cooper campaign told us via email. “From groceries to gas to health care – families are struggling while Whatley gets richer.” While we are unable to search Whatley’s day-to-day comments on the campaign trail, we didn’t find any interviews since January where he spoke about lower prices or no inflation. Whatley campaign spokesman DJ Griffin pushed back on Cooper’s campaign slogan “make stuff cost less,” claiming that Cooper’s policies had done the opposite. “Facts are that Michael Whatley supports policies that allow working families to earn more and keep more,” Griffin told us via email. title: Ossoff Ad Takes Collins’ Quote Out of Context
summary: In the Georgia Senate race, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has been running TV ads that take a sound bite from his opponent about Social Security out of context.
text: In the Georgia Senate race, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has been running TV ads that take a sound bite from his opponent about Social Security out of context. In a radio interview last year, Republican Rep. Mike Collins made the case for the tax cuts in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act , claiming that cutting taxes would spur economic growth and provide an incentive for people to “get off of Medicaid, get off of Social Security, get back into the workforce.” Collins, June 5, 2025: It’s just business 101. You’ve got spending and you’ve got revenue, and you set it up to where you can increase your revenue. And you do that by lowering taxes and making it more advantageous for people to work and to get off of Medicaid, get off of Social Security, get back into the workforce. And, and that decreases it on that side of the equation as well — on the mandatory side. But two Ossoff ads currently airing use only a snippet of the Collins interview — when he says, “get off of Social Security, get back into the workforce” — to claim that “he wants to push you off Social Security.” The ad shows images of older adults with gray hair when making that claim. The ads ignore that Collins also mentioned Medicaid, and, while his mention of Social Security is confusing, he wasn’t talking about pushing people off these programs, but rather “making it more advantageous for people to work.” One of the ads repeats the truncated audio clip for emphasis. “Listen again. ‘Get off of Social Security, get back into the workforce,’” that ad says. (See the ad below.) The Ossoff campaign has spent more than $2.8 million on the ad since it first aired on Aug. 8, according to AdImpact, an advertising tracking service. The Ossoff campaign defended its use of the clip, saying in a memo to us that its ads don’t imply that Collins would use coercion or force to get people off Social Security. Rather, “Collins makes it clear he wants to exert influence and pressure to push Social Security beneficiaries into the workforce,” the campaign memo said. In an interview, an Ossoff campaign spokesperson told us, “We are taking the quote as he said it, and he did not provide additional context.” But the full quote from the interview does provide some additional context, although getting off of Social Security to rejoin the workforce isn’t easy. And it can be costly. Social Security recipients can work and receive benefits . They can also withdraw their benefits application – but only within the first 12 months after being approved for Social Security payments. Those who do withdraw from Social Security must repay whatever they received in Social Security and Medicare benefits during the 12-month period. It’s also possible to temporarily suspend benefits between full retirement age and age 70, as AARP explains . We asked the Collins campaign what the Republican congressman meant when he said “lowering taxes” would make it “more advantageous for people” on Medicaid and Social Security to “get back into the workforce.” Sam Densmore, a spokesperson for the Collins campaign, said the candidate “misspoke” about Social Security. “In that interview, Rep. Collins misspoke and did not intend to make that statement. Instead, he was referring to getting off of Medicaid and onto their employer’s health insurance,” Densmore said. “He corrected himself immediately afterward, but his opponent clipped the remark short intentionally to mislead the voters.” Collins did not correct himself in the interview , which was a little more than 15 minutes long. We asked Densmore when and where Collins “corrected himself,” but we did not get a response. Regardless of what Collins meant to say, the Ossoff campaign took the quote out of context to claim that Collins said “he wants to push you off Social Security and back to work.” The ad above ends by saying that Collins is “attacking your retirement.” More on Social Security Both Ossoff ads also claim that “Collins voted to gut Social Security,” citing his vote in March for a balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The House resolution would have been the first step in a long and difficult process to amend the Constitution – but it failed, as many other proposed balanced budget amendments have in the past. It’s true that the balanced budget amendment – however unlikely to ever take effect – potentially could have made the program’s financial situation worse, if Congress didn’t do anything else. As it is, the federal government has had to borrow to cover full Social Security retirement benefits every year since 2010, the Social Security Board of Trustees said in its 2026 report to Congress. That’s because the total cost of the program exceeds non-interest revenue – which includes Social Security payroll taxes, income taxes on Social Security benefits and general fund reimbursements, the report said. Under current law, Social Security retirement benefits will have to be cut by 22% in 2032, if Congress doesn’t act, the trustees’ report projected. The House resolution made no exception for Social Security and made it more difficult for Congress to raise revenue by requiring a two-thirds majority to raise taxes. Unless Congress raised taxes or exempted Social Security from the balanced budget amendment, Social Security benefits would likely have to be reduced earlier than 2032. We asked the Collins campaign to respond to the ads’ claim that the balanced budget amendment would “gut Social Security.” Densmore, the campaign spokesperson, said only that Collins “has always supported Social Security … and that will not change” in the Senate. In its memo to us, the Ossoff campaign provided additional support for its claim that Collins would “gut Social Security.” The campaign document said Collins has a long history of voting to “jeopardize” the nation’s retirement program, dating to his first House campaign in 2014 when he advocated raising the retirement age for full Social Security benefits. Collins is also a member of the conservative Republican Study Committee , which has repeatedly proposed budgets that would gradually raise the retirement age, the Ossoff campaign noted. Raising the full retirement age from 67 to 69 for future retirees, as proposed by the RSC in its 2025 budget proposal, would reduce lifetime benefits for “[a]ll people affected by such an increase,” the Congressional Budget Office said in a September 2024 letter to the ranking Democrat on the House Budget Committee. But raising the retirement age would also shore up the program’s finances. In 1983, Congress and President Ronald Reagan agreed to “significant reforms” that “put the program on a stable footing for decades,” including raising the retirement age for full Social Security benefits and increasing taxes on Social Security benefits, as explained in a Brookings Institution report. The Ossoff campaign also cited Collins’ vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, saying the new law “accelerated Social Security’s insolvency.” That’s accurate. In its 2026 report , the Social Security trustees projected that the new law will “have a substantial effect on Social Security’s financial status,” because the program “will receive lower levels of revenue in the future from income taxation of Social Security benefits.” Health Insurance The Ossoff ad in heavy rotation that has been airing since Aug. 8 also criticized Collins on health insurance. “Collins voted with Trump to double health insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians,” the ad says, citing Collins’ vote against a Democratic bill that would have extended more generous Affordable Care Act subsidies for three years. The House bill passed Jan. 8 but didn’t become law, and out-of-pocket premiums for ACA plans went up. But how much did premiums increase for Georgians? The Ossoff campaign cited a KFF analysis published last year that said without the enhanced subsidies, premiums on average would “more than double what subsidized enrollees currently pay annually for premiums—a 114% increase.” Because of the higher costs, many have dropped their ACA coverage, as we’ve explained , and others shopped for lower-premium plans. KFF, a health policy research organization, published an updated analysis in May that said premium payments in 2026 have increased by an average of 58%. “This is lower than the 114% increase KFF projected if everyone had stayed in the same plan because many people bought down to higher-deductible plans and because those just past the subsidy cliff with the steepest increases dropped ACA coverage at higher rates,” KFF said. “Additionally, the 114% increase was among people receiving a tax credit whereas the 58% increase is among all consumers, including the most number who did not receive a tax credit in 2025.” KFF also said that more than 1.3 million Georgians signed up for health insurance on the ACA marketplace this year, down about 187,000 from 2025’s open enrollment, but we don’t know how many of them have seen or would have seen their premiums double. An Ossoff campaign spokesperson told us that it didn’t know, either. Instead, the spokesperson said there are about 350,000 fewer state residents who now get their insurance on the ACA marketplace, citing a report in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution based on state data this spring. “We are focusing on 300,000 have already lost their insurance,” the spokesperson told us. We don’t know how many of those may have obtained insurance from another source. The Georgia Senate race, which is rated “ lean Democrat ” by the Cook Political Report, is critical to the Democrats’ chances of regaining control of the Senate, where the Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage . Ossoff, who had no primary opponent , so far has raised and spent more money this campaign cycle than any other congressional candidate, according to the Federal Election Commission. title: Social Media Posts Push False Claim of Trump Chopping Down 60 Cherry Trees
summary: Q: Did the Trump administration have 60 cherry blossom trees cut down in D.C. to build a golf course? A: In what the Department of Interior called “routine maintenance,” about 60 trees were removed from East Potomac Park, according to the Washington Post. But only one cherry tree removal was mentioned in that article, and an advocacy group opposed to major changes to the park told us it only knew “for certain” of one cherry tree being cut down.
text: Q: Did the Trump administration have 60 cherry blossom trees cut down in D.C. to build a golf course? A: In what the Department of Interior called “routine maintenance,” about 60 trees were removed from East Potomac Park, according to the Washington Post. But only one cherry tree removal was mentioned in that article, and an advocacy group opposed to major changes to the park told us it only knew “for certain” of one cherry tree being cut down. FULL ANSWER In a June 28 Truth Social post, President Donald Trump said that renovations to Washington, D.C.’s East Potomac Golf Links would begin Sept. 1 to build “one of the Greatest Golf Courses anywhere in the World” that could “host Major Golf Tournaments.” No major renovations have begun yet. The public golf courses include two nine-hole courses, an 18-hole course, a driving range and other facilities. As of Sept. 3, tee times were available for booking on the website over the following week for all three courses. The East Potomac Park area also includes bicycle lanes and picnic areas. It’s unclear what the exact renovation plans are, and the project is subject to a lawsuit filed by a preservation group and two D.C.-area golfers. People play golf as the Washington Monument is visible in the background at the East Potomac Golf Links on May 3 in Washington, D.C. Photo by Pete Kiehart for The Washington Post via Getty Images. The potential removal of historic cherry trees became a concern this summer, after Trump was photographed at the golf course on June 28 holding renderings of a redesigned course. The Washington Post wrote at the time that those plans “do not appear to show several of the park’s best-known public amenities, including the riverside bicycle trail, the miniature golf course and Washington’s oldest grove of cherry trees.” Then, on Aug. 28, the Washington Post reported that more than 60 trees had been removed in recent weeks in the area surrounding the East Potomac Golf Links. The newspaper mentioned only one cherry tree that was removed. Social media posts are distorting the Washington Post report. Several readers have asked us about social media claims that the Trump administration had cut down 60 cherry trees. One reader asked us to validate a post claiming: “Trump just illegally chopped down SIXTY historic cherry trees in Washington D.C. WITHOUT court approval so that he could ‘renovate’ a GOLF COURSE!” The post goes on to cite the Washington Post, falsely saying that the newspaper “has reported that Trump has gone ahead and chopped down dozens and dozens of beloved cherry and sycamore trees at the historic East Potomac Golf Links.” As we said, the article doesn’t say that “dozens” of cherry trees were removed. It mentions one cherry tree, as well as two sycamore trees. It doesn’t provide details on what other types of trees were chopped down. Alex Rosen, a spokesman for the advocacy group Save East Po , told us that the social media claims were false. “I have noticed people online saying ‘60 cherry trees.’ I can tell you that this is totally untrue. We know for certain that 1 cherry tree was cut down.” Save East Po describes itself as “an independent, grassroots coalition of DMV neighbors, runners, cyclists, picnickers, fishers, families, and the golfers who actually play this course, who all want the same thing: keep East Potomac Park public, accessible, and affordable.” “There might have been one other [cherry tree] cut down but I am not certain on that,” Rosen said in an email. “What we are worried about is that more will come down as the admin continues to operate in very closed door ways.” The Department of the Interior told us — as it told the Washington Post — that “[a]rborists are doing routine maintenance at East Potomac Park with selective removal of hazard trees, non-native invasive trees and declining and dying trees that cannot be brought back to good health through any degree of intervention. Trees throughout the park are regularly monitored for potential safety impacts to visitors, and when a tree is determined to be dying, declining or hazardous our arborists may make the decision to remove it.” The Washington Post reported that workers with the company RTEC Treecare were cutting down trees at the park on Aug. 27, but RTEC told the Post that it hadn’t removed any cherry trees. RTEC Treecare now has a pop-up message on its website saying, “We want to be clear: RTEC Treecare has not removed any cherry trees at East Potomac Park Golf Course. Our work has been limited to trees identified by the National Park Service as hazardous, non-native, or invasive.” We asked the Interior Department if it could clarify whether any of the trees were cherry trees, but we did not get a response. We also did not receive a response from the National Park Service. East Potomac Golf Links Renovation Tee times at East Potomac Golf Links for the 18-hole course start at $42 for non-seniors, below the national average of $48 for public courses. Rosen’s group and others are concerned that the administration’s renovations could lead to higher prices and reduced access to the courses and other public spaces in the larger park. In May, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum shared a rendering of the renovated course, saying it would offer “championship-quality golf at affordable, highly discounted rates.” The rendering posted by Burgum would combine the existing courses into one, 18-hole course, and add a short, par-3 course and an expanded practice area, as the New York Times explained . Burgum credited the plan to Fazio Design, led by golf course designer Tom Fazio. The Fazio family has designed many of Trump’s golf courses. The Times reported that “Washington’s oldest grove of cherry trees — a gift from Japan in 1910 — currently sits between the fourth and the ninth holes on the White Course. In the Fazio plan, the grove is shown in the middle of the practice range. Its fate is uncertain.” In July, Rosen told us the publicly released image from Burgum “differs significantly from the one Trump was recently photographed holding” in late June. In the designs Trump was holding, there was no short par-3 course, and it was unclear what would happen to the existing bicycle path and mini-golf course. On Sept. 1, Rosen said there has been no further clarity on the future of the renovations. He pointed out that the potential renovation isn’t included in the Sept. 3 National Capital Planning Commission meeting agenda . The NCPC is responsible for reviewing the federal government’s plans for developing the National Capital Region. The New York Times reported on Sept. 2, “The administration has not submitted plans to any review panel.” Fazio told Golf.com in June that the president’s vision did not include removing the cherry trees. “The president has mentioned that several times he loves the trees,” Fazio said. “He wants to make sure we protect those trees and take care of the trees.” The fight over the legality of the golf course renovation is ongoing. The DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit in February, arguing that the administration’s actions threaten to “wrest the Park from the people.” The suit asked the courts to block the administration from dumping dirt and debris — from the White House East Wing renovations — at East Potomac Park and to block the administration from implementing a renovation plan without going through environmental and preservation approval protocols. U.S. District Court Judge Ana C. Reyes is overseeing the case. In May, the Associated Press reported that she “told the National Park Service that it should first discuss any plans with government lawyers if it was going to cut down more than 10 trees.” In July, the AP reported that Reyes asked for assurances that the plaintiffs wouldn’t “suddenly learn in the ‘middle of the night’ that there were bulldozers at the course ‘chopping down cherry trees.'” Michael Robertson, an attorney from the Justice Department, “told Reyes repeatedly that there was still a lengthy process to undergo that would include signoffs from various planning organizations, the National Capital Planning Commission and the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts,” the AP said. The National Park Service said in an April court filing that it would “complete its compliance in accordance with all applicable laws and regulations prior to authorizing construction activities at the East Potomac Golf Course.” Reyes has asked both sides in the suit to convene for a status conference on Sept. 3.
